Title: The project scheduling interdiction problem with delay groups
Authors: Fei Wu, Erik Demeulemeester, Jannik Matuschke
Abstract: Large-scale projects are frequently delayed by correlated disruptions: when a shared input such as a common supplier, a specialized team, or a supporting platform degrades, all dependent activities are slowed down simultaneously. This paper introduces delay groups to capture such disruptions: a delay group is a set of activities whose delays stem from a common cause, described jointly by an uncertainty set. Our model takes the perspective of an interdictor that, subject to a budget of $k$ groups, selects which groups to disrupt so as to maximize the project makespan. The interdictor can extend activity durations within each disrupted group by delays from a group-specific uncertainty set, while non-disrupted activities keep their nominal duration. We study the complexity of the resulting Project Scheduling Interdiction Problem with Delay Groups (PSIP-DG), which provides a worst-case stress test of the schedule. The problem is computationally intractable ($N\!P$-hard) for general polyhedral uncertainty sets, even for a single delay group with a continuous knapsack constraint. For budgeted uncertainty sets, we prove $N\!P$-hardness both when all activities of a disrupted group are delayed and when only one activity per group may be delayed, and derive an inapproximability bound of $1-1/e+\epsilon$ for the former case. We further develop a greedy heuristic with approximation guarantee $k$ and two structure-based heuristics with initializations and neighborhoods from tractable special cases. Experiments on $5{,}000$-activity networks show that the heuristics match the solution quality of an exact solver at substantially lower running times, in some cases finding strictly better solutions.

Title: A DeepSets-guided scheduling framework for total tardiness minimization in single-machine scheduling
Abstract: We present the DeepSets-Guided Scheduling Framework (DGSF), a hybrid machine learning and optimization framework for the single-machine total tardiness scheduling problem with release times. DGSF employs a geometric instance-classification rule to characterize scheduling instances using aggregate structural parameters. This classification enables targeted machine learning models to be trained across diverse instance types while leveraging training on smaller instances within the same instance class. The machine learning model is designed to accommodate varying numbers of jobs and uses attention to combine each job's features with information about the other jobs, learning priorities that reflect their relationships. These priorities define an initial sequence, which is refined through local swaps and restricted optimization to generate high-quality schedules. Computational tests show that DGSF generates better solutions than the tested heuristics for instances with all jobs released at time zero; and near optimal solutions (within 0.65–2.56%) for instances with staggered release times. Stronger sequential dispatching results for staggered-release instances motivate future work on learning sequential priority updates. The framework also remains interpretable, as the learned job priorities align with established heuristic principles, supported by permutation-importance analysis of input features. Overall, DGSF establishes a structured framework for integrating data-driven priority estimation with constrained optimization in single-machine scheduling, with strong potential to serve as a sequencing module within more complex multi-stage and multi-machine scheduling problems.

Title: An exact aggregation–disaggregation method for a class of mixed-integer linear programs
Authors: Jiarui Zhang, Alessio Trivella, Xiaojie Luan
Abstract: Although aggregating items such as commodities, vehicles, or resources into groups is widely used in planning and operations, the structural conditions under which aggregation is exact have not been systematically characterized. In this paper, we provide a mathematical foundation for aggregation techniques using mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs). Specifically, we prove that a class of MILPs can be solved to optimality by aggregating certain sets of variables and constraints, solving a smaller model with fewer symmetries and the same linear relaxation value, and then disaggregating the solution in polynomial time. The method applies to MILPs with block-diagonal and coupling constraints in which variable vectors share identical coefficients in the objective and coupling constraints. The exactness of the aggregation holds when (i) the diagonal blocks are identical totally unimodular matrices with proportional right-hand sides, or (ii) their constraints represent the balance of network flows with the same source or same sink. This aggregation–disaggregation method has both theoretical and computational value. On the theoretical side, it formalizes the fundamental mechanisms underlying existing aggregation techniques, extends and/or strengthens the theory and applicability of several structure-based methods for MILPs, and establishes polynomial-time solvability for a class of MILPs. Computationally, we verify the effectiveness of the method on variants of the service network design, vehicle scheduling, and interval scheduling problems. Using Gurobi, we show that, compared to directly solving the original formulations, the method brings speedups of one to three orders of magnitude.

Title: Designing and adapting dropshipping virtual distribution networks
Authors: Thomas B. Cassidey, Emily C. Griffin, Burcu B. Keskin, Ozgur Satici

Title: Strategic timing of buyer financing in supply chains with stochastic costs: The role of wholesale price-locking leadership
2026 Editors’ awards for excellence in reviewing
Minimizing network development costs using reverse p-median models
Abstract: The reverse p-median problem seeks network modifications that improve the accessibility of predetermined facility locations subject to budget and network-design constraints. Solving this problem on general networks with discrete edge length choices is computationally challenging because shortest-path distances must be repeatedly recalculated across a large number of feasible network configurations. To address this challenge, we develop a globally optimal solution framework, called the Reverse p-Median Solver (RPM), which combines structured enumeration with two complementary search procedures to efficiently explore the feasible budget domain. A key feature of RPM is its ability to identify globally optimal networks over the entire feasible budget range and construct the corresponding Pareto-efficient frontier between network cost and investment budget, enabling decision-makers to systematically evaluate trade-offs between infrastructure investment and network performance. Computational experiments on illustrative electricity-grid examples and a large-scale transportation network case study in Virginia demonstrate the practical applicability and scalability of the proposed framework.

Title: A new perspective on multi-objective project scheduling problems: Evaluating with multiple reference profiles
Authors: Ziyang Tang, Tom Servranckx, Mario Vanhoucke, Zhengwen He
Abstract: This paper addresses the multi-objective resource-constrained project scheduling problem (MORCPSP) under a non-compensatory preference structure over conflicting objectives. From the decision maker’s perspective, objectives reflecting distinct stakeholder concerns (such as minimising project tardiness and minimising resource leveling cost) often exhibit a non-compensatory relationship, in which good performance on one objective cannot fully offset unacceptable performance on the other. This characteristic makes it difficult for decision makers to specify precise compensatory weights between objectives. Moreover, existing multi-objective heuristic algorithms (MOHAs) typically generate large sets of non-dominated schedules without using preference information during the search, thereby leaving decision makers with the burden of selecting from numerous alternative schedules. To address these limitations, we develop MOHA-EMP, a preference-guided framework that integrates the Evaluating with Multiple Reference Profiles (EMP) procedure into the fitness evaluation and selection of the evolutionary search. Computational experiments conducted on 2700 RanGen2 instances and 480 PSPLIB J30 instances show MOHA-EMP achieves higher preference satisfaction than its standard MOHA counterparts for five benchmarking MOHAs (NSGA-II, ECGA, NTGA2, bNTGA and MOEA/D), improving the average EMP-measure by 12.5%–27.1% while reducing the number of output schedules by 89%–95%. The sensitivity analysis further shows that the method remains robust under varying project sizes, deadlines, resource constraints and network structures. These findings indicate the broad applicability of preference-integrated evolutionary search for decision support in MORCPSP.

Title: Multi-visit truck-drone pickup and delivery problem with release dates and drone resupply
Authors: Shuang Liang, Yanru Chen, Bo Du
Abstract: This study addresses a novel integrated truck-drone routing and demand allocation problem that captures three underexplored real-world complexities simultaneously: item release dates, time windows, and simultaneous pickup and delivery. Unlike existing studies that rely on a single drone type, we introduce resupply drones as a distinct second type that delivers newly released items from depot to en‑route trucks. This combination of features, including release dates, time windows, simultaneous pickup and delivery, and dual drone type service, has not been jointly addressed in prior literature. Decisions include customer assignment to truck, drone, or locker service; truck and delivery drone routes; delivery drone launch and retrieval nodes; and resupply drone-truck matching and rendezvous coordination. We formulate the problem as a mixed-integer bilinear programming model that captures payload- and waiting-dependent delivery drone energy consumption and truck load variations. To strengthen exact solution methods, we develop valid inequalities that reduce computational time by 37.53% on small instances. For large-scale problems, we develop a customized adaptive large neighborhood search (ALNS) with acceleration rules that exploit relationships among release dates, time windows, and delivery modes to prevent infeasibility, alongside a node-based feasibility test and efficient drone-scheduling mechanism that cuts waiting-induced energy use. On medium and large instances, the ALNS outperforms three benchmark algorithms, with reported average cost reductions of 37.87%, 54.75%, and 21.37%. Sensitivity analysis provides valuable managerial insights for logistics practitioners.

Title: Structural concentration in weighted networks: A class of topology-aware indices
Abstract: This paper develops a unified framework for measuring concentration in weighted systems embedded in networks of interactions. While traditional indices such as the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index quantify the dispersion of node weights, they ignore the topology of the relationships among the corresponding units. To address this limitation, we introduce a family of topology-aware concentration indices that jointly account for weight distributions and network structure. At the core of the framework lies a baseline Network Concentration Index (NCI), defined as a normalized quadratic form that measures the fraction of potential weighted interaction realized through the observed network. Building on this foundation, we develop a flexible class of extensions obtained by modifying either the interaction matrix or the normalization benchmark, including weighted, density-adjusted, null-model, degree-constrained, transformed-data, and multi-layer variants. The proposed framework preserves key properties such as normalization, invariance, and interpretability, while providing a common representation for topology-aware concentration measures under different interaction structures. Its general formulation allows alternative notions of interaction, including higher-order relationships or tail dependence, to be incorporated through an appropriate specification of the interaction matrix. Theoretical results establish the main properties of the proposed indices and clarify their relationship with classical concentration measures and standard network statistics. Simulation studies and empirical applications demonstrate that systems with identical weight distributions may exhibit substantially different levels of structural concentration depending on their network topology, highlighting the additional information captured by the proposed framework. The methodology is broadly applicable to economic, financial, and complex systems in which weighted entities interact through networks.

Title: Single machine optimistic bilevel scheduling problems with selection: State-of-the-art and new results
Authors: Vincent T’kindt, Alessandro Agnetis, Federico Della Croce
Abstract: We consider bilevel optimization for machine scheduling problems where two agents, the leader and the follower, take decisions on the same jobset. We survey the somewhat limited relevant literature, and thereafter we present a large set of new complexity results, focusing on single machine bilevel scheduling in the context of optimistic setting. Here, the leader acts first with the aim of selecting a subset of jobs to optimize his/her own objective function. Next, the follower schedules these selected jobs in order to optimize a given criterion. The optimistic setting is such that, among all his/her optimal solutions, the follower returns the one that is minimum for the leader’s objective function. We consider several basic scheduling criteria for both the leader and the follower and establish the complexity of the corresponding problems.

Title: Integrating response time and attention duration in Bayesian preference learning for multiple criteria decision aiding
Authors: Jiaxuan Jiang, Jiapeng Liu, Miłosz Kadziński, Xiuwu Liao, Jingyu Dong

Title: A two-stage optimization framework for maintenance depot location and technician allocation in urban rail transit systems
Authors: Guojian Hu, Yu Zheng, Siqi Qiu
Abstract: The strategic configuration of maintenance resources is essential for ensuring the efficiency and reliability of urban rail transit systems, requiring coordinated decisions on depot location and technician capacity allocation. However, existing studies have paid limited attention to the joint consideration of heterogeneous maintenance demand, response efficiency, and service-capacity adequacy under stochastic demand. To address these gaps, this study develops a two-stage optimization framework for maintenance resource sharing in urban rail transit networks. In the first stage, a depot location model is formulated to minimize the weighted maintenance response distance, incorporating heterogeneous station-level maintenance demand. In the second stage, a technician allocation model, formulated in both aggregate-capacity and generalized skill-compatible forms, maximizes system reliability subject to workforce budget constraints, enabling the framework to accommodate different levels of data granularity. For the aggregate-data computational implementation, a local search-based heuristic and a marginal benefit-based greedy algorithm are developed for the location and allocation models, respectively, while an exact integer linear programming reformulation provides allocation benchmarks. Experiments on networks derived from the Shanghai Metro show that the location heuristic obtains optimal or near-optimal layouts and the allocation algorithm matches the exact benchmark objective values in all tested instances. The combined heuristic process also substantially reduces total computation time relative to exact optimization. Sensitivity analysis reveals diminishing marginal benefits from depot and technician investments. It further shows that, under a limited workforce budget, increasing the number of depots improves response efficiency but may reduce system reliability because of capacity dilution.

Title: Optimization under uncertainty for energy infrastructure planning: A synthesis of methods, tools, and open challenges
Authors: Rahman Khorramfar, Aron Brenner, Lara Booth, Ana Rivera, Ruaridh Macdonald, Priya Donti, Saurabh Amin
Abstract: Energy infrastructure planning under uncertainty has become increasingly complex as electrification, interdependence between energy carriers, decarbonization, and extreme weather events reshape long-term investment decisions. This paper surveys recent advances at the intersection of generation and transmission expansion, and optimization under uncertainty, with a focus on stochastic programming, robust optimization, and distributionally robust optimization. We then categorize modeling needs along the axes of modeling fidelity, uncertainty characterization, and solution methods to identify dominant modeling features and trace research gaps. We further examine emerging directions at the interface of optimization and machine learning, including forecasting, scenario generation, and learned surrogates and discuss how these tools can be embedded within infrastructure planning models.

Title: Trust builder or defensive moat? Blockchain adoption and incentive mechanisms in a food supply chain with asymmetric competition
Authors: Xiaofei Gao, Bin Liu, Chunqing Chang
Abstract: Recurring food safety incidents have severely eroded consumer trust. While blockchain may mitigate this problem, its strategic adoption under asymmetric competition remains underexplored. We develop a three-stage game-theoretic model with an e-commerce platform and two asymmetric manufacturers to investigate adoption equilibria, platform preferences, and welfare effects. Our analysis shows that blockchain-enabled credible traceability can create a trust-based differentiation opportunity for the weaker manufacturer. Under the baseline conditions, this opportunity is endogenously covered because the dominant manufacturer also has an incentive to adopt, so weaker-manufacturer-only adoption does not survive on the equilibrium path. Within a stricter parameter region, universal adoption emerges even though both manufacturers earn higher profits under mutual non-adoption; we refer to this outcome as the Defensive Transparency Paradox. Weaker-manufacturer-only adoption can re-emerge under specific departures from the baseline assumptions. We also uncover an incentive misalignment between manufacturers and the platform and show that a conditional subsidy mechanism can reshape equilibrium adoption and surplus allocation. Finally, within the common feasible region, universal adoption maximizes consumer surplus, whereas dominant-manufacturer-only adoption can yield higher total welfare over an intermediate range of implementation costs.

Title: Leveraging 0–1 linear programming for partitioning and sampling in simulation-based optimization: The case of nested partitions
Authors: Tommaso Schettini, Fausto Errico, Jorge E. Mendoza, Carolina Osorio
Abstract: Discrete Simulation-based Optimization (DSO) problems typically involve highly complex stochastic systems such as urban road networks or electric grid networks. For such problems, computing the value of the objective function requires computationally intensive simulations. Many solution methods rely on iteratively sampling and partitioning the feasible space to progressively concentrate the sampling effort on its most promising portions. To boost the effectiveness of such methods, it is fundamental to quickly identify which portions of the feasible space are relevant to explore through an effective partitioning scheme. In this paper, we focus on binary DSO problems and introduce Nested Clusters, an enhancement of Nested Partitions that leverages the mathematical formulation of the feasible space to construct auxiliary 0–1 linear programming formulations for partitioning and sampling. Additionally, we expand Nested Clusters by introducing a biasing technique that improves the average quality of the sampled solutions, boosting the overall performance. Finally, we apply Nested Clusters to a simulation-based charger location problem for an autonomous fleet of ride-hailing taxis in New York City, which serves as our primary benchmark. We conduct further controlled synthetic tests on four binary simulation–optimization problems spanning different combinatorial structures and stochastic evaluators. On the tested ride-hailing charger-location instances, both proposed partitioning and biased sampling strategies independently improve solution quality relative to Nested Partitions; combining them yields an average 2.2% improvement in the best solutions found.

Title: Competitive distribution channel strategies in three-tier supply chains with horizontal product differentiation
Authors: Junsong Bian, Chenchen Yang, Suzhen Liang

Title: Channel operations and performance improvement of a green supply chain considering risk aversion and carbon abatement
Authors: Qingguo Bai, Shihao Liu, Guoqing Zhang
Abstract: While vertical integration optimizes resource allocation and enhances market competitiveness, it remains unclear how the decision-maker's attitude toward risk affects the operational performance of the integrated green supply chain. Furthermore, a manufacturer's decision to invest in abatement technology may be affected by the challenges arising from carbon taxation. These facts motivate us to study the channel operations and performance improvement in a green supply chain subject to carbon taxation comprising of one risk-averse manufacturer and multiple risk-neutral component suppliers. This issue has not been comprehensively explored in the current body of literature. Under the mean–variance framework, we first formulate a decentralized benchmark system where the risk-averse manufacturer does not adopt abatement technology. We then consider the case in which the manufacturer invests in abatement technology within the decentralized setting, so as to examine the impact of investment on channel operations. We propose a corresponding centralized model, which serves as an efficiency benchmark to evaluate the performance loss of the decentralized system We further propose a hybrid contract that combines the revenue- and cost-sharing contract with the Shapley value method and study the conditions for performance improvement under which the green supply chain can achieve a multi-win outcome. Finally, we analyze a real case in the new energy vehicle industry to verify the influences of the major parameters on the channel performance.

Title: Robust Dynamic Network Data Envelopment Analysis for Supply Chain Performance Evaluation
Authors: Adel Hatami-Marbini, Per J. Agrell, Aliasghar Arabmaldar, Pegah Khoshnevis
Abstract: Supply chains pose a challenging performance assessment problem because decentralised decision-making creates trade-offs between system- and firm-level objectives, exacerbated by intertemporal effects from inventory accumulation and demand fluctuations, task heterogeneity such as product differentiation, and competitive–cooperative interactions that impose system-level constraints. To address this challenge, this paper develops a dynamic network data envelopment analysis (DN-DEA) framework with robust counterparts, based on three complementary perspectives on supply chains: strategic behavioural, intertemporal and competitive-cooperative. We extend DN-DEA to cost-minimising networks, enabling a Farrell-style decomposition of cost efficiency into technical and allocative components, while linking system-, firm- and plant-level performance in a networked and dynamic setting. Robust formulations account for typical data perturbations in supply chains, protecting efficiency estimates from uncertainty. Applied to detailed panel data from a pulp and packaging supply chain, the approach decomposes efficiency into system- and firm-level components, demonstrates how dynamics affect efficiency rankings over time, and shows that robustness substantially reduces rank volatility, providing actionable insights for supply chain performance measurement and coordination.

Title: Static resource allocation: Maximizing revenue and ensuring fairness
Authors: Mosayeb Jalilian, Hamed Jalali, Mozart B.C. Menezes, Roel Leus
Abstract: In this study, we focus on a static multi-resource allocation problem where customers pay to obtain resources from which they derive utility. Resources can be allocated either dynamically, over time, or statically, in a single-shot process. In this study, we explore the trade-off between revenue and fairness in a static setting. We distinguish between fairness-aware decision makers, who prioritize fairness among allocations with equal revenue, and fairness-unaware ones, who randomly select an allocation among all revenue-maximizing options. When the number of customers exceeds the number of available resources, we prove that fairness can be achieved without any revenue loss, but only under fairness-aware decision-making. In contrast, fairness-unaware decision makers are at high risk of selecting allocations with substantially lower fairness, despite achieving the same revenue. We also find that both fairness and revenue are maximized when customers have low price sensitivity and prefer more expensive resources. In contrast, when resources outnumber customers, trade-offs between fairness and revenue become inevitable, especially when customers are highly price-sensitive and prefer cheaper options. In our numerical experiments, we also study the impact of merging resource categories and heterogeneity in customer preferences on the revenue-fairness trade-off. Finally, we complement these analyses with an empirically calibrated case study, showing that our fairness insights remain robust in realistic allocation settings.

Title: A metaheuristic algorithm for locomotive rescheduling in freight transportation under disruptions
Authors: Roberto Maria Rosati, Valentina Cacchiani, Vera C. Hemmelmayr
Abstract: We address a weekly Locomotive Rescheduling Problem (LResP) in the context of rail freight transportation, based on the real-life Austrian setting, in the event of severe disruptions. The main objective is to minimize trip cancellations and deviations from the original plan while meeting locomotive availability and maintenance constraints. To solve LResP, we design a Multi-Neighborhood Search metaheuristic (MNS) that effectively combines both traditional and problem-tailored neighborhoods. The proposed MNS relies on stochastic exploration and uses a simulated annealing scheme to guide the search. In addition, for a comparative analysis, we define a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation that significantly extends a model from the literature for the planning problem by incorporating a new objective function and additional constraints required for the rescheduling setting. We tested the proposed approaches on instances from a real-world setting of the Austrian railways under severe disruptions. While a few good-quality feasible solutions can be obtained for small-scale instances by solving the MILP model with a general-purpose solver, MNS is both fast and scalable, obtaining good quality solutions on instances with thousands of trips, thus highlighting its reliability and applicability in real-world scenarios.

Title: Evaluating dynamic efficiency: Multi-layer dynamic non-radial data envelopment analysis with time-lagged effect structure
Abstract: Economic systems are inherently dynamic, often characterised by temporal lags between the firms’ resource inputs and the realisation of outcomes. Static data envelopment analysis (DEA) approaches, which are widely used in efficiency measurement, largely overlook these intertemporal dynamics. While existing dynamic DEA frameworks account for temporal dependence, they typically capture limited source of efficiency variation and are unable to simultaneously accommodate time-lagged effect, data heterogeneity and the asymmetric contributions of individual inputs. As a result, such models may yield misleading efficiency benchmarks. To address these limitations, this study set up a multi-layer dynamic non-radial DEA (ML-DNRDEA) model that accommodates time-lagged interdependencies and non-proportional input adjustments in efficiency measurement. We adopt the ML-DNRDEA to assess efficiency in the technology industry using a completed panel of 1190 firm-year observations from 2012 to 2021. The results demonstrate that production delay effects have a significant impact on technical efficiency (TE) assessment, with the underlying drivers of TE variation differing across sub-industries. In particular, in the Semiconductors and Software sub-industries, production delays primarily operate through scale efficiency (SE), whereas in IT Services and Technology Hardware , pure technical efficiency (PTE) is more strongly affected. Moreover, the contribution of individual inputs to efficiency is asymmetric rather than proportional. The proposed ML-DNRDEA model provides more granular sources of inefficiency, such as intertemporal dependence and input-specific effects, providing managers and policymakers with richer diagnostic information to support informed decision-making and policy design.

Title: Original equipment manufacturer’s sourcing strategy with production cost information asymmetry
Authors: Qiao Zhang, Jing Chen, Tsan Ming Choi

Title: Beyond the pitch: An integrated machine learning and operations research methodology for financially sustainable squad formation
Abstract: Conventional squad planning methods struggle to reconcile the two-dimensional reality inherent in professional sports: assembling a competitive team capable of winning games while accounting for financial and regulatory constraints. These methods often treat on-pitch performance and the financial implications of player recruitment as separate challenges, without a structured approach to objectively incorporate both dimensions and balance quality-cost implications effectively. Furthermore, scouting has traditionally relied heavily on scout domain expertise, making it a highly subjective process. The ascendance of Big Data has introduced sports data resources that can help objectify scouting decisions and support decision-making with quantitative and analytical approaches. The development of an intelligent decision support system that seeks to integrate these multiple dimensions into a unified operations research framework is proposed. First, a two-stage min-max normalization process merges objective event-level performance statistics with subjective scout assessments to produce a standardized player-quality score for each player. Second, machine learning models are used to estimate each player's fair market value, quantify their undervaluation, and construct a pair-wise matrix to reflect team synergy. These insights will feed into a binary/mixed integer linear programming model that tackles the squad composition problem by maximizing the squad's depth quality and captured undervaluation, while adhering to roster size, foreign-player limits, and budget ceilings. The framework is validated through a case study with Sporting Cristal, one of Peru's most successful yet financially constrained football (soccer) clubs. Numerical results show the system can recommend balanced squads that raise projected performance while staying within budget and favoring undervalued signings.

Title: Inter-terminal collaboration: Optimizing multi-terminal berth allocation with container ground transfers
Authors: Di Zhang, Jian Gang Jin, Hai Wang
Abstract: This paper studies a multi-terminal berth allocation problem, where multiple container terminals collaboratively optimize berthing decisions to improve port efficiency. Upon a vessel's arrival, its contracted terminal decides whether to berth it locally or divert it, balancing waiting time and diversion costs. Existing studies focus on the vessel diversion and berth allocation, without considering their impact on containers. However, vessel diversion often necessitates additional container transfers: export containers may need to be moved to the new terminal before loading, import containers may require post-unloading transfers, and transshipment containers may require coordinated handling between two vessels. Moreover, since container transfers rely on limited truck resources, the assignment of trucks directly determines the feasibility and timing of these transfers, and thus influences the vessel diversion decision. This study fills this gap by integrating container ground transfers — including container transfers and truck assignment — into vessel diversion and berth allocation decisions. To solve the problem, we propose an integer programming model and develop a Branch-and-Price algorithm based on a set partitioning re-formulation with two types of columns, decomposing the complex problem into two manageable sub-problems, and facilitating the attainment of optimal solutions. Numerical experiments demonstrate the superiority of our approach over a solver, a matheuristic, and a sequential algorithm. We also assess the value of collaboration, confirm the importance of container ground transfers, and analyze key inputs, revealing the robust benefits of inter-terminal collaboration.

Title: Minimum risk consensus model based on consensus breakdown probability
Authors: Weiwei Guo, Yunyun Wang, Zaiwu Gong, Xiaoqin Chen, Xiao Tan, Shuli Yan
Abstract: In group decision-making (GDM) and consensus reaching process (CRP), the imbalance in interest distribution can easily induce consensus risks, and even lead to consensus breakdown. However, most existing consensus models focus on cost minimization, overlooking the importance of risk quantification and control. To address these issues, we propose the concepts of consensus risk and consensus breakdown probability, construct a basic paradigm of the minimum risk consensus model (MRCM), and provide four fundamental theorems that characterize the essential properties of consensus risk. Furthermore, we define the consensus level, fairness index and consensus breakdown index in the CRP, and reveal the geometric significance of fairness index in consensus analysis, thereby providing theoretical support for analyzing the consensus risk mechanism. Subsequently, we categorize the sources of consensus risk into two types: return imbalance and output-to-input ratio imbalance, and construct two types of MRCMs—one based on consensus level and fairness index, and the other based on Equity Theory. These models are simplified and transformed to enhance computational tractability, and the corresponding minimum risk CRP and algorithm are developed. Finally, we use a consensus problem based on carbon emission benchmark value to verify the rationality and effectiveness of the proposed models. Sensitivity analysis is conducted to examine the effects of parameter changes on consensus results, while a comparative analysis highlights the differences among models across multiple dimensions.

Title: Applying Distributionally Robust Optimization frameworks to tackle travel-time uncertainty in the ambulance location and dispatching problem
Authors: Imanol Gago-Carro, Unai Aldasoro, María Merino, Angel Ruiz
Abstract: The efficient management of Emergency Medical Services (EMS) relies on the strategic location of ambulances and their optimal dispatching, two decisions that are inherently challenged by considerable uncertainty. This paper addresses the ambulance location and dispatching problem under uncertain travel times, a factor often overlooked in the literature that nonetheless plays a critical role in response times. Travel-time uncertainty is represented by a finite, data-driven set of candidate probability distributions fitted to historical data. On this set we build three distribution-aware frameworks: a min–max model over the candidate set (Distributionally Robust Optimization), a model that averages performance over the set (Distributionally Stochastic Optimization), and a scenario-robust extension (Distributionally scenario Robust Optimization). The performance of the solutions they produced to a manageable subset of scenarios (in-sample experiments) is evaluated on different realizations of travel-time uncertainty (out-of-sample experiments) constructed on historical data from the EMS in the Basque Country (Spain). The results highlight the importance of explicitly modeling travel-time uncertainty in EMS system design. Finally, a Discrete Event Simulation model allows assessing the behavior of those solutions when the spatial and temporal variability of emergency call patterns are incorporated. The distribution-aware solutions align with Stochastic Optimization in similar average response time while improving the response time attained under the most adverse candidate distribution, and they avoid the conservatism of Robust Optimization.

Title: Integrated deployment and operational planning of offshore wind–aquaculture coupled systems
Authors: Zhiyuan Yang, Miaomiao Wang, Lu Zhen, Shuaian Wang
Abstract: The integration of offshore wind energy generation with marine aquaculture offers a promising pathway for jointly supporting renewable energy production and sustainable seafood supply. Existing studies have mainly examined the techno-economic feasibility of such integration, while optimization-based research on the deployment and operation of such systems remains limited. This study fills this gap by developing an integrated optimization framework for an offshore wind–aquaculture coupled system (OWACS) with pre-screened candidate turbine platforms. The purpose is to quantify the economic value of coupling offshore wind with marine aquaculture, identify the operational mechanisms that drive system profitability, and provide practical guidance for early-stage OWACS planning. To this end, we formulate a two-stage stochastic programming model that coordinates strategic decisions (e.g., platform commissioning and aquaculture species allocation) and operational decisions (e.g., energy storage, electricity sales, and aquaculture production), while also incorporating uncertainties in energy production and market prices. To solve the resulting model, we develop a tailored exact Benders-based algorithm and strengthen the master problem with problem-specific valid inequalities and lower bounds. Computational experiments based on offshore wind–aquaculture planning instances demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model and algorithm. The results offer several insights into OWACS planning: aquaculture integration improves profitability, co-culture can better balance revenue generation and emission limits, earlier platform commissioning increases system value, and front-loaded carbon reduction mitigates profit losses under tighter emission targets. As an additional extension, we incorporate commissioning-dependent wake losses and an endogenous radial inter-array cable network into the model and develop a customized adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm for larger instances.

Title: Privacy-preserving multi-source transfer learning for credit risk prediction with mixture cure models
Authors: Xiaoyan Wang, Ankang Jiao, Jingmao Li, Kuangnan Fang
Abstract: A central challenge in credit risk management is the dynamic assessment of borrower default risk, particularly under conditions of data scarcity. To address this issue, this study proposes a multi-source transfer learning framework for the mixture cure model (MTL-MCM). The MCM first distinguishes long-term non-defaulters from potential defaulters through the incidence model and then predicts the time-dependent default probabilities of the latter via the latency model, thereby enabling more accurate dynamic default prediction. To enhance model performance in target data with limited sample size, the proposed framework facilitates knowledge transfer from multiple heterogeneous sources and accommodates diverse types of information. Only summarized knowledge, rather than raw data, is utilized, thereby ensuring privacy protection. A two-level adaptive weighting mechanism is developed to dynamically evaluate the quality of each source, enabling more efficient transfer learning. Model estimation is performed using a regularized Expectation–Maximization algorithm. Simulation studies show that MTL-MCM outperforms alternative methods in variable selection, parameter estimation, and dynamic risk prediction. Moreover, an empirical analysis using cross-platform credit data further demonstrates the model's practical utility in constructing dynamic credit scoring systems for new business applications.

Title: A new cut-and-solve-based approach for the single-source capacitated facility location problem
Authors: Guilherme Barbosa de Almeida, Marcone Jamilson Freitas Souza, Elisangela Martins de Sá, Sérgio Ricardo de Souza
Abstract: The Single-Source Capacitated Facility Location Problem involves locating facilities so that each customer’s demand is met by a single facility and capacity constraints are not violated. This paper focuses on developing an exact algorithm to handle this problem. In this sense, we propose an algorithm that uses four strategies: (i) strengthening the problem formulation through a cutting-plane procedure; (ii) exploiting partial linear relaxations to obtain good lower bounds; (iii) applying a heuristic to obtain a good upper bound; and (iv) applying a Cut-and-Solve-based scheme to construct a binary search tree. We evaluate and select cutting-plane generation procedures that differ from those previously used for the problem and propose a new heuristic procedure. The results of the computational experiments showed that the proposed algorithm found a greater or equal number of optimal values with lower runtime than the state-of-the-art exact algorithm in 22 out of 26 subsets, and than the CPLEX solver in 19 out of 26 subsets.

Title: Strategic cooperation: Winning in live-streaming e-commerce with key opinion leaders
Authors: Peng He, Henry Xu, Zhongyi Huang, Helen Cai, Victor Shi
Abstract: In live-streaming e-commerce, brands, Key Opinion Leaders (KOLs), and social platforms must make complex decisions about collaboration structures, balancing sales incentives against the risk of long-term reputation loss. Using differential game theory, this paper investigates three cooperation modes in a three-echelon social e-commerce supply chain: the independent-KOL mode, the brand-signing KOL mode, and the platform-signing KOL mode. Our findings indicate that when the live-streaming promotion effect is relatively strong, a higher KOL commission rate enhances brand goodwill when the reputation loss effect is relatively weak, but diminishes brand goodwill when the reputation loss effect is relatively strong. Moreover, the brand-signing mode enhances brand goodwill and KOL influence when both platform and KOL commission rates are relatively low. Conversely, when these rates exceed certain thresholds, the platform-signing mode becomes more advantageous and expands market demand. Additionally, signing a KOL accelerates profit growth for the signing parties, while non-signing members can also benefit from others' cooperative arrangements. Finally, the brand- or platform-signing KOL modes yield higher total cooperative profit than the independent-KOL mode when live-streaming efficiency is lower, whereas the opposite holds when efficiency is higher. These results offer strategic guidance for brand managers and platform operators in optimizing partnership structures and mitigating the dynamic risks inherent in KOL live-streaming.

Title: Permutation tests on common production frontiers in nonparametric models
Authors: Anders Rønn-Nielsen, Dorte Kronborg, Mette Asmild
Abstract: Permutation techniques, which involve recomputing a test statistic over permutations of data, have a long history in statistics and have become increasingly useful with the availability of greater computational power. However, until now, there have been no permutation tests available for statistical analysis within non-parametric models for production frontiers. We develop new permutation-based tests for comparing production technologies. These tests can be used to determine general differences between production technologies and to assess whether one production possibility set is nested within another. They can be applied both for comparison of frontiers for independent groups and for analysing frontier shifts across time for panel data. Our permutation tests all make use of Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) for estimating efficiencies, and indirectly the production possibility set, through linear programming. The tests are easily implementable. We show that our suggested permutations of the observations satisfy the necessary randomisation assumptions, and hereby that the tests have the desired sizes and, consequently, are exact. Further we show that our tests are consistent. The main advantage of permutation tests is that they are particularly useful for relatively small samples. However, one needs to be careful about the hypotheses that are being tested.

Title: From global to local? Designing optimal climate-linked industrial policy for global supply chains under sustainability gaps
Abstract: In developed countries, local sourcing is typically more expensive than global alternatives due to sustainability gaps in supplier carbon intensity. Climate policies seek to promote cleaner inputs through incentives such as consumer tax credits, but their effectiveness on economic efficiency and climate externalities remains uncertain. To address this, we develop a game-theoretical model of a local original equipment manufacturer (OEM) that allocates orders between a less sustainable, cost-efficient global supplier and a more sustainable, costlier local supplier, subject to a government-imposed eligibility threshold that conditions consumer tax credits. Our analysis reveals a non-decreasing, three-zone structure for the optimal threshold: it starts at zero in emerging markets, rises gradually in transitional markets, and maximizes in mature markets. Complete localization arises only when the sustainability gap is narrow, while wider gaps restrict thresholds to an interior value to avoid disengagement. Stricter thresholds always increase economic surplus, but emission reductions occur only in intermediate-scale markets, especially when supplier sustainability differs substantially. Extending the model to competitive settings, we find that under global competition, localization policies take effect sooner but reach the maximum value more slowly, while local competition accelerates both the initiation and finalization of the localization process. Competition also alters economic and environmental effects: economic efficiency initially declines with market growth before recovering, and stricter thresholds fail to reduce emissions due to either policy exemptions or reduced output responsiveness. These results underscore that effective climate policy must be adaptive and aligned with market maturity, competition, and supplier characteristics.

Title: Competitive implications of spectrum subleasing on pricing, quality and sourcing decisions
Authors: Manish Tripathy, Hans Sebastian Heese, Tim Kraft
Abstract: In the last decade, a new class of service providers, known as Mobile Virtual Network Operators (MVNOs), has emerged in the cellular market. MVNOs minimize infrastructure investments by subleasing bandwidth from traditional Mobile Network Operators (MNOs). In this paper, we study a duopoly cellular service market in which two MNOs compete on price and quality while potentially subleasing spectrum to an MVNO. The MNOs decide the price for their own service as well as the quality level and wholesale price to offer the MVNO. We consider two MNO pricing cases: (i) No Anticipation, where the MNOs ignore the MVNO's potential entry in setting retail prices, and (ii) Anticipation, where they account for the MVNO's entry. The MVNO decides where to source from and the price to set for its service. Using a vertically differentiated spatial model of product positioning, we examine how service quality, price, and market structure change with the presence of an MVNO. We find that the MVNO never sources from only the low-quality MNO. Instead, the MVNO chooses between sourcing from the high-quality MNO or from both MNOs based on the benefits of bundling spectrum and the MVNO's reputation. If the interaction of the two significantly enhances the MVNO's quality, the MVNO sources from both; otherwise, it sources only from the high-quality MNO. We find that all firms can coexist in the No Anticipation case; however, the low-quality MNO can be pushed out of the market under the Anticipation case if the MVNO's reputation is sufficiently high.

Title: Deep reinforcement learning for aging cheese inventory management under correlated prices
Authors: Alexander Pahr, Paula Krumm, Anna Kolemesina, Martin Grunow
Abstract: In aging cheese inventory management, producers must jointly consider auto-correlated and cross-correlated prices for raw milk and age-differentiated cheese products. Issuance flexibility arises because the cheese age label specifies a minimum maturation time, allowing deliberate target-age excess. We develop a generic Markov decision process model for ameliorating inventory systems that captures auto-correlated and cross-correlated purchase and sales prices. Because state and action spaces grow exponentially in the number of age classes, we use deep reinforcement learning (DRL). However, standard actor-critic DRL algorithms struggle with the high-dimensional action spaces induced by issuance flexibility. For a reduced two-period hedging problem, we prove that the value of issuance flexibility declines with purchase-price auto-correlation. Building on this result, we develop two dimensionality reduction approaches. The first curtails issuance flexibility, whereas the second retains it via actor pipelining, with issuance actions determined by simple decision rules. On average, actor pipelining provides the best trade-off between policy quality and computational effort. Further, full factorial experiments reveal that, in contrast to prior work, the benefit of issuance flexibility is limited under cheese-specific price processes. It becomes substantial only in highly volatile, fast mean-reverting environments and can be omitted entirely in highly correlated settings. Additionally, we show that multi-agent actor designs provide limited value at substantially higher computational cost. Our DRL policies outperform a rolling-horizon planning benchmark by 16.7% on average. Moreover, modeling cheese-specific price dynamics yields a 7.1% profit improvement over simplified price assumptions.

Title: Fast but reliable? Consistency of preference elicitation with ranking and rating for multicriteria decision analysis in Real‑World cases
Authors: M. Kuller, P. Beutler, J. Lienert
Abstract: Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) methods require stakeholder preference elicitation, but standard approaches like Swing weight elicitation can be time-consuming and cognitively demanding for practical applications. This study investigated whether fast preference elicitation methods—direct ranking and rating of objectives—can effectively substitute for rigorous Swing weight elicitation in real-world public decision-making contexts. Data were collected from three case studies involving flood early warning system development in West Africa and wastewater management transitions in two Swiss rural communities. Individual stakeholder preferences for objectives were elicited through ranking, rating, and Swing weight methods across multiple workshops. Consistency between ranking and rating was high for most stakeholders (median γ-values around -0.9). Weights derived from objectives ranking correlated better with Swing weights than rating weights, particularly in the largest case study. When aggregated across stakeholders, fast elicitation methods implemented in MCDA produced nearly identical rankings of alternatives compared to Swing weights (Kendall's τ > 0.84), with no rank reversals in top-5 alternatives between weights derived from objectives ranking and Swing. However, holistic, direct ranking of alternatives showed poor correlation with MCDA-calculated rankings (τ < 0.5), supporting value-focused thinking principles. These findings demonstrate that fast ranking of objectives can approximate Swing weight elicitation outcomes while significantly reducing time and cognitive burden, offering a practical approach for consensus-seeking in resource-constrained public decision processes.

Title: Agency vs. resale: Selling format choice on competing platforms with asymmetric suppliers
Authors: Benrong Zheng, Guoxuan Huang, T.C.E. Cheng
Abstract: This study investigates how competing online platforms choose between agency and resale selling formats when sourcing from exclusive suppliers with differing cost efficiencies. Utilizing a game-theoretic framework, we analyze how supplier cost asymmetry and platform competition influence equilibrium selling strategies, firm profitability and consumer welfare. Our findings reveal a key trade-off: the resale model mitigates competition through double marginalization, while the agency model enables more cost-efficient suppliers to exploit their advantages via aggressive pricing. Platforms adopt the resale-resale (RR) strategy when supplier cost differences are minimal and the commission rate is low. As cost asymmetry or the commission rate increases, the equilibrium shifts toward agency-based or asymmetric formats: high commissions induce the agency-agency (AA) equilibria, whereas sufficiently large cost asymmetry leads to asymmetric equilibria, with RA arising under low commissions and AR under high commissions. Notably, we identify an agency trap, a prisoner's dilemma outcome where platforms choose the AA equilibrium even though both would earn higher profits under the RR model. This outcome arises when the commission rate is sufficiently high and supplier cost asymmetry is either low or lies within a narrow high-asymmetry range. Welfare analysis indicates that agency-dominated models (AA or AR) tend to maximize consumer surplus and social welfare, albeit at the expense of supplier profits. These findings remain robust across various extensions, including platform-side asymmetry, service competition, and endogenous commissions. These results suggest that platforms should align their selling format choices with supplier cost asymmetry and market competition, rather than adopting a one-size-fits-all strategy.

Title: When manufacturer encroachment backfires: Effects of cross-selling in Internet of Things product supply chains
Authors: Rui Hou, Yongjiao Ruan, You Zhao
Abstract: This paper studies a supply chain in which a manufacturer sells an Internet of Things (IoT)–enabled product through an e-commerce platform and may also open a direct channel (i.e., encroachment). The manufacturer endogenously chooses the IoT functionality level, while the platform and the manufacturer benefit from cross-selling of consumables enabled by IoT data, regardless of the sales channel. We examine how the presence of cross-channel externalities affects the manufacturer's encroachment and investment strategies. We develop a game-theoretic model includes a subscription-based charging mode for IoT service. Contrary to prior research, we show that higher platform cross-selling revenue can discourage the manufacturer from investing in IoT functionality under encroachment. We also find that encroachment can increase wholesale prices rather than reduce them when the platform lacks pricing power. Surprisingly, even when channels are equally efficient, encroachment may harm the manufacturer while benefiting the platform. Our results highlight that cross-selling externalities can distort investment incentives and decouple encroachment from profit gains. Manufacturers should reconsider encroachment when platforms extract disproportionate value via cross-selling. Platforms, in turn, can shape channel outcomes through pricing structures and IoT fee designs, and may even subsidize encroachment to boost ecosystem-level monetization.

Title: Surge pricing and multi-agency interaction in humanitarian logistics: An equilibrium approach
Abstract: In this paper, we develop a network model for hurricane relief logistics in which multiple agencies choose pre-positioned stock and response shipments while sharing depots and freight lanes. The pre-positioning decision carries a procurement or reservation cost and is limited by available depot storage. After landfall, agencies ship relief supplies through lanes whose freight prices increase with total use. We formulate both a centralized planner model and a decentralized agency model on the same physical network using a variational inequality framework. The model also includes time-based shortage penalties, service balance across demand zones, and a budgeted expected-shortage hedge. Numerical examples calibrated to a U.S. Gulf Coast setting examine lane expansion, early shortage costs, service balance, expected-shortage protection, coordination surcharges, and stochastic planner-GNE comparisons. Replicated sample average approximation checks and independent out of sample evaluations are used to support the stochastic comparisons. The results show that, among the tested individual stresses, the increase in demand has the largest effect on cost, that local lane expansion has diminishing returns when congestion shifts to other lanes, and that decentralized decisions can create service gaps even when total cost gaps are small.

Title: Platform contracts for emission-reducing smart products with consumers’ privacy concern
Authors: Prasenjit Mandal, Debashree Ray, Abhishek Chakraborty, Tania Saha, Ou Tang
Abstract: IoT-enabled smart home devices, such as smart thermostats, can help reduce household carbon emissions through data-driven energy optimization. However, their reliance on continuous data collection poses significant consumers’ privacy concerns, creating a fundamental tension between sustainability benefits and privacy risks. This paper studies a supply chain where a manufacturer sells smart home devices via an online platform that chooses an optimal contract: the reselling or agency contract. The manufacturer invests in emission-reducing technologies. Given that consumers are emission-sensitive and privacy-concerned, and consumer data has a significant monetizable value for the platform, we examine how these factors influence smart product pricing, emission reduction efforts, and stakeholders’ contract preferences. Our results reveal that higher emission sensitivity does not always lead to greater emission reductions, particularly when investment costs in emission reduction are high. Next, under the reselling model, a higher marginal value of consumer data incentivizes the manufacturer to increase emission reduction, while the product price response depends on the cost of emission reduction. In contrast, under the agency model, the equilibrium outcomes are unaffected by data value. Further, our results indicate that the platform chooses the reselling contract when the data value is significantly high or very low, whereas the agency model is preferable for intermediate data values. Moreover, under specific market conditions, both contracts can lead to ‘win-win-win’ outcomes for the manufacturer, the platform, and the consumers. Most importantly, we also show that our key findings on ‘win-win-win’ outcomes are robust to alternative leadership structures, including manufacturer-led contract choice.

Title: Decision-focused learning for distributionally robust multi-agent dynamic vehicle routing in e-commerce last-mile delivery
Authors: Ruowei Liu, Yuhao Ma, Rongfei Ma
Abstract: E-commerce last-mile delivery requires coordinated vehicle routing under uncertain demand, travel times, and dynamically arriving orders. We develop DFL-DRO-DVRP, a sequential decision architecture that integrates regret-based learning, samplewise adversarial robustification motivated by Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization, and best-response coordination among delivery agents. The architecture first trains the predictor with a robustified SPO+ objective and then adjusts deployed routes through agent-level best responses. A nested formulation makes these interfaces explicit, while a conditional error decomposition separates prediction, perturbation, and centralized deployment terms. Across four benchmark settings, DFL-DRO-DVRP attains the lowest total cost on Solomon, distribution-shift, and multi-agent instances, improving on the data-driven hybrid ALNS baseline by 1.5%, 1.4%, and 2.5%, respectively; on the nominal e-commerce benchmark, its 0.5% cost difference is not statistically significant. Under demand, time-window, and travel-time shifts, the method limits cost increases to 6.1%, 8.7%, and 5.2%, compared with 6.8%, 9.5%, and 5.8% for the strongest competing baseline. These results show that the proposed composition remains competitive under nominal conditions and provides its clearest advantages when distributional robustness and decentralized coordination are operationally relevant.

Title: Covariance matrix estimation for positively correlated assets
Abstract: The comovement phenomenon in financial markets creates decision scenarios with positively correlated asset returns. This paper addresses covariance matrix estimation under such conditions, motivated by observations of significant positive correlations in factor-sorted portfolio monthly returns. We demonstrate that fine-tuning eigenvectors linked to weak factors within rotation-equivariant frameworks produces well-conditioned covariance matrix estimates. Our Eigenvector Rotation Shrinkage Estimator (ERSE) pairwise rotates eigenvectors while preserving orthogonality, equivalent to performing multiple linear shrinkage on two distinct eigenvalues. Empirical results on factor-sorted portfolios from the Ken French data library demonstrate that ERSE outperforms existing rotation-equivariant estimators in reducing out-of-sample portfolio variance, achieving average risk reductions of 10.52\% versus linear shrinkage methods and 12.46\% versus nonlinear shrinkage methods. Further checks indicate that ERSE yields covariance matrices with lower condition numbers, produces more concentrated and stable portfolio weights, and provides consistent improvements across different subperiods and estimation windows.

Title: Condition-based maintenance for multi-component systems under spatio-temporal degradation propagation
Authors: Ziyu Wang, Shuguang He, Yi Luo, Bin Liu, Xiujie Zhao
Abstract: For complex industrial systems, a commonly witnessed phenomenon is that degradation occurring in one component propagates spatially over time, aggravating the degradation of adjacent components, which is referred to as spatio-temporal degradation propagation. In this paper, we propose a maintenance optimization framework for systems where component degradation is jointly governed by intrinsic generation and propagation processes: the Wiener process is adopted to model the degradation generation process, while a convolution-based model is employed to characterize the degradation propagation process. The maintenance decision problem is formulated as a Markov decision process (MDP), and further transformed into a factored Markov decision process (FMDP) by decomposing the system's factor structure to reduce computational complexity. We formulate the maintenance optimization problem under an expected discounted cost criterion and derive structural properties of the optimal policy. Numerical examples show that the proposed approach achieves a lower expected discounted cost than alternative policies. It is further demonstrated that the degradation propagation process exerts a significant impact on the optimal maintenance policy, highlighting the importance of preventive maintenance for components strongly affected by propagation effects.

Title: Learning-driven multi-start local search for the multiple row equal facility layout problem
Authors: Wen Sun, Qi Yue, Jin-Kao Hao, Qinghua Wu, Fengshun Wang
Abstract: Given a set of facilities, integer numbers k and r , a facility flow matrix, and a group distance matrix, the multiple row equal facility layout problem (MREFLP) aims to determine a facility-to-group assignment with the minimum aggregate of the products of the flow cost and the facility distances, such that the number of the facilities assigned to each group does not exceed r . The MREFLP is a general model for various applications including operating theater layout in hospitals. However, due to its NP-hardness, solving this problem is computationally difficult. This paper proposes an effective learning-driven multi-start local search algorithm for this problem, which features a learning-driven solution construction procedure and a dedicated two-phase local search. Experiments on 572 benchmark instances demonstrate that the algorithm surpasses the state-of-the-art algorithms. Specifically, it achieves 165 new upper bounds and 407 equal results (including 289 known optima). An ablation study is performed to show the influence of each algorithm component.

Title: Two-stage one-dimensional cutting stock problem with flexible item sizes in steel industry
Authors: Ying Meng, Lixin Tang, Roberto Baldacci, Marco Antonio Boschetti, Jiyin Liu, Md Al Amin
Abstract: The classical cutting stock problem (CSP) consists of efficiently producing items with different sizes and demands using the minimum number of bins (stock materials), ensuring that the total size of the items assigned to each bin does not exceed its capacity. Various CSP variants have emerged to address specific constraints and objectives across different applications. This paper focuses on a new two-stage one-dimensional CSP with flexible item sizes (TS-1DCSP), which arises in the steel industry. In TS-1DCSP, each order is associated with a length range and a total length demand. For the TS-1DCSP, we develop compact, arc-flow-based, and pattern-based mathematical formulations, and enhance the latter by adding cuts to improve its linear programming relaxation. A novel label-setting-based pricing algorithm is designed for the pattern-based formulation. This pattern-based model forms the basis for an exact algorithm within a branch-and-price (BP) framework, using a two-level branching rule to achieve integrality. The exact algorithm also includes a primal heuristic that uses a depth-first search in the BP tree. We validate the method's performance through extensive computational experiments on benchmark instances from literature and real-world scenarios, confirming its effectiveness in solving TS-1DCSP instances with up to 150 orders.

Title: Exact methods for disabling interdiction problems
Authors: Alberto Boggio Tomasaz, Roberto Cordone, Pierre Hosteins
Abstract: Interdiction problems are a class of adversarial combinatorial optimisation problems where two agents compete to optimise the same objective function in opposite directions. In this work, we focus on the case in which the leader disables a subset of elements from the instance, preventing their use in the follower's solution. We introduce methodological improvements for three existing methods, providing a tighter version of two Benders decompositions and a generalised version of a covering decomposition which exploit the availability of super-optimal bounds. Such bounds are obtained through three novel heuristic methods based on a bi-objective auxiliary problem that generates diverse, high-quality solutions for the follower, in order to reduce computation times. The framework is applied to the Shortest Path Interdiction Problem and the Set Covering Interdiction Problem. The experimental results suggest that the proposed approaches outperform the existing Benders decompositions and perform comparably with the basic covering decomposition, but scale better for large sizes and interdiction budgets.

Title: To cooperate with Top-tier streamers or not? A sequential bargaining approach in live-streaming supply chains
Authors: Tong Xu, Dong Yang, Junjun Kong, Minyue Jin
Abstract: In live-streaming supply chains, manufacturers face a strategic choice between cooperating with a Top-tier streamer, who offers broad market exposure but stronger bargaining power, and a Small-scale streamer, who provides greater pricing flexibility but limited reach. To examine this trade-off, we develop a three-party sequential bargaining model with one manufacturer and two asymmetric streamers, incorporating the effect of streamers’ engagement effort on consumer demand. Interestingly, we find that cooperation with a Top-tier streamer does not necessarily lead to a higher negotiated price. When the Top-tier streamer's reservation profit is sufficiently high, the manufacturer may lower the price to satisfy the streamer's participation constraint, resulting in a lower price than under cooperation with the Small-scale streamer. We also show that lower production costs can strengthen the manufacturer's incentive to cooperate with the Top-tier streamer by amplifying the value of broader market reach. Finally, our welfare analysis identifies two win–win regions in which both the manufacturer and consumers benefit. These findings offer insights into manufacturer–streamer cooperation and pricing decisions in live-streaming commerce.

Title: The impact of resale price maintenance on a legitimate retailer’s decision to sell counterfeits in dual-channel competition
Authors: Jing Chen, Shanshan Guo, Hang Wei, Lei Xie, Chaonan Zheng
Abstract: The higher profits from selling counterfeits may tempt legitimate retailers to engage in such practices. When brands gain channel advantages through direct stores or pricing power, this can intensify intra-brand competition and further incentivize counterfeit sales. Two common scenarios are widely observed in practice. The brand enforces a Resale Price Maintenance (RPM) policy to control the retail price (RPM model) and the retailer can set retail price freely (Non-RPM model). We consider a dual-channel competition game where a brand sells its products through its direct channel and a licit retailer in a distribution channel. The licit retailer could procure deceptive counterfeits from an outside supplier. The channel competition is captured by a standard Hotelling model and the quality difference represents the quality competition between deceptive counterfeits and brand-name products. We find that selling counterfeits provides the cost-saving force and the market-loss force which drive the retailer to increase and decrease the proportion of deceptive counterfeits respectively. RPM may boost the flood of counterfeits with intense channel competition. Interestingly, allowing the retailer to set retail prices can generate an anti-counterfeiting benefit at the cost of a reduction in brand and retailer's profits when channel competition becomes excessive. Under moderate channel competition and low-quality competition, granting pricing right to retailers reduces consumer surplus but enhances overall supply chain performance and social welfare by reducing counterfeiting and elevating retail prices across both channels.

Title: A unified learning framework for the block relocation problem: A new performance baseline
Authors: Woo-Jin Shin, Ji-Kwang Jung, Sang-Hyun Cho, Inguk Choi, Shunji Tanaka, Hyun-Jung Kim
Abstract: This study addresses the block relocation problem (BRP), a key challenge in container yard operations. In the BRP, containers are stacked vertically, and retrieving a target container may require relocating those above it. The objective is to retrieve all containers in a predefined order while minimizing the total number of relocations. Recent reinforcement learning (RL) approaches have been explored for the BRP, but they face fundamental limitations. In particular, the unrestricted variant allows any topmost container to be relocated, which may lead to cyclic relocations, non-termination, and arbitrarily long decision trajectories. These issues can produce unreliable learning signals and substantial training-time and memory overhead. To address these challenges, we propose L2BR, a unified learning framework for both the restricted and unrestricted BRP that sequentially combines imitation learning (IL) and self-improvement learning (SIL). IL mitigates cycle-related issues by training an initial policy from pre-generated (near-)optimal solutions, while SIL enables scalable improvement by imitating the best complete solutions found by the policy itself. Experiments on well-known benchmark sets show that L2BR consistently finds optimal solutions for many instances and establishes new best-known results within only a few seconds. L2BR substantially outperforms existing RL-based methods and also surpasses state-of-the-art optimization-based approaches, particularly for the unrestricted variant and large-scale instances.2

Title: Robust and fair ticket allocation under strategic passenger behavior for enhancing railway system resilience
Authors: Rui Chen, Chunpeng Fan, Hua Wang
Abstract: Ticketing practices in railway systems face growing challenges under demand uncertainty, exposing operators to risks of segment-level overloads. These risks are amplified by strategic passenger behaviors such as buy-short-to-ride-long, whereby travelers initially purchase short-haul tickets and subsequently extend their journeys by paying the additional fare onboard. Such behavior generates hidden passenger flows that distort planned load profiles, substantially increasing the likelihood of localized capacity overloads and potentially leading to severe congestion or even service disruptions. These challenges underscore the need for more robust and behavior-aware ticket allocation policies. This study develops a distributionally robust optimization framework for railway ticket sales. The model integrates three key features: (1) distributionally robust optimization to hedge against demand-distribution uncertainty; (2) segment-level capacity-risk constraints that account for BSRL-induced continuation patterns; and (3) fairness-aware constraints that safeguard equitable ticket availability across passenger markets. By combining a duality-based reformulation with a conditional value-at-risk approximation, the resulting model is tractable and interpretable. Extensive numerical experiments based on realistic railway settings demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently outperforms classical benchmarks, yielding higher revenues, fewer overload incidents, and more equitable seat allocations. Beyond methodological contributions, the results provide operational guidance for railway operators and policymakers seeking to modernize ticketing strategies in ways that jointly enhance efficiency, fairness, safety, and resilience.

Title: Outsourcing under cost information asymmetry and tariffs pressure: When multinationals prefer their local competitors
Authors: Yingying Teng, Bo Li, Hubert Pun, Pengwen Hou
Abstract: Escalating geopolitical tensions are prompting many local governments to impose higher tariffs on imported goods, increasing the costs for multinational firms (MNFs) serving the local market via their established manufacturing bases. To avoid these tariffs, MNFs may consider outsourcing production to local suppliers. However, such decisions are strategically complex. First, MNFs often have limited visibility into the local supplier's cost structure. Second, local suppliers may also compete in the product market, creating risks of innovation spillover. In this paper, we develop a price-signaling game to examine the MNF's outsourcing decision between (i) a traditional supplier (TS) located in an established manufacturing country, where the MNF has prior working experience and hence with transparent cost but subject to tariffs, and (ii) a local supplier (LS) with private cost information who competes in the product market and poses innovation spillover. The main findings are as follows. First, when outsourcing to the TS, the MNF makes biased quantity decisions. By contrast, when outsourcing to the LS, the MNF can endogenously eliminate the LS's information advantage through the LS's wholesale price signal under a low or moderate innovation value. Second, even with significant cost advantages of the LS at high tariffs, the MNF may favor the TS when the innovation value is high. Finally, cost information asymmetry may actually make the MNF more willing to outsource to the LS, even in cases where outsourcing to the TS incurs a low tariff.

Title: Counting operations to analyze and compare Fast DEA procedures
Authors: Gregory Koronakos, José H. Dulá, Dimitris K. Despotis
Abstract: When introducing new procedures in OR/MS, particularly in Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA), standard practice involves describing the proposed approach and evaluating its performance through execution times. This metric depends on the hardware, software, implementation, and solver. The practice obscures the intrinsic computational effort and limits the reproducibility of the results. Solving linear programs (LPs) to classify and score entities represents the preponderant task in DEA procedures. This work proposes applying Representative Operation Counts (ROC) to large-scale DEA for measuring computational effort by counting the LPs solved and tracking their size. ROC is environment-independent since it does not depend on hardware or software configuration (programming platform, solver, simplex method, etc.). We use ROC for the foundational “Traditional” DEA approach and three “Fast” DEA procedures, i.e. approaches that have provided substantial speedups in DEA by using novel theoretical LP results and/or geometric properties. We derive analytical expressions for the DEA procedures to capture best, worst, and average case scenarios where possible. ROC, which can also be calculated empirically, enables pairwise comparisons, explains performance and how data characteristics affect computational effort. Thus, we propose using ROC to supplement execution time. Finally, we explore how ROC can be used to estimate execution time for specific data and environment. From this we empirically observe a near-linear relationship between ROC and execution time, primarily valid for large LPs, and dependent on simplex-based implementations.

Title: A dynamic programming algorithm for the Robotic Cell Problem with a fixed job processing order
Abstract: The Robotic Cell Problem (RCP) is a flow-shop scheduling problem in which jobs must be transferred from each machine to the next one by a robot. The robot movements require non-negligible time and must be optimized to minimize the makespan. The problem is practically relevant in the context of manufacturing systems. In this work, we study a variant of the RCP in which the processing order of the jobs is fixed.
