We present a dynamic programming algorithm for the exact optimization of this variant and show how it can be transformed into an accurate heuristic. Computational results are provided on instances with up to 30 jobs and 15 machines under different distributions of travel and processing times. The results indicate that our algorithm can solve significantly larger instances than existing methods. The proposed approach may also serve as a subroutine within future heuristic methods for the general RCP.

Title: The double-edged role of manufacturer corporate social responsibility: How selling formats and store brand entry shape platform-based supply chains
Authors: Hai Li, Bangyu Long, Yao Tang, Shouyu Ma
Abstract: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) has been widely studied in traditional supply chains, yet its strategic implications in platform-based markets remain relatively unexplored. Unlike conventional settings, e-commerce platforms introduce novel operational frictions, enabling manufacturers to choose between agency and reselling formats, while platforms can enter the market with their own store brands (SB). Departing from prior studies that treat the selling format or SB entry as exogenous, we model both decisions endogenously within a game-theoretic framework. This integrated framework allows us to uncover how CSR strategically reshapes the interactions between the manufacturer and the platform, revealing several counterintuitive results. First, the manufacturer's profit follows an inverted-U relationship with its CSR intensity: moderate CSR enhances profitability, whereas very low or very high CSR reduces it. Second, stronger CSR can paradoxically empower the platform by inducing the manufacturer to adopt the reselling format, thereby increasing the platform's strategic control and facilitating SB entry. Third, although CSR is intended to benefit consumers, excessive CSR may backfire by altering market equilibrium and ultimately reducing consumer surplus. We further extend the baseline model to incorporate platform CSR and endogenous commission setting, demonstrating that the main qualitative insights remain robust. Overall, our findings highlight the double-edged nature of CSR in platform-based markets and underscore the trade-offs among stakeholders, offering guidance for aligning social objectives with operational decisions.

Title: Fifty years of Robust Linear and Convex Optimization
Abstract: During the last 25 years Robust Linear and Convex Optimization (RLCO) has become an important subfield in optimization after several seminal publications in the late nineties. Several papers published during 1973–1997 already contain some of the ingredients of modern RLCO. In this paper, we describe the contributions of these papers during the first 25 years, and we describe the main achievements of modern RLCO during the last 25 years. We focus on generic principles and methodology.

Title: Optimization-based strategic planning for geographical healthcare accessibility in developing countries: A literature review
Authors: Laura Davila-Pena, Maria Paola Scaparra, Dick den Hertog
Abstract: Access to healthcare facilities is a critical issue in developing countries, where limited resources and significant challenges hinder progress toward universal health coverage, one of the targets pursued by the United Nations. As a result, the Operations Research (OR) community has become increasingly active in addressing this issue, employing various techniques, particularly optimization. However, making long-term strategic decisions remains challenging, as these often require substantial investments and directly affect large populations. Moreover, much of the existing literature is predominantly theoretical. This paper reviews studies published over the past two decades that use optimization techniques to inform strategic planning decisions aimed at improving health accessibility and specifically contain a case study conducted in a developing country. The review explores the nature of the problems tackled, considering factors such as the level of care, service delivery channels, objectives, criteria, or potential hierarchy, uncertainty, and multi-period settings. Additionally, we discuss the modeling approaches, solution methodologies, and the extent of practical implementation. The goal of this survey is not only to summarize existing work but also to provide a roadmap for future research, offering valuable insights for OR practitioners in the field.

Title: Sorting under multiple eyes: A multi-view preference learning framework for multi-criteria decision aiding
Authors: Yuan Gao, Zhen Zhang, Yu-wang Chen, Miłosz Kadziński
Abstract: Multi-criteria sorting (MCS) problems increasingly involve alternatives described through multiple views, where each view represents a distinct information source, descriptive perspective, or modeling lens providing partial support for a common class assignment. We propose a preference learning framework for multi-view MCS. First, we develop an Evidential Preference Learning (EPL) model for single-view sorting, combining a value-driven, threshold-based sorting procedure with a flexible preference model that can represent non-monotonic effects and pairwise criterion interactions. Rather than producing only deterministic assignments, EPL transforms the available information into an evidential opinion over the common class set, composed of class-wise belief degrees and predictive uncertainty. We then introduce Multi-view Evidential Preference Learning (MEPL), in which view-specific preference models are jointly trained and their opinions are fused at the decision level using evidential reasoning. The fusion mechanism accounts for predictive uncertainty and learned view importance, enabling convergent, complementary, or conflicting evidence to be combined into a coherent sorting recommendation. Experiments on four real-world datasets instantiate views as statistical measurement perspectives, client information sources, health-related assessment domains, and relational data sources describing the same alternatives. An additional analysis considers views induced by alternative preference-model specifications applied to the same evaluation data. The results show improved predictive performance over single-view and multi-view baselines, robustness to noise, and flexibility across preference-model configurations. An illustrative credit-risk case further demonstrates how MEPL supports decision aiding by explaining assignments through view-specific evidence, predictive uncertainty, and the relative contributions of different views to the final decision.

Title: Long memory score-driven models as approximations for rough Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes
Abstract: This paper investigates the continuous-time limit of score-driven models with long memory. By extending score-driven models to incorporate infinite-lag structures with coefficients exhibiting heavy-tailed decay, we establish their weak convergence, under appropriate scaling, to fractional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes with Hurst parameter $H<1/2$. When score-driven models are used to characterize the dynamics of volatility, they serve as discrete-time approximations for rough volatility. We present several examples, including EGARCH($\infty$) whose limits give rise to a new class of rough volatility models. Building on this framework, we carry out numerical simulations and option pricing analyses, offering new tools for rough volatility modeling and simulation.

Title: Optimal allocation of embedding dimensions under finite-sample constraints
Abstract: The embedding dimension of categorical predictors is usually selected through heuristic tuning, although it directly affects model complexity, approximation quality, and finite-sample generalization. This paper formulates embedding dimension selection as a constrained allocation problem. The main contribution is to show that embedding capacity can be allocated across heterogeneous categorical predictors according to an explicit approximation–estimation tradeoff. We characterize approximation error through the singular-value tail of the latent category representation, while estimation error increases with total embedding complexity. Under a fixed global embedding budget and a tractable approximation model, this leads to a closed-form allocation rule in which the dimension assigned to each predictor is proportional to the square root of its approximation value relative to its parameter cost. Simulation experiments support the proposed approximation–estimation interpretation and show that the allocation rule improves budget efficiency relative to standard uniform and cardinality-based heuristics, particularly when the budget is binding and predictor heterogeneity is substantial. A real-data healthcare application further shows improvements in predictive accuracy and probabilistic calibration. Overall, the results establish embedding-dimension allocation as a principled finite-sample optimization problem rather than a purely heuristic modeling choice.

Title: A new critical realist approach for evaluating multimethodological practice in operational research
Authors: Jane S. Christie, John Mingers, Kathy Kotiadis, Martin Parr
Abstract: Understanding why practitioners take the actions they do in multimethodological operational research (OR), and the effects these actions have, is fundamental for evaluating and improving practice. But it is widely recognized in OR literature and amongst practitioners that objective, comparative evaluation of complex, real-world interventions is challenging if not impossible. It is not clear how multimethodology should be evaluated. Critical realism has been advocated for exploring causation to evaluate OR practice holistically, but not fully operationalized. For our collaborative research evaluating multimethodological practice supporting strategic decision-making in non-academic settings, we therefore developed a new approach. We synthesized and operationalized empirical research and theories in OR and recent developments in critical realism and social science. In this paper, we present our theoretical framework – a new critical realist ontology of multimethodological OR practice and methodologies – and our empirical research design. We illustrate the approach with a case study of an OR analysis for a business case for government investment in a national capability. We demonstrate how we investigated the intervention context and the complex process of practitioners’ choice of methods using interviews and project documents, thematic and comparative analysis, rich description, and structural and causal analysis. We explore how this new operationalization of critical realism for identifying and comparing causal mechanisms across practitioner case studies can be used: (1) to examine mechanisms leading to other actions and outcomes, including intervention success; and (2) to theorize and evaluate mixed methods research projects across disciplines, including their causal complexity and practical utility.

Title: Route and schedule adjustment for liner shipping service under anticipated disruption events
Authors: Shuaiqi Zhao, Hualong Yang, Zaili Yang, Yadong Wang
Abstract: This paper studies the route and schedule adjustment problem under anticipated disruption events in liner container shipping. We propose an innovative route and schedule adjustment strategy by jointly optimizing scheduled port removal, port sequencing, sailing speeds, and along-route port insertion to proactively recover the schedule under anticipated disruption events. The problem is formulated as a stochastic mixed-integer programming model, where the expected voyage profit is maximized. A scenario-based Benders decomposition algorithm is developed to solve the computational challenges in large-scale scenarios. Numerical experiments based on an actual shipping route validate and evaluate the applicability and effectiveness of the proposed model and solution algorithm. The numerical results also provide some meaningful management insights.

Title: Scheduling of cooperative twin yard cranes under bidirectional container flows
Abstract: Coordinating twin automated stacking cranes is essential for reducing bottlenecks in complex container yards. This study addresses the Flexible-Handover Twin-Crane Scheduling Problem, in which two non-passing yard cranes can transfer containers through inter-crane handovers. A handover splits a request at an intermediate location, allowing the remaining operation to be completed by the other crane. Although handovers can reduce empty travel and waiting, excessive use adds loading/unloading operations, making it crucial to decide which requests to hand over and where. Existing flexible-handover approaches mainly consider unidirectional container flows; we extend this setting to bidirectional container flows, where opposing crane movements generate frequent interference. We propose a two-stage framework that separates handover planning from detailed crane scheduling. The first stage uses an integer linear programming (ILP) model to construct a handover plan by optimizing a surrogate objective derived from a relaxed problem. The second stage determines sequences and interference-resolution priorities using exact or heuristic methods. Comparisons with an integrated mixed-integer programming model show the value of decomposition. Computational experiments demonstrate the robustness and superior schedule quality of the ILP-guided handover strategy. Operational analyses further show that the proposed strategy reduces not only makespan but also empty travel and waiting.

Title: When blockchain creates value? Financial leasing for the newsvendor under data source uncertainty
Authors: Wenyi Zhang, Feng Yang, Chen Bi, Ziming Wang, Dawei Wang, Stephen Shum
Abstract: Small and medium-sized manufacturers often lack liquidity to upgrade equipment needed for manufacturing transformation. Financial leasing provides a solution by separating ownership from control rights, but its efficiency is constrained by multi-dimensional data assessments and complex claiming processes. Blockchain technology may alleviate these concerns through more efficient and transparent verification processes, but its operational value remains uncertain when source data are distorted at the point of entry. We develop a game-theoretical model of a pull supply chain with a capital-constrained manufacturer, a retailer, and an external lessor to examine blockchain's role in financial leasing. The results show that data source uncertainty affects supply chain decisions in a non-monotonic way. Under moderate data source uncertainty and high claiming costs, blockchain adoption unexpectedly reduces default risk and increases overall supply chain profit. Furthermore, the manufacturer, even as a follower, can achieve higher profitability and improve system outcomes when the benefits of reduced transaction failure risk and lower financial costs outweigh the additional manipulation costs. These findings suggest that semi-transparency where moderate data source uncertainty remains, can sometimes outperform full transparency. In such cases, blockchain adoption offers a more effective balance between profit and risk in financial leasing systems.

Title: Collaborative routing problems in automated warehouses
Authors: Julian Golak, Lara Nehrke, Dominik Kress, Malte Fliedner
Abstract: The pick-and-drive system is a novel solution for warehouse automation. It integrates two types of autonomous mobile robots (AMRs). Storage and supply AMRs (S-AMRs) navigate to a storage area, where they lift unit loads and transport them to a disposition area. Picking AMRs (P-AMRs) move freely within this disposition area. They carry bins and meet S-AMRs to collect items from the unit loads attached to the S-AMRs by means of robotic arms. We take an operational perspective on the pick-and-drive system and focus on the problem of determining and scheduling meeting locations and sequences of the AMRs, so that all required items are picked. This setting is interpreted as a vehicle routing problem, where the customers (S-AMRs) collaborate with the vehicles (P-AMRs). We consider two objective functions, minimizing the total distance driven by the AMRs and minimizing the sum of completion times of the P-AMRs. We translate these routing problems into a mathematical framework and provide theoretical insights by examining a specific case where the potential meeting points lie along a line. For this scenario, we present an approximation algorithm for the case of minimizing the overall distance traveled and demonstrate that minimizing the sum of completion times is strongly NP-complete. Additionally, we prove strong NP-completeness of the general case when minimizing the overall distance traveled. Leveraging the structural insights, we develop heuristics that are evaluated in a numerical study. Our results highlight the potential impact of the system in practice.

Title: Semi-strong efficiency schemes and indexes for arbitrary technologies with compact dominating sets
Abstract: An efficiency scheme is a general optimization program that encompasses a large category of various specific efficiency indexes or measures. This theoretical paper establishes general results for three weak schemes: the input/output-variables scheme, the slack-variables scheme and the Russell-type scheme. The optimization programs offer a unified analysis of the entire category of efficiency indexes that are characterized by semi-strictly monotone improvement functions as objectives. It includes all common strong measures, but also many weak ones, especially the oriented (non-graph) slacks-based measures and the radial models of data envelopment analysis (DEA). The paper demonstrates that the three schemes produce equivalent, well-defined efficiency indexes when the improvement functions are specified accordingly. Several useful general theorems are proven for technologies with compact dominating sets of the assessed production activities. In general, the technologies do not need to satisfy any further properties on disposability, convexity, scalability, closeness or boundedness and may even be discrete. The findings are illustrated by numerical examples and are concretized by specific technologies and improvement functions that lead to the standard DEA models and to unoriented biradial efficiency indexes. In particular, the radial DEA models, known as path-based measures, are slacks-based as well.

Title: Pros and cons of service pooling considering price and congestion-sensitive service users
Authors: Baozhuang Niu, Yikang Hong, Lingfeng Wang
Abstract: With the rapid growth of service demand, both users and providers increasingly suffer utility and economic losses due to service congestion. To improve service quality, collaboration between competing service providers (service pooling hereafter) has been widely recognized as a potential mechanism to improve service efficiency through better resource utilization, although aligning incentives between competitors remains super challenging. This study examines the conditions under which service pooling is feasible for competing providers and compares them with separate operations. We find that pooling collaboration can help break the prisoner's dilemma that leads to significant customer congestion disutility in separate operations. However, pooling does not universally resolve congestion aversion as it generates more demand from enhanced service attraction. We further demonstrate that an appropriate revenue-sharing contract can achieve a Pareto improvement for both providers, rather than simply dividing profits based on capacity share. Nevertheless, an all-win outcome is unattainable. Such an outcome would require service pooling to increase both providers’ profits and consumer surplus while alleviating customer congestion disutility, but improving consumer surplus and alleviating congestion disutility are at odds.

Title: Parameterized complexity of scheduling problems in robotic process automation
Authors: Michal Dvořák, Antonín Novák, Přemysl Šůcha, Dušan Knop, Claire Hanen
Abstract: This paper studies the growing domain of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) problems. Motivated by scheduling problems arising in RPA, we study the parameterized complexity of the single-machine problem with precedence constraints, release times, and deadlines (i.e., the problem known as $1|\operatorname{prec},r_j,d_j|*$ in the three-field notation). We focus on parameters naturally linked to RPA systems, including chain-like precedences, the number of distinct processing times, and the structure of the time windows. We show that the problem is strongly XNLP-hard parameterized by the number of chains, even with only two prescribed processing times and two distinct time-window lengths. The problem remains XNLP-hard even under prec-consistent time windows. On the positive side, we obtain polynomial-time algorithm when all jobs share a single time-window length and FPT when the processing times, release times and deadlines are chain-uniform. We also show that the problem lies in XNLP when parameterized by the width of the precedence relation either when the instance is encoded in unary or the processing times are bounded.

Title: Integrated berth allocation and yard assignment with conflict-induced preemptive operations in bulk cargo ports
Authors: Jiefu Yang, Defeng Sun, Roberto Baldacci
Abstract: Frequent conflicts among stacking and reclaiming operations within the stockyard are a common challenge in the operation of bulk cargo ports. This paper incorporates the practically relevant setting of preemptive operations induced by stacking-reclaiming conflict into the integrated berth allocation and yard assignment problem (IBYP) in bulk cargo ports. Compact mathematical formulations and branch-and-price (B&P) solution methods tailored for preemptive stacking are developed to jointly optimize the interdependent decisions of vessel unloading sequences and storage locations, thereby improving operational efficiency in bulk materials. To speed up the column generation procedure at each branching node, we first disaggregate each pricing problem and introduce a set of easier surrogate subproblems. Then, a unified label-setting algorithm framework is developed to efficiently solve all surrogate subproblems sequentially, potentially leading to a negative reduced-cost column and thus skipping the time-consuming exact pricing procedure. Furthermore, by leveraging this label-setting procedure, we propose a greedy-and-repair heuristic that delivers fast, near-optimal solutions for practice and provides high-quality warm starts for B&P. In particular, we also investigate the non-preemptive special case and design a time-indexed dynamic programming algorithm for exact pricing, which is orders of magnitude faster than solver-based methods while preserving optimality. Experiments on instances derived from real port data demonstrate strong scalability and competitive runtimes on large-scale cases. We publicly release code, instance data, and detailed results to support future research.

Title: Robust e-waste recycling facility location problem with decision-dependent uncertain customer behavior
Abstract: The recycling of electronic waste (e-waste) has emerged as a critical global issue. Consumer recycling behavior plays a significant role in e-waste recycling, which directly influences return quantity and, consequently, the strategic design of recycling networks. While existing research has highlighted the impact of facility convenience on recycling willingness and considered uncertainty in return quantity separately, few studies have integrated both features. To bridge this gap, we tackle a robust facility location problem considering uncertain, location-dependent e-waste recycling behavior. We characterize the uncertainty in the proportion of customers’ choices between returning to a collection center and opting not to recycle, where the empirical value is estimated via the proportional choice rule. We propose a two-stage robust model featuring a norm-based decision-dependent uncertainty set. To solve this problem exactly, a Benders decomposition-based algorithm is developed and enhanced through various acceleration techniques. A case study utilizing real-world data from Tianjin, China, is conducted to derive managerial insights. We compare our decision-dependent proportional choice model with robust models that assume decision-independent recycling rate, the nearest choice rule, or centralized allocation rule, elucidating decision-making mechanisms when accounting for decision dependence and decentralized allocation. Our results demonstrate that neglecting these features yields suboptimal performance, manifested as diminished collection rates, underutilized capacity, and decreased profit. Robustness and sensitivity analyses are also conducted to provide managerial suggestions.

Title: Pattern-based adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm for roll-on roll-off vehicle routing problem
Authors: Sangil Han, Seungyeop Lee, Byung-In Kim
Abstract: The roll-on roll-off vehicle routing problem (RRVRP) is a variant of the waste collection vehicle routing problem (WCVRP), in which waste is not collected directly in a vehicle's body but stored in large containers, called roll-on roll-off containers. Vehicles transport these containers, either empty or full, between customers, yards for storage or supply, and landfills for disposal. Despite its practical importance, the RRVRP has received little scholarly attention compared to other WCVRP variants, such as residential and commercial waste collection problems. Moreover, existing studies simplify the problem by omitting several operational constraints to reduce complexity. This study investigates a more practical RRVRP by explicitly incorporating multiple operational constraints, including staging and thirteen service types, representing the most comprehensive set observed in real-world operations. To manage the resulting problem complexity, customers are classified as either pick-up or delivery stops based on the requested service, and a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation is developed. Because repeated visits are inevitable in the RRVRP, minimizing their frequency is critical for improving solution quality. To exploit the importance of reducing repeated visits, pre-generated trip patterns are introduced as the core building blocks of a pattern-based adaptive large neighborhood search (PALNS) algorithm. Computational experiments show that PALNS consistently outperforms the most comprehensive prior study and achieves significant improvements on large-scale problems. Comparisons with the MILP model confirm PALNS can find optimal solutions for small instances, while further experiments validate the effectiveness of both the trip pattern design and PALNS search strategy.

Title: Strategic adoption of 3D printing in multi-product supply chains: cost and capacity considerations
Abstract: This paper explores the integration of Additive Manufacturing (or 3D printing) into decentralized supply chains, focusing on the strategic decisions manufacturers and retailers make when facing capacity constraints. Using a Stackelberg game framework, we analyze how AM impacts traditional wholesale pricing across two scenarios. First, a manufacturer producing two distinct products and second, a case involving multiple products, each affected by AM's capacity limitations. For the first scenario, we derive sufficient conditions to find the equilibrium under a generic demand distribution, and for a uniform distribution, we fully derive the equilibrium and identify the critical cost threshold below which AM adoption is preferable. For the second scenario, we determine the conditions for the equilibrium, offering insights into the feasibility of AM relative to traditional manufacturing. Furthermore, we find that, contrary to some literature, even when AM incurs higher per-unit costs than traditional methods, it remains viable for some supply chains. However, limited AM capacity, particularly under high demand, may restrict its adoption, highlighting capacity constraints as a pivotal factor in AM decision-making. This study extends current research by examining multi-product and capacity-driven scenarios, providing valuable guidance for supply chain managers weighing the benefits of traditional manufacturing against those of AM.

Title: Tractable conditions for stochastic arbitrage in index options: Theory and evidence
Abstract: This study develops and applies tractable conditions for stochastic arbitrage in equity index options. The conditions, derived from the dual formulation of asset pricing restrictions, take the form of a relatively small set of linear inequalities and can incorporate bid-ask spreads and potential portfolio constraints. Because return distributions vary across volatility regimes, the inequalities must be tested conditionally, as unconditional tests cannot establish market inefficiency. Using the proposed arbitrage conditions and statistical dominance tests, we reexamine efficiency in one-month S&P 500 index options. Out-of-sample performance analysis points at arbitrage opportunities in high-volatility regimes, predominantly in the form of call front spreads. These opportunities often remain undetected unless both the volatility dependence of the market risk premium and the negative conditional skewness of index returns are taken into account. When volatility is low to moderate, no significant arbitrage opportunities are detected, consistent with higher pricing efficiency.

Title: Robust optimization for urban metro operations: Solving train timetabling and rolling stock circulation planning problems via facility location models
Authors: Housheng Zhou, Jianguo Qi, Lixing Yang, Hongyang Wang, Ran Yan
Abstract: The dynamic and uncertain nature of passenger demand presents significant challenges for the operation of urban metro systems. We study the robust train timetabling and rolling stock circulation planning problem under uncertain passenger demand to improve metro service stability and operational efficiency. Passenger demand is modeled using a continuous polyhedral uncertainty set to capture real-world variations. A novel modeling framework is introduced that reformulates the train timetabling and rolling stock circulation planning problem as a capacitated facility location problem, which enables more effective integration of complex operational decisions. To solve this problem efficiently, we propose a progressive optimality gap reduction algorithm, which iterates between a master problem and a subproblem. This algorithm accelerates early iterations and enables the computation of (near) optimal solutions for large-scale instances. Two sets of numerical experiments based on Beijing Metro Yizhuang Line and Xi'an Metro Line 6 show that our method outperforms traditional column and constraint generation and Benders decomposition algorithms. The robust model exhibits reliable performance compared with deterministic and stochastic models, producing high-quality operational plans under uncertainty.

Title: Optimization methods for assigning positions under multiple objectives
Abstract: We study a problem arising in the administration of staff positions in organizations with a fixed set of given positions, e.g., public institutions. When a new employee is hired, one or more of the available positions need to be (partially) assigned to her while respecting that they are already (partially) assigned to other staff members, possibly only during certain time intervals. Some positions are better suited for the new hire due to their associated pay grades or other administrative reasons. Furthermore, one seeks an assignment to only few positions and with only few changes over time. This yields a multi-objective optimization problem with a lexicographic objective function that models the mentioned considerations. Our problem can be seen as a scheduling problem with non-availability periods for the machines, where one of the objectives is to minimize the number of job preemptions. We derive structural insights into this problem and present three MIP-formulations based on them. Their solutions are optimal with respect to the three most important sub-objectives and optimal or near-optimal with respect to the least important sub-objective, respectively. We show that, using our formulations, we can find provably optimal solutions considerably faster than with a straightforward approach and near-optimal solutions even faster. In addition, we present a combinatorial algorithm for an important special case of the problem with even better running times. Our results form the backbone of an optimization tool we developed in collaboration with the administration of the Technical University of Munich where it is now used regularly whenever a new employee is hired.

Title: Refining demand accuracy for competing retailers
Authors: Meng Wu, Xiaoyin Cao, Tian Bai
Abstract: With recent advancements in technology significantly boosting forecasting accuracy, more retailers are investing in enhancing their forecasting capabilities to reduce demand uncertainty. This paper examines how refining demand accuracy affects demand competition between two retailers in a market where consumers could freely transact across multiple retailers. Employing a mean-preserving framework alongside a forecast correction approach to model demand accuracy improvement, we derive equilibrium demand accuracy, order quantities, and profits. Our findings suggest that while improving demand accuracy enhances supply–demand matching in the absence of competition—benefiting both low- and high-margin products—it can deteriorate supply–demand matching for medium–high margin products when retailers compete, potentially leading to profit losses. Importantly, enhanced demand accuracy does not always translate into a competitive advantage, challenging the prevailing view that greater accuracy tends to be beneficial.

Title: Repeated near misses and risk perception in newsvendor decisions
Authors: Florian Mathis Federspiel, Robin L. Dillon, Matthias Seifert
Abstract: Near misses are common in inventory management, yet little is known about how they influence decision makers’ perceptions and subsequent choices. We conceptualize an inventory near miss as a situation in which a stockout almost occurred but did not because of good fortune. Drawing on theories of near misses and risk perception, we argue that repeated near misses may be misinterpreted as evidence that an inventory strategy is safe and effective, thereby reducing perceived risk. Across two experimental studies, we find consistent evidence that repeated near misses lead decision makers to evaluate outcomes more positively, perceive inventory decisions as less risky, and become less willing to protect themselves against future losses. These effects are substantially attenuated when decision makers also experience repeated stockouts, suggesting that actual losses sensitize individuals to the risks obscured by repeated close calls. We further find evidence that these perceptual shifts are associated with reductions in order quantities, although these behavioral effects are more modest than the corresponding changes in risk perception. Together, our findings identify a previously unexplored mechanism through which repeated operational success without failure increase exposure to future inventory risk.

Title: Drone-enabled early diagnosis of human immunodeficiency virus in infants
Abstract: Africa, where only one-third of the population resides within 2 km of functioning routes, carries over 85% of the world's infant HIV burden. Drones hold great potential for transporting samples crucial to the early infant diagnosis of HIV in hard-hit regions. We consider a resource-limited environment where efficient sample transfer between scattered clinics and laboratories is indispensable. We first develop a mixed-integer non-linear program to model this complex supply chain and optimize the clinics-labs-transportation mode assignment. Despite highly non-linear objectives and constraints, we derive a tractable linear approximation. Using country-level data from Mozambique, we find that the bottleneck is caused by a confluence of prolonged transportation time, long waiting at the clinics until a transportation opportunity becomes available, and batching delay at the labs. A drone network relieves the bottleneck in three ways: (i) Drones significantly reduce sample transportation time; (ii) By eliminating waiting for transportation opportunities, drones remarkably decrease clinic delays while increasing dispatch frequencies; (iii) Increased dispatch frequency smooths clinic-lab sample flow which decreases the variation in random time between creation of two sample batches at labs. This, in turn, decreases the total lab delay. Our analysis also demonstrates that effectiveness-first designs compromise fairness less than equity-first designs do effectiveness. We finally find that optimizing fairness concentrates drones in villages rather than cities. Conversely, optimizing effectiveness allocates drones mainly to urban areas: i.e., in cities, drones impact many infants less while in villages, they impact fewer infants more. Therefore, the network structure should be tailored to the policy-maker's needs.

Title: An exact approach for the Train Single-Routing Selection Problem
Authors: Anna Livia Croella, Fabio Furini, Ivana Ljubić, Bianca Pascariu, Paola Pellegrini, Pablo San Segundo
Abstract: Given a set of train routes with route costs and a set of compatible route pairs with pairing costs, the Train Single-Routing Selection Problem (TSRSP) seeks to assign one route to each train, minimizing the total cost while ensuring pairwise compatibility among the selected routes. This problem is of significant practical relevance in rail traffic management and it is a special case of the Train Routing Selection Problem. We introduce a Binary Quadratic Programming formulation for the TSRSP and apply a linearization technique from the literature that requires a linear number of additional variables and constraints. This yields a novel and effective Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation for the TSRSP. By exploiting the structure of the problem, we further propose a method to strengthen the Linear Programming (LP) relaxation of the MILP formulation, substantially improving its computational performance. The resulting formulation is the first to efficiently solve real-world TSRSP instances to optimality within short computational times—instances that, until now, have only been addressed using heuristic approaches in the literature. Extensive computational results show that our MILP model consistently outperforms existing formulations, both in terms of computational time and the number of instances solved to optimality, primarily due to the strength of its LP relaxation.

Title: A parameterized complexity view on robust scheduling with budgeted uncertainty
Abstract: In this study, we investigate a robust single-machine scheduling problem under processing time uncertainty. The uncertainty is modeled using the budgeted approach, where each job has a nominal and deviation processing time, and the number of deviations is bounded by Γ . The objective is to minimize the number of tardy jobs where a job is considered tardy if there is some scenario in which it is completed after its due date. Since the problem is NP-hard in general, we focus on analyzing its tractability under the assumption that certain natural parameters of the problem are each bounded by a constant . We consider three parameters: the robustness parameter Γ , the number of distinct due dates in the instance, and the number of jobs with nonzero deviations. Using parameterized-complexity theory, we prove that the problem is W[1]-hard with respect to Γ , but can be solved in XP time with respect to the same parameter. With respect to the number of distinct due dates, we establish a stronger hardness result by showing that the problem remains NP-hard even when there are only two different due dates and is solvable in pseudo-polynomial time when the number of due dates is upper bounded by a constant. To complement these results, we show that the case of a common (single) due date reduces to a robust binary knapsack problem with equal item profits, a problem we prove to be solvable in polynomial time. Finally, we prove that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the number of jobs with nonzero deviations.

Title: Traffic diversion vs. self-built e-commerce: The content and e-commerce platform operations considering spillover effect and consumer loyalty
Authors: Nenggui Zhao, Youqing Wu, Qiang Wang, Jie Wu
Abstract: With the rapid development of content platforms (CPs), their operational modes have become increasingly diverse. Inspired by real-world practices, CPs such as Zhihu and Douyin can choose to collaborate with traditional e-commerce platforms (TPs) by directing traffic to them (traffic diversion mode), or establish their own e-commerce to sell products competitively with TPs while continuing to provide content creation (self-built e-commerce mode). To investigate the optimal mode choice, we model a supply chain consisting of one CP and one TP, where the CP can invest in content creation efforts that generate spillover effects on the TP. Our findings indicate that the CP will enter the market and operate in the traffic diversion mode only when a certain proportion of loyal consumers exists. Conversely, it will enter the market with content creation effort and operate in the self-built e-commerce mode only under negative spillover effects, specifically when it attracts consumers away from the TP to its own marketplace. Moreover, regardless of the CP's effort investment, both the CP and TP can achieve win-win outcomes under specific conditions in either operational mode. Additionally, the CP always benefits from efforts to enhance the content creation level, and it is consistently advantageous for the CP to operate in both modes simultaneously, whereas this is detrimental to the TP. Finally, the TP exerts effort (e.g., live streaming) in the diversion mode, benefiting itself but harming the CP, whereas it never exerts such effort in the self-built e-commerce mode.

Title: Interval optimization coupled with statistical feasibility robust optimization for hydrogen data center microgrid scheduling
Authors: Juntao Duan, Yuanzheng Li, Yang Li, Wei Yao, Lin Jiang, Yang Shi
Abstract: The growing power demand of data centers poses new challenges for its energy-efficient and robust operation. This paper investigates the scheduling of hydrogen-enabled data center microgrids with integrated renewable energy (RE) and hydrogen energy storage systems, under uncertainties in both renewable output and the equivalent meteorological index. To address these challenges, we propose a statistical feasibility-based robust interval optimization (SFRIO) framework that jointly minimizes operational cost and RE curtailment. The framework relaxes over-conservative constraints in traditional robust optimization by introducing statistical feasibility, and employs interval optimization with Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) reformulation. To reduce the computational burden associated with the dual variables in the KKT conditions while guaranteeing statistical feasibility, we further develop a statistical guarantee-based externally tangent (SGET) algorithm that constructs uncertainty sets involving fewer dual-related constraints. Numerical experiments validate that the proposed SFRIO framework, combined with the SGET algorithm, achieves improved solution quality and significantly reduced computational complexity. Simulation results show that the proposed method reduces the mean RE curtailment by 79.17%–87.19% compared with stochastic optimization, robust optimization, and statistical feasibility-based robust optimization, while incurring only minor constraint violations, and reduces the average computational time from over 3×104 seconds to several seconds.

Title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for path planning and storage policy in automated warehouses
Authors: Hanzhao Wu, Zhenyong Wu, Wenyan Song, Mark Goh, Yuan Wang
Abstract: Efficient routing of vehicles and storage assignment of stock in automated warehouses reduce the operational costs and improve service levels. However, most approaches to the Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) in warehouses treat routing and storage assignment separately, often overlooking the effects of three-dimensional layouts, item priorities, and real-time traffic congestion. This paper addresses the VRP in three-dimensional warehouse environments through a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) framework based on the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)-Attention network. The GRU-Attention network effectively captures complex temporal dependencies and dynamically identifies critical storage and routing features, which enables more adaptive and coordinated decisions in warehouse settings. This method jointly optimizes Automated Guided Vehicle (AGV) routing paths and item storage assignment while considering storage priorities, item turnover rates, and physical weights. In this framework, DRL handles path planning and storage assignment decisions. The proposed model integrates a dynamic storage allocation with an DRL architecture to minimize operational costs. Computational experiments are conducted on real-world and synthetic datasets across various storage policies and warehouse layouts. The experimental results suggest that the GRU-Attention network achieves reductions of 12.65%–19.60% in warehouse scenarios with 50 items compared to traditional and existing algorithms. Additionally, the semi-circle storage policy proves superior to the random, within-aisle, and across-aisle approaches by minimizing AGV travel distances and alleviating congestion within the warehouse. A comparative analysis of warehouse layouts reveals that designs without a central main aisle improve efficiency by minimizing bottlenecks. These findings offer practical insights for optimizing real-time, multi-objective warehouse management automated warehouse systems.

Title: A novel equilibrium efficient frontier for evaluating network decision-making units with shared undesirable fixed-sum outputs
Authors: Tao Ding, Jingfang Zhang, Ping Wang, Qingxian An
Abstract: Data envelopment analysis (DEA) methods for fixed-sum outputs have received increasing attention in recent years. Among them, the generalized equilibrium efficient frontier DEA method (GEEFDEA) has gained widespread application due to its computational convenience. However, its uniform weight assumption is inconsistent with the differentiated weighting principle of traditional DEA models, which simplifies the structure of the generated equilibrium efficient frontier (EEF), limiting its ability to accurately reflect real-world production processes. Although recent studies have addressed the uniform weighting issue in single-stage systems, their approaches are not readily applicable to more complex systems. To address this limitation, this study develops a novel evaluation approach for network decision-making units (DMUs) with shared undesirable fixed-sum outputs. The proposed approach extends the relaxation of the uniform weight assumption to the two-stage network setting, allowing DMUs to select their preference weights when constructing the EEF. Depending on the presence of a central authority, EEF construction models are developed under centralized and decentralized scenarios. After obtaining the adjusted DMUs, the adjusted extreme efficient DMUs are further identified to form the corresponding locally supported extreme efficient DMU set (LSEEDS) for evaluating the original DMUs. Notably, the model for constructing the EEF is nonlinear. We demonstrate that it can be linearized when there is a single fixed-sum output and propose a parametric iterative algorithm for the case of multiple fixed-sum outputs. Finally, we verify the proposed algorithm through a numerical example and apply the approach to evaluate energy production-utilization efficiency in 30 Chinese provincial administrative regions.

Title: On the approximability of covering problem under a quadratic constraint
Authors: Trung Thanh Nguyen, Khaled Elbassioni, Areg Karapetyan, Majid Khonji
Abstract: Motivated by recent applications in power and energy scheduling, this work investigates a class of nonlinear Knapsack problems, called the covering problem under a constant-rank quadratic constraint. In this problem, the constraint is represented as a sum of a constant number of squared linear functions. Since the problem is NP-hard, existing research has primarily focused on developing polynomial-time approximation algorithms with provable performance guarantees. In this work, we advance this line of research by presenting the first polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for the case where the constraint consists of the sum of two squares of nonnegative linear functions, thereby significantly improving upon the previously best-known quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme (QPTAS) for this setting. For the more general case involving a constant number of linear functions, we present an n-approximation algorithm and establish the existence of a resource-augmentation algorithm. In addition, we conduct numerical experiments to demonstrate the practical relevance and effectiveness of the proposed approximation scheme.

Title: The role of suppliers’ sustainability in improving airline efficiency and financial performance: An Integrated Approach
Authors: Fahimeh Chomachaei, Hirofumi Fukuyama, Sepideh Kaffash
Abstract: A substantial body of literature has examined the link between a firm's sustainability and its operational and financial outcomes. However, limited attention has been given to how supplier sustainability is associated with the performance of buying firms. This study addresses that gap by empirically investigating the relationship between supplier sustainability and both airline efficiency and financial performance, using a unique panel dataset covering U.S. airlines and their suppliers. We also propose a novel framework that integrates the ESG pillars into a Network Data Envelopment Analysis model to assess airline efficiency. By embedding ESG pillars as model outputs, our approach enables a more comprehensive evaluation of both operational and sustainability efficiency, offering deeper insights into sustainability-driven performance. The results show that airlines benefit from more sustainable suppliers, improving both efficiency and financial outcomes. Among ESG dimensions, the Environmental pillar is most strongly associated with airline efficiency, whereas the Governance pillar shows the strongest relationship with financial performance. These findings offer key managerial insights, showing that partnering with ESG-conscious suppliers boosts both operational and financial performance. From a policy standpoint, the study highlights the need for greater ESG transparency and supportive regulations to integrate sustainability across aviation supply chains. The results provide managerial guidance for integrating supplier ESG performance into sourcing and evaluation decisions and offer policy insights for encouraging sustainability-driven partnerships in the aviation sector. By linking ESG and DEA methods, this research contributes theoretically and provides practical guidance for sustainable decision-making.

Title: Algorithms for traceability adoption in complex supply chain networks
Authors: Luis A. Guardiola, Ana Meca, Greys Sošić
Abstract: Today’s supply chains are increasingly complex, creating challenges in achieving transparency and leading to issues such as recalls, reputational risks, susceptibility to disruptions, and compliance difficulties. Legislative measures like the California Transparency in Supply Chains Act and the U.S. Dodd-Frank Act require companies to disclose efforts addressing human trafficking, slavery, and the use of conflict minerals within their supply chains. Emerging technologies such as blockchain and artificial intelligence offer promising solutions for enhancing supply chain traceability and transparency. However, achieving comprehensive traceability requires participation from most, if not all, supply chain members to avoid undetected irregularities. While the benefits of traceability are clear, implementation entails costs. Some participants may find the benefits outweigh these costs, but to encourage broader adoption, downstream firms might consider subsidizing upstream partners. Supply chain leaders, such as Inditex, are often assumed to pursue traceability to enhance transparency and reduce risk, and may take on a leadership role in promoting and implementing such a subsidization model. This paper employs a cooperative game framework to explore scenarios within supply chain networks, aiming to distribute the benefits of technology implementation and foster widespread adoption. Starting with a basic supply chain modeled as a tree graph, we propose an algorithm to identify allocations that promote technology adoption. The analysis then extends to broader supply chain networks, introducing an algorithm that simplifies the problem and reduces dimensionality for efficient analysis. When the full network is not immediately solvable, we propose two complementary interventions: game reduction, for which the exact optimization problem is NP-hard and for which we provide both an exact algorithm and a polynomial-time min-cut heuristic, and benefit augmentation, which we formulate as a polynomial-time linear program that identifies the minimum additional benefit or cost reduction required for full adoption. We conclude with a simulation that applies the proposed framework to a larger, hypothetical apparel supply chain inspired by Inditex.

Title: The interplay between arm’s length regulation and innovation investment: Implications for Co-opetition incentives
Authors: Wei Li, Dan Luo, Jing Chen, Xuan Zhao
Abstract: This study investigates the incentives of a competitive supplier (CS) and an original equipment manufacturer (OEM) to engage in a co-opetitive supply partnership. The CS is an internally decentralized firm comprising a component supply subsidiary and an end-product retail subsidiary. It chooses whether to supply a key component to the OEM, while the OEM chooses between the CS and a non-competitive supplier (NS). Both suppliers can invest in innovation to increase component quality. In setting wholesale prices, the CS may offer its retail subsidiary a discount, which is, however, restricted under the arm's length regulation (ALR). By exploring the interaction between the ALR and innovation investment, we show that without the ALR, innovation investment can shift the equilibrium from competition to co-opetition, as the CS's higher innovation level enhances its attractiveness to the OEM relative to the NS. In contrast, under the ALR, while co-opetition is the equilibrium without innovation investment, such investment can lead to a competition equilibrium. This shift occurs because supplying the OEM may reduce the CS's profit, even though the OEM consistently prefers to source from the CS. Our analysis therefore reveals that the ALR fundamentally reshapes the co-opetition game by reallocating decision-making power from the OEM to the CS. Moevoer, we show that the ALR's impact on the CS's innovation level and firms’ profits varies with investment efficiency and market competition intensity, potentially leading to lose-lose or win-win outcomes for both the CS and the OEM.

Title: Robust optimization of prepack-based inventory control and demand fulfillment for two-echelon e-commerce distribution networks
Authors: Song Jiu, Chengjie Li, Shangqing Luo
Abstract: E-commerce retailers are increasingly establishing forward distribution centers to preposition inventory for rapid delivery. Benefiting from economics of scale, prepacks that bundle stock keeping units with fixed batch sizes, have been widely used in retail supply chains. However, their inherent rigidity and discrete handling requirement introduce significant complexity for operating two-echelon distribution networks. Motivated by this practical challenge, this paper studies the joint optimization of inventory and fulfillment using retail prepacks over a multi-period horizon. In each period, multifaceted operations including prepack procurement, prepack unpacking, inventory allocation, and demand fulfillment must be seamlessly integrated to minimize the expected total cost. Given the distributional ambiguity, we formulate a distributionally robust optimization model based on partial demand information. To solve the model efficiently, we propose a two-phase decomposition framework. Phase 1 applies an optimal static rule for integer prepack decisions under a target-oriented reformulation. We also develop an exact binary search algorithm to enhance the computational efficiency for the deterministic counterpart. Fixing prepack decisions, Phase 2 utilizes a linear decision rule to approximate adaptive continuous decisions. We evaluate the performance, benefit, and practical applicability of implementing the proposed framework through extensive numerical experiments using both synthetic data and real-world demand data from JD.com. Some technical and managerial insights are derived from the numerical results.

Title: Branch-and-cut for mixed-integer robust chance-constrained optimization with discrete distributions
Authors: Daniela Bernhard, Frauke Liers, Michael Stingl
Abstract: We study robust chance-constrained problems with mixed-integer design variables and ambiguity sets consisting of discrete probability distributions. Allowing some classes of non-convex constraint functions, we develop a branch-and-cut framework using scenario-based cutting planes to generate lower bounds. The cutting planes are obtained by exploiting the classical big-M reformulation of the chance-constrained problem in the case of discrete distributions. Furthermore, we include the calculation of initial feasible solutions based on a bundle method applied to an approximation of the original problem into the branch-and-cut procedure. We conclude with a detailed discussion about the practical performance of the branch-and-cut framework with and without initial feasible solutions. In our experiments we focus on gas transport problems under uncertainty and provide a comparison of our method with solving the classical reformulation directly for various real-world sized instances.

Title: Logic-based Benders decomposition for additive manufacturing scheduling with sequence-dependent setup times
Authors: Wenjing Ma, Jian Chen, Yaowen Sang, Yingqian Zhang, Yaoxin Wu
Abstract: This paper studies an additive manufacturing (AM) scheduling problem on unrelated machines with sequence-dependent setup times, where the objective is to minimize the overall makespan. The problem requires simultaneously grouping parts into batches, assigning batches to machines, and determining the processing sequence of batches on each machine. To address this problem, three mixed-integer programming (MIP) formulations are developed and strengthened by valid inequalities, symmetry-breaking constraints, and analytical bounds to improve computational efficiency. In view of the problem's complexity, a logic-based Benders decomposition (LBBD) algorithm is proposed to decompose the problem into a master problem (MP) for part grouping and assignment, and multiple subproblems (SPs) for batch sequencing on individual AM machines. Each SP is formulated as an asymmetric traveling salesman problem (ATSP) and solved using the Dantzig-Fulkerson-Johnson (DFJ) formulation. Based on the SP solutions, optimality Benders cuts are dynamically generated and added to the MP to strengthen the solution process. In addition, a local search heuristic is embedded in the LBBD framework to produce high-quality feasible solutions from incumbent MP solutions. Computational experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed formulations and enhancements, verify the efficiency of the LBBD algorithm, and further reveal the impact of sequence-dependent setup times on the makespan.

Title: Authorization or outsourcing in OEM–TPR remanufacturing: The impact of grandfathering and benchmarking in emissions trading
Authors: Xiqiang Xia, Zhaohan Huang, Victor Shi, Junsong Bian, Xuefeng Shao
Abstract: In emissions trading, carbon allowance allocation rules shape the carbon compliance costs of original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), thereby affecting how they organize remanufacturing with third-party remanufacturers (TPRs). This study examines OEM–TPR remanufacturing under two common allocation mechanisms, namely grandfathering (based on historical emissions) and benchmarking (based on sector-wide standards), and compares two remanufacturing modes, authorization and outsourcing. We develop four analytical models to examine how allocation rules and remanufacturing modes affect pricing, production, recycling, firms’ profits, consumer surplus, and environmental outcomes. Our main findings are as follows. First, OEMs consistently prefer outsourcing because it gives them greater control over remanufacturing and improves profitability. Second, TPRs benefit more from grandfathering than from benchmarking. Authorization is preferable when both consumer preference for remanufactured products and the recovery scale are low, whereas outsourcing dominates when both are high. Third, benchmarking improves consumer surplus and expands new product sales but weakens remanufactured product demand and recycling incentives. In contrast, grandfathering raises product prices, yet shifts demand toward remanufactured products, increases recycling, and reduces environmental pollution. Finally, outsourcing better aligns OEM profitability with government environmental objectives. Our model extensions and further analyses show that a contract combining revenue sharing, cost sharing, and a fixed fee can achieve coordination. Furthermore, our main findings remain robust when both OEMs and TPRs are subject to carbon regulations.

Title: Impact of social preferences on demand information sharing and corporate social responsibility investments in a triadic supply chain
Authors: Junlin Chen, Chunyue Deng, Yizhi Wang, Yue Li
Abstract: We study a triadic supply chain with a retailer and two complementary suppliers. The retailer is closer to the market and can privately observe the proportion of prosocial consumers, which is reported to the suppliers. The suppliers then independently decide on CSR investment levels, which generate positive demand externalities and expand the prosocial market. We consider supply chain members’ social preferences, including the retailer's lying cost when manipulating shared information and the suppliers’ trust in the retailer's report. The results show that: (1) Information sharing influences suppliers’ CSR investment decisions only when trust and credibility shape their responses to reported information, relative to the rational benchmark. (2) Outcomes are determined by the trade-off between distortion and spillover effects, as trust amplifies both the impact of misreporting and the demand spillovers from CSR investments. (3) A win–win–win outcome arises when the retailer's lying cost is high, and suppliers’ trust is high and aligned, enabling CSR spillovers to be effectively internalized. (4) An extended analysis shows that supplier cooperation and peer-induced fairness concerns, although driven by different mechanisms, both mitigate free-riding and can improve the profit of the overall supply chain.

Title: Product customization and returns: A supply chain perspective
Authors: Qing Zhang, Yan Zhang, Bing Li
Abstract: While advanced technologies enable firms to offer customized products that reduce mismatch before purchase, consumers may still request returns due to dissatisfaction after purchase, highlighting a critical yet underexplored issue. This paper develops a unified framework in which customization mitigates pre-purchase mismatch, whereas return services address post-purchase mismatch. By incorporating an endogenous customization degree into game-theoretic models, we investigate the interaction between customization and returns under one-echelon and two-echelon supply chain structures. Our analysis yields three main results. First, the manufacturer tends to choose a high customization degree when post-purchase mismatch is low, but as pre-purchase mismatch intensifies, the customization degree may first rise to mitigate mismatch and then fall once customization investment becomes excessive. Moreover, both the return service provision and the retailer involvement weaken the manufacturer's incentive to invest in customization. Second, the manufacturer is consistently incentivized to offer customized products in both one-echelon and two-echelon supply chains. Unlike a one-echelon supply chain where the manufacturer withdraws return services under low consumers’ return costs, the retailer involvement can make the manufacturer favor return services for customized products. Additionally, the manufacturer's customization strategy can generate mutually beneficial outcomes for both supply chain members, regardless of whether the retailer offers return services. Third, when return services are transferred to the retailer, the two-echelon supply chain may become more profitable for the manufacturer by leveraging its specialized allocation of responsibilities. These findings provide insights into how firms coordinate customization and return strategies and allocate related responsibilities across different supply chain structures.

Title: Supplier encroachment and retail service effort: The role of carry-over effect and strategic inventory
Authors: Faizul Haque, Sumanta Basu, Peeyush Mehta, Vishal Bansal
Abstract: The growing prevalence of direct-to-consumer channels has intensified supplier encroachment concerns for retailers. While retail service effort is commonly used to stimulate demand and deter supplier encroachment, its effects often persist across selling seasons through a carry-over effect. Despite its practical relevance, the role of the carry-over effect in shaping supplier encroachment decisions remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we examine how the carry-over effect of retail service effort influences supplier encroachment and the effectiveness of retailer deterrence strategies. We develop a two-period Stackelberg game-theoretic model between a supplier and a retailer, informed by consumer survey data and practitioner interviews with retailer and supplier firms. Our results show that retail service effort does not always deter supplier encroachment. When the carry-over effect is sufficiently strong, the supplier can partially free-ride on the retailer's past service effort, making supplier encroachment attractive even at higher direct selling costs. We further find that strategic inventory complements service effort only when the retailer carries a limited amount of inventory across selling periods. Interestingly, moderate order quantity restrictions imposed by the supplier facilitate supplier encroachment, whereas excessive restrictions suppress demand and reduce the supplier's incentive to encroach. Finally, under upstream supplier competition, supplier encroachment becomes more likely when competing products are highly substitutable, and the carry-over effect is strong. Overall, our findings demonstrate that the carry-over effect is a critical driver of supplier encroachment decisions and alters the effectiveness of traditional retailer deterrence mechanisms.

Title: A large neighborhood search matheuristic for the two-dimensional guillotine flexible stock size cutting stock problem
Abstract: This paper introduces the two-dimensional flexible stock size cutting stock problem (2D-FSSCSP), where stocks of flexible (bounded) sizes are available. The problem consists of cutting a set of smaller rectangular items, each with given dimensions, from a set of larger rectangular plates with bounded height and width. Cutting patterns are restricted to two-stage non-exact guillotine cuts and are subject to two-dimensional constraints. The objective is to minimize the total amount of used materials. The 2D-FSSCSP is first formulated using three mixed integer linear programming models: item-, strip-, and pattern-based. Different dominance properties and lower and upper bounds of the 2D-FSSCSP were considered to reduce the search space. To handle large-scale instances, a large neighborhood search (LNS) is employed. The LNS framework eliminates a few patterns and reconstructs new ones by solving subproblems such as the minimum waste pattern problem. We evaluate these approaches using newly generated instances. The numerical results enable us to analyze and evaluate the impact of different modeling strategies for managing stock-size flexibility in this variant of the 2D-CSP.

Title: Integrated workforce assignment in identical parallel machine scheduling with compressible setup times
Authors: Saurabh Chandra, Debashish Jena, Atanu Chaudhuri
Abstract: In this paper we present a problem of scheduling identical parallel processes with setup times dependent on workforce assignment. The objective is to minimize the workforce requirement in meeting a specified production demand. The problem considered has many practical applications, such as assigning gig workers to customer deliveries, in large scale baking operations in the confectionary industry, printing presses operating multiple identical printers, agent-assisted automated kiosks in service centers, etc. We present a case study of a production unit dealing with the assignment of temporary workforce to setting up baking processes across multiple identical ovens in malt-based beverage mix production. We present an integer programming formulation for the problem and a novel constraint programming formulation. We prove that this problem is NP-hard. To solve real-size problem instances, we propose a decomposition strategy to split the problem into two parts- machine scheduling aimed at minimizing the required workforce size followed by a satisfiability problem assigning workforce to the pre-scheduled tasks. Consequently, a three-step solution heuristic based on a combination of mathematical programming and constraint programming is developed. Analysis related to the impact of required capacity utilization on workforce size and worker utilization, relationship of the target objective with the objective of makespan minimization and the impact of break policies on the stated objective and worker utilization level are presented to generate insights.

Title: Exact clique number manipulation via edge interdiction
Authors: Yi Zhou, Haoyu Jiang, Chenghao Zhu, André Rossi
Abstract: The Edge Interdiction Clique Problem (EICP) aims to remove at most k edges from a graph so as to minimize the size of the largest clique in the remaining graph. This problem captures a fundamental question in graph manipulation: which edges are structurally critical for preserving large cliques? Such a problem is also motivated by practical applications including protein function maintenance and image matching. Because of its bilevel nature, the EICP is considerably more difficult than most classical NP-hard optimization problems like the maximum clique problem. Existing approaches rely on general mixed-integer bilevel linear programming solvers or reformulate the problem into a single-level mixed integer linear program. However, they are still not scalable when the graph size and interdiction budget k grow. To overcome this, we investigate new mixed integer linear formulations, which recast the problem into a sequence of parameterized Edge Blocker Clique Problems (EBCP). This perspective decomposes the original problem into simpler subproblems and enables tighter modeling of clique-related inequalities. Furthermore, we propose a two-stage exact algorithm called Clique Edge Manipulation Algorithm (CEMA) that first applies problem-specific reduction techniques to shrink the graph and then solves the reduced problem using a tailored branch-and-cut framework. Extensive computational experiments on maximum clique benchmark graphs, large real-world sparse networks, and random graphs demonstrate that CEMA consistently outperforms existing approaches.

Title: Authorized remanufacturing and financing for capital-constrained contract manufacturers under cap-and-trade regulation
Abstract: Motivated by carbon-peaking and carbon-neutrality targets, governments implement cap-and-trade (CAT) regulations to curb emissions. Authorized remanufacturing (AR) is a key strategy for the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) to balance environmental sustainability and profitability. We develop a Stackelberg game between an OEM and a capital-constrained contract manufacturer (CM) to study how CAT regulation shapes AR supply chains and characterize equilibrium production, emissions-reduction level, and financing under bank financing and trade credit. Our main results are: (i) OEMs can charge higher authorization fees under the bank financing regime, which mitigates the cannibalization effect from authorized remanufacturing; (ii) the CM's financing choice is jointly shaped by the interest rate and the carbon trading price; bank financing is preferred over a wide region because it better balances emissions-reduction investment and AR output; and (iii) under comparable financing rates, the financing channel does not change the optimal emissions-reduction level, but it affects net emissions through the remanufacturing scale. An extension incorporating outsourced remanufacturing (OR) reveals that market acceptance of remanufactured products critically influences the OEM's preferred remanufacturing mode. When market acceptance is low, the OEM prefers the AR mode under both bank financing and trade credit. When market acceptance is high, the OEM's choice between AR and OR depends on the carbon trading price and the financing regime.

Title: More is less? The newcomer port’s service diversification under hinterland-transshipment competition and government subsidies
Authors: Baozhuang Niu, Hongzhi Wang, Kee-hung Lai, Dong Yang
Abstract: Ports mainly collect revenue from hinterland and transshipment services. For ports that are newcomers to a specific service market, one natural question is: Would focusing on a single service be better than providing both services? In this study, based on tri-port competition analysis with two incumbents, we reveal interesting “2 < 1″ zones in which providing two services (i.e., hinterland and transshipment services) yields lower profitability for the newcomer port than focusing on a single service (i.e., hinterland service only). We highlight the role of government subsidies in shaping the newcomer port's incentive to provide two services, which may also benefit customer surplus. We also identify the conditions under which government subsidies either fail to promote port diversification or impose excessive fiscal burdens. To make matters worse, uncoordinated subsidies across local governments may generate the prisoner's dilemma, where both governments incur high subsidy costs but achieve poorer performance than under the no-subsidy scenario. Therefore, our work shows the significance of coordinated regional governance within port systems, differentiated port service operations, and targeted government subsidies.

Title: Single-machine scheduling with learning dates
Authors: Yiwei Jiang, Haibo Lin, Jianming Dong, T.C.E. Cheng, Min Ji
Abstract: This paper studies a single-machine scheduling problem with learning dates to minimize the makespan. Each job has a distinct learning date, and its processing time differs before and after the learning date. All jobs have the same learning ratio, i.e., the ratio of the processing time after learning to that before learning is ρ(0<ρ<1) for each job. We consider two variants of the problem according to whether the jobs are preemptible, namely the preemptive model and the non-preemptive model. For the preemptive case, we develop an O(nlogn)-time solution algorithm with at most one preemption. For the non-preemptive case, we show that the problem is NP-hard and design an approximation algorithm whose worst-case ratio is no greater than [Formula presented], with a time complexity of O(nlogn).

Title: An oracle-based approach for price-setting problems in logistics
Authors: N. Pommerening, M. Hügging, D. Henke, C. Buchheim, U. Clausen
Abstract: We study a price-setting variant of the hub location problem where a shipment service provider not only builds a transportation network, but also sets the prices of shipments on each possible transportation relation. In doing so, it must account for the customers’ reaction, as their decision to purchase transport services may depend on their individual budget or on the prices of competing offers. The objective is to maximize the generated profit. This problem can be modeled as a bilevel program. Since the classical hub location problem is well known to be NP-hard, we focus on the additional complexity induced by the price-setting decisions. We propose an oracle-based approach that assumes availability of an algorithm for the prize-collecting variant of the hub location problem. Our main contribution is an efficient reduction of our price-setting problem to the latter oracle, showing that it is not significantly harder. We achieve the reduction through a novel Lagrangian decomposition approach in which the optimal multipliers can be determined analytically. Moreover, we prove that strong duality holds. Computational experiments highlight the advantages of our method. It significantly outperforms standard solvers applied to a compact single-level MIP formulation as well as a general purpose bilevel LP solver. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm can be adapted to numerous price-setting variants of classical combinatorial optimization problems, even beyond logistics.

Title: Combinatorial auctions for green supplier selection and bundled order allocation
Authors: Sadeque Hamdan, Chefi Triki, Simona Mancini
Abstract: Outsourcing has become a key strategy for firms seeking efficiency and competitiveness, leading to a growing emphasis on effective supplier selection and order allocation (SSOA). While combinatorial auctions have been recognized as a powerful tool for procurement, their integration into multi-sourcing SSOA decisions remains underexplored. This paper develops a novel Winner Determination Problem model that generalizes prior work by allowing suppliers to submit multiple, potentially even overlapping, bundles. We also propose four original heuristic approaches inspired by Kernel Search, tailored to address both the cost and environmental sustainability dimensions of procurement.
