Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the strong performance of the proposed methods, with the weighted frequency-based rarity and value density heuristic achieving the best trade-off between solution quality and computational time. Managerial insights reveal that auction-based SSOA mechanisms can achieve significant cost savings compared to traditional models due to economies of scope, and highlight critical trade-offs between supplier diversification, cost efficiency, and risk management. This study advances the field by offering both methodological and practical contributions, with future research directions suggested in stochastic and dynamic auction settings.

Title: Maintenance schedules by conditional inference trees
Authors: Shixuan Wang, Aris A. Syntetos, Simme Douwe P. Flapper, Carla Di Cairano-Gilfedder, Mohamed M. Naim
Abstract: Maintenance represents a large part of the total operational costs of vehicle fleets. We perform reliability analysis based on a dataset of maintenance records from the fleet of light commercial vehicles used by BT Fleet Solutions and their customers (Post Office, National Grid, etc.). In our preliminary analysis, we first verify that reliability deteriorates with age, mileage, and the number of historical maintenance activities, as we also find heterogeneous behavior associated with different geographic locations and vehicle makes. Drawing on this background, we propose a dynamic maintenance policy. We build it on a data-driven method, Conditional Inference Trees (CIT), which provides a good balance between applicability (with loose assumptions) and interpretability (being a “white-box” solution). Since there is no closed-form solution for maintenance costs based on tree-structured reliability, we develop a simulation-based method to estimate the maintenance cost for the CIT-based maintenance policy, along with a new backward optimization procedure for the operational parameters. Based on the cost analysis, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the CIT-based maintenance policy in comparison to two prevalent maintenance policies. Finally, we identify opportunities for further improvements in the operations of the company, and for maintenance operations in general.

Title: Distributionally robust bilevel optimization for last-mile delivery with delivery options and demand steering
Authors: Xiaoshuai Peng, Lele Zhang, Cui Zhao
Abstract: The rapid growth of e-commerce and increasing expectations for expedited shipping have intensified last-mile delivery challenges, especially for home delivery. Many operators offer financial incentives to encourage customers to accept delayed delivery or alternative delivery modes such as pickup-point collection. While combining these levers can further improve efficiency, determining incentives that are both operationally beneficial and acceptable to customers remains challenging, particularly under uncertain parcel demand. We study this problem by proposing a distributionally robust bilevel model in which the operator determines financial incentives and the resulting a priori delivery plan, while customers decide whether to accept these offers. Exploiting the model structure, we develop a three-level matheuristic capable of solving realistically sized instances. Using this framework, we derive managerial insights into when postponement, delivery-mode switching, or their combination is most effective, and how their relative value varies with key factors including demand level, parcel-size variability, vehicle capacity, compensation, and customer spatial distribution. Numerical results show that joint incentive–routing optimization across the two flexibility levers yields substantial cost reductions relative to single-lever and no-flexibility benchmarks. The proposed matheuristic consistently outperforms existing algorithmic baselines on instances adapted from standard two-echelon last-mile delivery benchmarks and scales to large instances where those baselines fail. We further show that the approach extends to related two-echelon inventory- and production–routing problems.

Title: From cognitive maps to value trees. Supporting conflict transformation and management
Authors: H. Berkay Tosunlu, Joseph H.A. Guillaume, Alexis Tsoukiàs
Abstract: Conflict transformation and management are complex decision processes with extremely high stakes, benefiting greatly from formal decision support approaches. This paper presents a structured methodology to enhance conflict management by integrating Cognitive Maps (CM) and Value Trees (VT), two prominent tools in Problem Structuring. In doing so we introduce a methodological innovation introducing a formal procedure (an algorithm) transforming cognitive maps to value trees when this is possible. This transformation helps revealing decision drivers and allows the design of actionable policies. The paper presents a simulation of supporting a conflict management process concerning the protracted Turkish-Kurdish conflict. We show that our procedure allows to share the conflicting drivers and thus, facilitates the identification of common ground potentially leading to the design of policy alternatives. We show that our findings have a much wider validity since they allow to enhance decision support tools with advanced problem structuring facilities and algorithms.

Title: A novel dynamic programming approach for minimum fleet size in electric bus transit lines
Authors: Liming Li, Jinpeng Liang, Chenghao Zhuang, Zaihan Gao, Yue Bao
Abstract: The widespread adoption of electric buses (EBs) in urban transit systems offers significant environmental benefits but poses operational challenges due to their shorter driving ranges and longer charging times compared to conventional diesel buses. Optimizing the EB fleet size is crucial for transit operators to reduce capital expenditure while maintaining service reliability. This paper investigates the minimum fleet size problem in EB transit lines, aiming to determine the minimum number of EBs and generate corresponding scheduling decisions to complete a pre-determined timetable. We formulate the problem as a mixed-integer programming model and prove its complexity and structural properties. We then develop a novel heuristic dynamic programming-structure-based (HDP) approach that sequentially adds EBs to the transit line and determines their scheduling to minimize the fleet size required to cover the remaining trips. Extensive numerical experiments using both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our HDP approach in minimizing fleet size, optimizing computational efficiency, and maximizing vehicle utilization compared to benchmark approaches from the literature and practice. The results highlight the promising performance of our approach in determining the minimum EB fleet size and generating efficient EB scheduling results for transit operations.

Title: Strategic incentives and efficiency: A non-cooperative approach to Data Envelopment Analysis
Authors: Juan Aparicio, Victor J. España, Juan Carlos Gonçalves-Dosantos
Abstract: In competitive environments, organizations face increasing pressure to optimize operational efficiency while balancing limited resources and strategic objectives. This paper presents a novel incentive-based framework that integrates Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) with Game Theory to evaluate and enhance the efficiency of Decision-Making Units (DMUs) under non-cooperative scenarios. The proposed methodology incorporates both technical efficiency and strategic decision-making by considering Nash equilibria to model the interactions among DMUs competing for limited shared revenue. Two incentive models are introduced: (i) a model rewarding technical efficiency and (ii) a model driven by incremental effort. To evaluate the cost of projecting each DMU onto the frontier, this paper also develops a DEA projection approach based on the cost per unit of input reduction or output increase. This versatile approach can be applied across sectors such as corporate, healthcare, education, and public administration, promoting a culture of continuous improvement and better use of resources.

Title: Formulations and an exact algorithm for the Traveling Thief Problem
Authors: Tomás Kapancioglu, Raquel Bernardino, Maria Cândida Mourão
Abstract: The Traveling Thief Problem (TTP) is a combinatorial optimization problem that combines two well-known NP-hard problems: the Traveling Salesman Problem and the Knapsack Problem. The thief must perform a Hamiltonian circuit on a set of nodes, starting and ending at a depot. Items are scattered across the nodes and may be collected as long as the knapsack capacity is not exceeded. Collecting items slows the thief down, and a renting rate is paid for each time unit taken to complete the circuit. The objective is to maximize the profit given by the difference between the value of the collected items and the total rent. This paper proposes mixed-integer linear programming formulations and an exact algorithm to solve the TTP. The computational experiment revealed that the algorithm performs well in instances with similar item weights, and new optimal values are reported for 15 benchmark instances, including two instances with over 50 nodes.

Title: Industrial incentive design for domestic manufacturing and skill diffusion: Comparing production-linked and cost-sharing schemes
Abstract: Emerging economies increasingly use industrial incentive schemes to promote domestic manufacturing and build technological capabilities. We study two such schemes: a Production Linked Incentive (PLI), under which firms receive subsidies based on sales from local production, and a Cost Sharing Incentive (CSI), which subsidizes firms’ quality-enhancing investments in the local economy. We develop a stylized model featuring a firm and a social planner. The firm invests in quality improvement at the local production site, which increases consumer demand and generates social value through workforce skill development and local technology diffusion. We compare the two incentive schemes in terms of quality effort, pricing, firm profit, and the social planner's net utility. Our analysis reveals that high skill-diffusion benefits or a large consumer market make the CSI scheme more attractive to the social planner, as it generates higher net utility than the PLI scheme. Conversely, when the downstream market is highly price-sensitive, the PLI scheme generates higher net utility. We also find that when the market size is small (large), both the firm and the social planner prefer the PLI (CSI) scheme when the skill-diffusion benefit is moderate. Overall, our results suggest that industrial incentive schemes should reflect sector-specific skill potential and demand characteristics, with the CSI scheme better suited to sectors with high skill-diffusion potential or large markets, and the PLI scheme better suited to nascent or highly price-sensitive markets.

Title: A game-theoretical model for green urban logistics coordination: Exact and data-driven methods
Authors: Adejuyigbe O. Fajemisin, David Rey, Xavier Brusset
Abstract: This study presents a single-leader, multi-follower game aimed at minimizing carbon emissions in urban logistics. First-Mile (FM) delivery service providers transport parcels to satellites at city outskirts, after which Last-Mile (LM) service providers with eco-friendlier vehicles finalize delivery to customers. In this game, FM and LM delivery service providers are follower players that form a two-echelon logistics network which is coordinated by a leader player representing a green urban logistics platform. The leader optimally assigns parcels to satellites and LMs to minimize emissions across both echelons, while FM and LM followers adjust their operations accordingly. To determine optimal strategies, an exact cutting-plane algorithm is developed and benchmarked against a scalable data-driven heuristic approach based on constraint learning. To model followers’ best responses to leader assignment decisions, we implement a network-oriented learning approach where we learn FM and LM predictive models that can be used with large city-sized network instances. The proposed approaches are tested on realistic problems instances from Berlin, Madrid and Bologna. Our findings highlight the potential of the proposed game-theoretical model for reducing emissions while ensuring that stakeholders’ preferences such as on-time deliveries are taken into account.

Title: On the service time in the close-enough traveling salesman problem
Authors: Weiwei Cui, Jianhui Zhu, Lan Peng
Abstract: The rapid advancement of drone technology and long-range sensors attracts researchers to revisit the close-enough traveling salesman problem (CETSP), where customers can be regarded as visited whenever the traveler gets close enough. As the concept of “visiting” alters, the questions of how, where, and when the customers are served arise. We introduce the close-enough traveling salesman problem with service time (CETSPST), which requires the traveler to remain within the customer's neighborhood for a period of time to complete services. According to different paradigms of service, a family of service time assignment problems (STAPs) along with the circle touring problem with service time (CTPST) is proposed as the subproblems of CETSPST. Due to the complexity of geometric features, the CETSPST is challenging to model and to solve. Thus, we develop a matheuristic approach that optimizes routing and service-time allocation jointly across multiple service modes and finds the fastest path to serve all customers. The numerical results show that joint route and service-time optimization can reduce the total completion time relative to assigning service time to CETSP shortest paths. In addition, analyzing similarities and differences in solution performance across four service modes serves as a valuable guide for facilitating wide-ranging real-world applications.

Title: Multi-period predictive inventory routing for battery swapping in shared e-micromobility
Authors: Deyi Li, Yaoming Zhou, Jiuh-Biing Sheu
Abstract: The rapid extension of shared electric micromobility systems (SEMS) as sustainable urban transportation solutions has underscored the demand for efficient battery swapping to ensure uninterrupted operations. However, due to the absence of inventory management, current battery swapping practices under the vehicle routing optimization-based strategy fail to align station inventory with the riding demand of micro electric vehicles (MEVs), resulting in untimely battery swapping or unnecessary station visits. This paper proposes a novel predictive inventory routing method for multi-period battery swapping in SEMS, where battery swapping vehicles are periodically dispatched from a warehouse to visit MEV stations for battery swapping operations. First, a continuous-time Markovian model is developed to forecast station-level inventory dynamics and system-wide performance, considering both the number and power level of MEVs at stations. Leveraging these predictions, the multi-period battery swapping problem is formulated as an inventory routing problem incorporating timing decisions, structured as a mixed-integer programming to maximize total expected profit across the entire planning horizon. To address computational complexity, a two-phase iterative matheuristic integrating adaptive large neighborhood search and dynamic programming is then designed to solve the problem, enabling coordinated cross-period resource allocation and better decision-making regarding station visits and their optimal swapping timing. Real-world case studies demonstrate that the proposed inventory routing optimization-based strategy achieves a 23% profitability improvement over conventional vehicle routing-based methods. This paper explores the value of multi-period inventory management in SEMS operations and offers a transferable decision-support framework for dynamic systems managing analogous resource-service trade-offs.

Title: Lifted branching: Learning to improve branching strategies
Authors: Simon Renard, Quentin Louveaux, Bernard Fortz
Abstract: Branch-and-bound (B&B) is a widely used algorithm for solving mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs). One of the elements of its efficiency is the branching strategy. While strong branching empirically produces small B&B trees, its high computational cost makes it impractical for real-world applications. Recent advances in machine learning explored imitation learning to replicate the effectiveness of strong branching. However, these approaches are limited to mimicking existing strategies rather than discovering new ones. In this work, we propose lifted branching, a novel framework that iteratively improves an existing branching strategy by using imitation learning to learn from an improved version of the strategy. Lifted branching is designed to generate smaller B&B trees while avoiding the computational overhead of strong branching, making it suitable for offline training and efficient real-time deployment. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on four different problem classes, showing that our learned lifted branching models can outperform state-of-the-art strategies, such as reliability pseudo-branching and learned strong branching, depending on the problem of interest.

Title: Assessing operational efficiency, financial stability, and profit efficiency in hotels with negative value observations using firm accounting data
Authors: Hirofumi Fukuyama, Yong Tan, Peter Wanke
Abstract: This study develops a novel Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) framework that integrates a three-stage network structure with a translation-invariant directional slack inefficiency measure to derive an accounting-based composite measure of financial health. Relying exclusively on balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow data, the method accommodates negative values without transformation and decomposes performance into operational efficiency, financial stability, and profit efficiency, where profit efficiency is further divided into profit-generation efficiency and profit-retention efficiency. To enhance causal interpretability, we embed the DEA scores within a two-phase inferential framework that combines Kullback–Leibler divergence-based separability testing with a novel bootstrapped regression approach based on QR decomposition to a panel of UK hotels (2015–2023). The first-stage results indicate that efficiency dynamics in the UK hotel sector are largely shaped by macroeconomic shocks, with pronounced declines during Brexit-related uncertainty and the COVID-19 period, followed by a strong post-pandemic recovery, while regional disparities remain limited. The second-stage analysis reveals that efficiency determinants are highly dimension-specific: labour cost emerges as the only consistent positive driver of operational, financial stability, and profit-generation efficiency, whereas liquidity exhibits a significant but negative effect on profit-retention efficiency, with other financial and governance variables showing limited explanatory power. The framework advances DEA methodology by jointly addressing negative data, multi-stage production, and endogeneity in contextual analysis, and offers actionable, region-specific insights for managers and policymakers in the hospitality sector.

Title: Manufacturers’ selection of streamer type under competition: Streamer screening and manufacturer misrepresentation
Authors: Gaoke Wu, Wensheng Yang, Jiaying Zhang, Linfang Fan
Abstract: Live-streaming commerce has become a dominant sales channel, profoundly reshaping power structures and competitive dynamics within supply chains. Against this backdrop, manufacturers’ streamer selection strategies and top streamers’ product selection decisions are critical to market efficiency, while the risk of false claims by ordinary manufacturers seeking cooperation remains underexplored. To address this issue, this study develops a supply chain game-theoretic model comprising a brand manufacturer, an ordinary manufacturer, a top streamer, and a normal streamer. Based on different combinations of manufacturers’ streamer choices, we formulate four scenarios using Stackelberg games and Nash bargaining models to derive optimal pricing and commission rate decisions. The key findings are as follows: (i) the brand manufacturer should strategically leverage competition between streamers to optimize commission costs; (ii) manufacturers’ choice of streamer type and top streamers’ willingness to collaborate with ordinary manufacturers are primarily driven by the traffic effect of normal streamers and the slotting-fee coefficient; (iii) collusive false claims between top streamers and ordinary manufacturers can be effectively curtailed only when the traffic effect of normal streamers is moderate and the slotting-fee coefficient is extremely low or extremely high; and (iv) improving top streamers’ screening success rates significantly deters false representations by ordinary manufacturers, with particularly strong deterrent effects in collaborations involving brand manufacturers. This study contributes by uncovering the intrinsic mechanisms of competition and collusion in live-streaming commerce, thereby providing a theoretical foundation for strategic decision-making by manufacturers and streamers.

Title: A two-stage column-generation-based matheuristic for integrated scheduling in a cloud manufacturing environment
Authors: Qiao Wu, Naiming Xie, Roel Leus, Shaoxiang Zheng
Abstract: Cloud manufacturing is a new service concept that allows the effective coordination of geographically distributed manufacturing resources, enabling manufacturers to expand their markets and to significantly improve the service levels for customers. In this paper, we address an integrated scheduling problem based on a cloud manufacturing environment, which consists of a parallel batch scheduling problem in the production stage and a multi-vehicle routing problem with resource constraints in the transportation stage. We first provide a MILP model for the integrated problem and a set partitioning model for each stage. Then, a two-stage matheuristic framework is proposed to achieve near-optimal solutions. In the first stage, a column generation (CG) algorithm is provided to determine batch solutions, and heuristics are applied to accelerate the process, followed by a variable neighborhood search (VNS) algorithm to obtain additional feasible solutions. In the second stage, we apply the CG to generate routing decisions based on the inputs from the first stage, where the pricing problem is solved by a label setting algorithm. In addition, we design a feedback strategy that uses the routing information obtained in the second stage to improve the quality of the solutions generated in the first stage. Computational experiments show that the two-stage algorithm is an effective approach for the integrated problem.

Title: The impact of joint price dynamics and customer preference on the dynamics of closed loop supply chains
Authors: Jiawen Li, Junyi Lin, Jie Chu, Ou Tang
Abstract: Closed-loop supply chains (CLSCs) are becoming increasingly important for sustainable operations, but their dynamic behaviour remains underexplored when new and remanufactured products are not perfect substitutes. Furthermore, existing CLSCs dynamics studies rarely examine how market-level customer preference for remanufactured products and stochastic price dynamics jointly affect the bullwhip effect (BE) and net stock amplification (NSAmp). To address this gap, this study develops a two-echelon CLSC system dynamics model including an independent manufacturer and remanufacturer under the order-up-to policy. The demand model incorporates customer preference for remanufactured products and exogenous prices for new and remanufactured products, whose price dynamics follow first-order autoregressive processes. Exact closed-form expressions of the BE and NSAmp for both product types are derived based on variance analysis. Also, system dynamics simulation is conducted to examine the effects of customer preference, price dynamics, lead times, and return rate on the BE and NSAmp. The results show when the autoregressive parameter of the new-product price exceeds that of the remanufactured-product price, stronger customer preference for remanufactured products reduces BE for both products and lowers NSAmp for new products, but increases it for remanufactured products; the opposite holds when the remanufactured-product price is more autoregressive. Both price autoregressive parameters exhibit inverse U-shaped relationships with the BE and NSAmp. In addition, lead times and return rate significantly affect the BE and NSAmp, leading to dynamic instability. This study extends CLSCs dynamics research by relaxing the perfect-substitution assumption and providing analytical and managerial insights concerning pricing, remanufacturing promotion, and return management.

Title: Reinforcement learning for joint scheduling in robotic mobile fulfillment systems
Authors: Yunyang Lu, Lindong Liu, Yan Zhu, Chengcheng Yu
Abstract: Robotic mobile fulfillment systems (RMFSs) are revolutionizing e-Commerce by automating the transport of product pods to workstations, reducing labor costs, and improving order fulfillment efficiency. However, this automation introduces new operational complexities that require innovative solutions. In this paper, we tackle the primary scheduling issues that arise during the order processing phase, including pod retrieval, pod repositioning, and robot assignment. We utilize the Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework as our decision-making model to minimize the system's makespan. To solve the problem, we propose a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based method for the RMFS joint scheduling problem, and introduce several effective rules to constrain the search space, significantly accelerating the training process. We evaluate the performance of our algorithms on both small scenarios based on synthetic data and large-scale scenarios based on real-world data. The computational results demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms for daily use. In particular, joint optimization substantially outperforms decoupled optimization, highlighting the necessity of optimizing in an integrated manner. Through the analysis of the value function and numerical studies, we identify three key drivers of the makespan: task efficiency, visit frequency, and robot coordination. Reducing the makespan requires improving these three factors jointly. Our numerical study shows that adding more robots beyond a certain threshold yields diminishing returns, and robot coordination is more critical than individual efficiency during peak demand periods. Additionally, warehouses with a concentrated or a dispersed storage strategy perform better than those with a moderate storage strategy.

Title: A novel meta-frontier super-efficiency data envelopment analysis approach capable of unbiased identification of technology gaps
Authors: Dawei Wang, Feng Yang, Lili Liu, Sheng Ang
Abstract: Meta-frontier super-efficiency data envelopment analysis (MS-DEA) approach integrates super-efficiency concepts into the meta-frontier framework to improve the discriminatory power of group efficiency evaluations. However, existing MS-DEA approach often fail to accurately capture technology gaps between group frontiers and the meta-frontier. This paper re-examines this issue and proposes a revised MS-DEA model. The proposed method corrects the technology gap ratio calculation by resetting the super-efficiency scores of fully efficient units to unity, thereby removing the distortion caused by super-efficiency based reference frontiers. It also improves the decomposition of inefficiency in existing MS-DEA approach. In addition, the framework is extended to non-convex meta-frontiers and undesirable outputs. An empirical application to China's provincial transportation sector illustrates that the proposed model provides unbiased assessment of technology gap and superior discriminatory power.

Title: Collaborative vehicle routing with strategic request acceptance: The impact of profit sharing
Authors: Yannick Oskar Scherr, Margaretha Gansterer, Richard F. Hartl
Abstract: We investigate the operational problem of carriers receiving pickup-and-delivery requests that must be answered immediately and fulfilled the next day with a given fleet. Before fulfillment, carriers participate in a collaboration to exchange requests with other carriers in a combinatorial auction. Submitted requests are grouped into bundles that are redistributed according to carriers’ bids to minimize costs. Total auction profits are shared among carriers using a profit-sharing mechanism. We model each carrier's sequential optimization problem and use heuristic routing approaches. For making dynamic acceptance decisions, we propose a two-step policy considering strategic rejection, i.e., rejecting also requests that could be fulfilled with currently available capacities. The first step decides on accepting and fulfilling a request, while the second step decides on overbooking a request and submitting it to the auction. After modeling the carriers’ decision-making process, we investigate the impact of the exchange mechanism, particularly the profit-sharing mechanism, on carriers’ behavior. We propose a Shapley-Value based profit-sharing mechanism and a new adjustable mechanism in which the degree to which carriers receive equal auction outcomes can be adjusted. Experiments on homogeneous settings (carriers use the same strategy) show revenue gains (up to 15.19%) and cost savings (up to 10.43%) compared to benchmarks. Heterogeneous settings (different strategies) provide insights into incentives to deviate from the best strategies based on the profit-sharing mechanism. Our results suggest that intermediate settings of the adjustable mechanism are particularly effective in counteracting deviations. Thus, mechanism design impacts both the success of the collaboration and carriers’ customer acceptance.

Title: An extension of Hu’s algorithm for resource leveling and some related results
Abstract: In this paper we consider resource leveling problems with precedence constraints in which jobs requiring a common resource have to be scheduled in order to minimize a convex function of the resource usage over time. We consider two variants of this problem. In the first one, all the jobs have unit processing time, a common deadline and require one unit from the common resource. Moreover, the precedence constraints induce a set of disjoint in-trees on the job set. We propose a polynomial time algorithm which solves the resource leveling problem for arbitrary convex functions. Our method builds on some of the ideas of Hu's algorithm for solving the makespan minimization problem in a parallel machine environment with unit-time jobs and with precedence constraints inducing an in-tree. In the second variant, we have a parallel machine environment and unit-time jobs connected by arbitrary precedence constraints. Since deciding if a feasible schedule of a given makespan exists is NP-hard, our goal is to transform any feasible schedule by at most doubling its makespan while approximating the best possible resource usage cost among all schedules with a makespan bounded by that of the original schedule.

Title: Joint weak disposability in benefit-of-the-doubt models: methodology and structural analysis of country performance
Authors: Hirofumi Fukuyama, Yong Tan, Peter Wanke
Abstract: We extend the conventional Benefit-of-the-Doubt (BoD) approach by explicitly incorporating undesirable sub-indicators—variables typically excluded from standard models or treated under the unrealistic assumption that they can be reduced independently of desirable sub-indicators. Our method introduces the principle of joint weak disposability for both desirable (“good”) and undesirable (“bad”) outputs within the Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) framework, ensuring a consistent treatment of substitutability between them. By interpreting DEA outputs as sub-indicators in BoD, the framework acknowledges that bad sub-indicators cannot be reduced independently, nor offset by increases in good sub-indicators, reflecting the structural and economic constraints countries face in managing burdens. To demonstrate its value, we apply the model to a global panel of countries from 2013 to 2021 and conduct a second-stage analysis of the drivers of cross-country performance differences. The findings highlight three main insights: (i) burden-to-benefit ratios exert a strong negative effect on performance, (ii) returns-to-burden conditions play a significant moderating role, and (iii) systematic disparities persist across income groups. Taken together, the proposed framework delivers both methodological innovation and practical guidance for macro-level performance assessment, offering a more realistic and policy-relevant evaluation of national outcomes.

Title: An exact branch-price-and-cut algorithm for integrated waste collection system: Elementary shortest path and hop constraint Steiner Tree Problems
Authors: Maryam DehghanChenary, Christian Tilk, Richard F. Hartl
Abstract: This paper presents an exact solution approach to a waste collection problem, which combines traditional truck-based collection with an automated pneumatic pipe network. The problem jointly determines (i) whether each collection point is assigned to truck service or to the automated system, and (ii) the corresponding truck routes and a cost-minimizing pneumatic tree. The truck component is modeled as a Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem, while the pneumatic tree is represented by a variant of the Steiner Tree Problem. Our main contribution is the development and comparison of two decomposition strategies within a branch-price-and-cut framework. In the full decomposition, routing and tree generation are handled independently in two pricing problems. On the contrary, in the partial decomposition, the tree structure is modeled directly in the master problem, and column generation is applied only to the routing part. For the tree-part, we adapt two state-of-the-art formulations, resulting in four distinct branch-price-and-cut algorithms. Computational experiments on benchmark data sets with up to 80 nodes reveal apparent performance differences between the decomposition strategies depending on instance characteristics, demonstrating the substantial impact of modeling choices on solvability, scalability, and overall computational efficiency.

Title: Multiagent search and rescue planning for dynamic disaster settings
Authors: José Betancourt, Gina Galindo, Ruben Yie-Pinedo, Alfredo Moreno
Abstract: Natural disasters such as wildfires, hurricanes, and earthquakes pose significant threats to human life. Timely search and rescue operations are crucial during such events to minimize fatalities. A key challenge in these missions is that missing individuals face increasing risks of critical injury or death as the disaster progresses. Additionally, as the disaster evolves, the distribution of risk across the affected region changes dynamically, further complicating the decision-making process. This situation results in a complex problem where search planning must account for both the dynamic risk in high-risk areas and the need to quickly locate victims in regions where missing persons are most likely to be found. Despite the critical importance of this issue, it has received limited attention in the Search Theory literature. This paper presents a decision support model designed to address these challenges by prioritizing searches in areas of greatest danger and highest likelihood of finding victims. The model uses real-time risk data to generate optimized search paths for a team of heterogeneous agents. To solve this problem efficiently, a Pareto Ant Colony Optimization approach is employed.

Title: Joint order batching and picker routing under human–robot collaboration: An efficient heuristic and practical insights
Authors: Sina Khodaee, Melih Çelik, Vaggelis Giannikas
Abstract: The growing reliance of warehouses on automation to improve productivity introduces new challenges, particularly in coordinating interactions between multiple picking entities. In this study, we address the problem of human–robot synchronisation in a picker-to-parts system, where Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) transport bins across the warehouse, while human pickers move between locations to load them. This setting requires integrated order batching and routing of both pickers and AMRs. To tackle this, we propose mathematical models and an iterative decomposition-based heuristic to minimise makespan. The heuristic consists of two stages: (i) AMR batching and routing, and (ii) picker routing. In the first stage, we use a variable neighbourhood search to batch orders and route AMRs. In the second, we treat AMR arrival times at picking locations as due dates for human pickers and generate routes accordingly. Our computational experiments demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed approach and provide managerial insights. We show that collaborative picking under our setting decreases the makespan of a fully manual system by more than a half, and a fixed-resource-assigned system by 15% on average, with gaps reaching over 50% when a single picker is assigned to three or more AMRs. We also highlight the importance of resource balancing. Specifically, we find that increasing AMRs improves performance when picker capacity is sufficient, whereas adding pickers yields the greatest gains when AMRs outnumber them. Furthermore, fewer high-capacity resources outperform larger fleets of low-capacity ones. Finally, our findings are quite robust to varying speeds of picking entities.

Title: Virtual projection bias in two-stage network data envelopment analysis: A unified non-radial approach for efficiency decomposition
Authors: Chixiao Lu, Ali Emrouznejad, Dimitris Giraleas
Abstract: Two-stage network Data Envelopment Analysis (2SN DEA) is widely used to evaluate decision-making units (DMUs) with internal production structures. However, conventional 2SN DEA models may produce biased efficiency estimates when the generated virtual projection point lies outside the feasible input–output production frontier. From a managerial perspective, existing models also have important limitations. They usually explain inefficiency as a stage-level production problem, while paying insufficient attention to system-level managerial inefficiency and ripple effects between connected stages. More importantly, many conventional 2SN DEA models implicitly assume that supply-chain stages can be freely rearranged across DMUs. To address these issues, we propose a unified non-radial analysis framework that imposes additional restrictions on the reconfiguration of conventional network production technology. These restrictions ensure that the generated projection point remains feasible within the input–output production frontier. The proposed model is evaluated against existing approaches using an empirical case study from the supply chain of motor manufacturing industry, along with a sensitivity analysis based on alternative reference sets. The results, further supported by the proposed theorems, demonstrate that the new approach effectively relocates previously identified exterior projection points onto the boundary of the input–output production frontier. Through the corresponding dual programming model, we further introduce a novel mechanism to account for stage-level and system-level failures, as well as the ripple effect. The proposed model enables a decomposition of the overall efficiency of each DMU into stage efficiency and system efficiency, offering deeper managerial insights.

Title: Cascading disruptions in multi-factory supply chains: Stability-constrained distributionally robust planning
Authors: Mohammad Asghari, Hamid Afshari, Mohamad Y. Jaber, Cory Searcy
Abstract: Disruption-sensitive supply networks are highly vulnerable to capacity and delay shocks that propagate across multiple stages. Existing supply chain disruption models often see disruptions as isolated or static, missing multi-wave cascade propagation, robust hedge, and coordination. This study develops a framework connecting disruption spread, stability analysis, and distributionally robust planning in a unified optimization model. The approach combines a linear cascade model on a time-expanded network with spectral-radius and small-gain stability conditions. It constructs polyhedral (multifaceted) disturbance and ambiguity sets that are consistent with these dynamics and embeds them in a two-stage coordination model. Within this model, we (i) quantify resilience trade-offs between plant level autonomy and network-wide coordination, (ii) jointly optimize risk-aware inventory, production, and transport decisions under cascading disruptions, and (iii) evaluate performance and robustness through multiobjective criteria under distributional ambiguity. A mixed-integer master–recourse scheme combining logic-Benders and column-and-constraint generation is used to solve the model on an industry inspired multi-factory setting, illustrated through a semiconductor-style network. Computational results show that optimized hedging strategies substantially reduce amplification and disruption span, shorten recovery time by about 1.5–2 periods, and increase fill rates from 0.92 to above 0.97 with moderate additional investment. Ambiguity-aware designs further improve out-of-sample performance relative to nominal plans. These findings show that explicitly modeling cascade structure can satisfactorily improve resilience design and support valuing resilience investments, governed pooling, and structural hedges in tightly coupled supply networks.

Title: A branch-and-price approach for last-mile deliveries with capacitated robot stations
Authors: Yerlan Kuzbakov, Laurent Alfandari, Diego Delle Donne
Abstract: In the capacitated routing-scheduling problem (CRSP) for a multimodal delivery system, the first leg is performed by a truck that makes a tour starting from the depot, visiting some facilities from a set of candidate robot stations. The second and last leg of the delivery is performed by Autonomous Delivery Robots (ADRs), starting from the facilities and ending at the customer's doorstep. The demand that can be served at each robot station is limited. Each customer has a scheduled delivery time and must be served from a single station. If the robot arrives after this time, the difference between the time of the delivery and the scheduled time is counted as the tardiness for the customer. The CRSP asks to select a tour for the truck and a feasible assignment of customers to facilities such that the total tardiness of delivery is minimized. Existing literature tackles an uncapacitated version of this problem which is modeled with a compact formulation and solved by Benders decomposition. We propose an extended formulation and branch-and-price approach to solve the capacitated problem, which is shown to outperform a direct solving of the (adapted) compact formulation. We also perform a sensitivity analysis on key parameters such as the number and capacities of robot stations in the network and the tightness of delivery deadlines, to derive managerial insights.

Title: Adaptive relief logistics for predictable disasters: Integrating professional vehicles with flexible crowdshipping
Authors: Jing Li, Feng Chu, Ada Che, Junkai He
Abstract: This study investigates a new relief logistics planning problem for predictable natural disasters with an actionable warning window. It integrates professional vehicles with crowdshipping and combines centrally pre-positioned inventories with pre-contracted suppliers to improve distribution flexibility and supply reliability. For the problem, we propose a novel multi-period distributionally robust chance-constrained model that accounts for dynamic and random demands, crowdshipping capacity, and traffic conditions to minimize the total relief cost under the worst-case scenario. Strategic decisions on facility location and supplier selection are made pre-warning, while post-warning tactical decisions involve multi-period relief supply distribution and vehicle assignment. To address computational challenges arising from the model's nonlinearity and large problem size, we reformulate it as a mixed-integer linear program and develop an improved column-and-constraint generation algorithm. The proposed algorithm features a customized three-phase framework consisting of decompose-and-relax, explore-and-repeat, and refine-and-repeat. It accelerates convergence via problem relaxation, scenario filtering, and iterative optimality tightening, with theoretical guarantees of finite-step convergence. Experimental results from a case study on historical typhoons in Shenzhen City, China, and randomly generated instances demonstrate the strong performance of the proposed model and algorithm. Insights relevant to management are also derived.

Title: An enhanced graphical method for distributed job shop scheduling problems
Authors: Lin Huang, Dunbing Tang, Zequn Zhang, Haihua Zhu, Changchun Liu
Abstract: The Distributed Job Shop Scheduling Problem (DJSP) is a typical challenge in distributed manufacturing systems, inherently involving a two-stage scheduling process: assigning jobs to factories and sequencing operations within each factory. To address this complex problem efficiently, this paper proposes an Enhanced Graphical Method (EGM), which integrates both scheduling stages within a unified graphical framework, thereby overcoming the limitations of traditional approaches that treat the two stages separately. The EGM framework consists of four core modules: initial solution generation, graphical search, local search, and acceptance criteria. In the graphical search phase, two key enhancements are proposed. First, a bidirectional shifting mechanism is developed to construct an obstacle graph by left or right shifting the remaining operations, significantly expanding the neighborhood solution space. Second, a layered path planning algorithm based on non-dominated sorting is introduced to improve the search efficiency. Furthermore, three neighborhood structures are designed within the graphical framework to support integrated scheduling of job allocation and operation sequencing. In the local search phase, a dynamic tabu search mechanism is incorporated to optimize the scheduling of critical factories, further enhancing solution quality and stability. The proposed EGM was evaluated on 210 Taillard benchmark instances. Experimental results demonstrate that EGM consistently outperforms four state-of-the-art algorithms in both solution quality and robustness, especially by discovering the upper bounds of 71 benchmark instances.

Title: A systems multimethodology framework to address challenges of rural communities implementing ecotourism
Authors: Yunfei Gu, Bhakti Stephan Onggo, Martin H. Kunc, Steffen Bayer
Abstract: Ecotourism implementation is inherently complex, requiring the integration of ecological, economic, and social dimensions alongside diverse stakeholder interests. This study addresses these challenges by applying Soft System Dynamics Methodology to a real-world case study on Chongming Island, China. The research provides a structured procedural manual for the ontological-epistemological transition, operationalising the move from qualitative narratives to formalised causal feedback logic through an empirical thematic analysis empirical bridge. bridge. Furthermore, it demonstrates how adopting multiple systemic perspectives enables strategic initiatives within highly regulated environments to achieve regenerative feedback loops. Evidence of the study's impact is provided through the formal submission of strategic recommendations to the Chongming District Government for the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–2030) solicitation process. By shifting from top-down interventions to community-led co-creation, this study offers an innovative application of community operational research that enhances systemic resilience and legitimacy in data-scarce contexts. These insights provide a replicable path for practitioners seeking to apply multimethodology in complex, stakeholder-diverse rural environments.

Title: Mitigating disruption risk in multi-echelon supply chains via possibilistic networks: A robust decision-making approach
Authors: Lyu Chengrui, Chen Jing, Shi Jingyi
Abstract: Globalized supply chains face increasing complexity and vulnerability to disruptions, where local incidents can trigger systemic ripple effects. Traditional probabilistic risk assessment, like Bayesian Networks (BNs), struggles with the epistemic uncertainty of rare events or expert knowledge. To complement probabilistic approaches, especially in scenarios of high epistemic uncertainty, this study introduces possibility theory and possibilistic networks (PNs) as a robust alternative framework. We propose an integrated framework for implementing interventions on supply chain participants to mitigate the ripple effect. We construct two mixed-integer nonlinear programming models using the unique possibility measure (to assess potential risk) and necessity measure (to gauge operational resilience). The models aim to minimize the focal manufacturer's disruption possibility, with the second model adding constraints on operational necessity to ensure a resilience threshold. We analyze the properties of these models and develop a problem-oriented differential evolution algorithm for efficient solution. Numerical experiments demonstrate that: (1) The proposed PN-based models effectively reduce disruption risk and can achieve the same numerical minimum risk levels as BN approaches under sufficient budget, validating their consistency. (2) The PN framework's identification of multiple, equally effective optimal intervention strategies offers significant managerial decision flexibility. (3) The dual measures provide a qualitatively different and richer assessment of risk and resilience compared to single probability metrics, offering insights into both worst-case plausibility and operational confidence. This research offers a novel quantitative approach for supply chain intervention planning under epistemic uncertainty, enhancing decision support for building more resilient supply systems.

Title: Integrated poultry production–distribution optimization
Authors: Samuel Gbéya, Maryam Darvish, Jacques Renaud, Leandro C. Coelho
Abstract: . In this paper, we describe, model, and solve an integrated production-distribution planning problem encountered in the poultry supply chain. The production process involves raising chicks on farms before they are sent to slaughterhouses for processing. Production planning decisions include determining the number of chicks to be raised on each farm, the start time, and the duration of their breeding. Distribution planning focuses on scheduling the delivery of mature poultry from farms to slaughterhouses, specifying the timing and quantity of each delivery while accounting for transportation costs and slaughterhouse quota allocations. The objective is to develop cost-efficient production and delivery schedules that respect numerous industry-specific constraints. We formulate the problem as a mixed-integer linear programming model and propose a neighborhood search-based matheuristic to solve large-scale, real-world instances. Computational results on instances derived from data provided by a Québec poultry producer demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed solution approach.

Title: Integrated shift and break scheduling for airline ground staff under flight delay uncertainty
Authors: Jeroen Assink, Mahekha Dahanayaka, Dennis Prak, Rohit Gupta, Martijn Mes
Abstract: Efficient ground personnel scheduling is critical for reliable airline operations. This paper presents an integrated two-stage stochastic optimization framework for shift and break scheduling of airline ground staff, incorporating employee exchangeability and service-level constraints under delay uncertainty. Two model variants are developed: a baseline shift and break scheduling model with predetermined break times and an ex-post variant with scenario-dependent breaks. The models explicitly consider understaffing and overstaffing costs, and allow for limited cross-pool and cross-skill employee exchangeability. To address risk-sensitive planning requirements, the baseline model is extended with service-level constraints that ensure understaffing remains bounded in all but a specified number of extreme scenarios. The models are evaluated on six synthetic demand profiles representing different flight schedule patterns and on a case study inspired by a major European airline. The computational experiments examine the effects of demand shape, understaffing cost, delay variance, correlation, and workforce exchangeability. The results show that stochastic planning substantially outperforms deterministic planning, achieving cost reductions of up to 34%. The value of perfect information remains limited in most settings, indicating that the stochastic framework already captures most of the benefit of improved foresight. Ex-post break scheduling yields only modest additional gains, whereas employee exchangeability emerges as a major source of flexibility and cost efficiency, particularly under correlated disruptions. The service-level formulation provides a practical alternative when explicit reliability guarantees are preferred over penalty based modeling. This research highlights the importance of integrating uncertainty, operational flexibility, and performance in tactical workforce scheduling for complex airline operations.

Title: Resource-dependent process times in hybrid flexible flowshops: A Constraint Programming-oriented decomposition approach
Authors: Ioannis Avgerinos, Ioannis Mourtos, Dimitrios Papathanasiou, Georgios Zois
Abstract: The effect of resource allocation on manufacturing motivates us to examine a scheduling variant that is of practical significance yet remains overlooked. We examine a Hybrid Flexible Flowshop (HFFS), i.e., an environment where a set of jobs is scheduled across multiple stages (each stage having multiple identical machines) yet some jobs may skip some stages. In addition, we consider processing times that depend on the resources assigned to a job at each stage, transportation times between machines and limited-capacity buffers before and after each stage. We introduce a Constraint Programming (CP) formulation, which we then decompose through Logic-Based Benders Decomposition (LBBD). We tighten formulations by a set of makespan lower bounds, the strongest of which arises from a reduction to malleable scheduling. By modifying recent instance generators, we experiment with up to 400 jobs, 8 stages, and 10 parallel machines per stage. The results demonstrate competitive integrality gaps, highlighting the efficiency of our approach at scale and on an HFFS variant quite beyond the current literature.

Title: Suspense and surprise in European football
Authors: Raphael Flepp, Tim Pawlowski, Travis Richardson
Abstract: A key criterion for evaluating sports competitions is their attractiveness to consumers. In this paper, we propose using match-level suspense and surprise, which capture the entertainment utility generated by competitive balance and outcome uncertainty for sports spectators, to assess attractiveness. Through simulations, we derive a benchmark range for suspense and surprise based on an otherwise balanced match with home advantage, before analyzing more than 25,000 matches from Europe’s top five football leagues played between 2010/11 and 2023/24. Our findings reveal that mean match suspense is often lower than the benchmark range, particularly for top teams, while mean match surprise most often aligns with the benchmark. Moreover, we identify nuanced trends over time and highlight notable differences across leagues and clubs. These insights enhance our understanding of how the attractiveness of matches arises from competitive balance and carry important policy implications.

Title: Index policy for condition-based maintenance scheduling of aircraft fleet with limited technicians
Authors: Ying Zhu, Dong Li, Shiqiang Hu, Tangbin Xia, Ershun Pan, Lifeng Xi
Abstract: This paper investigates condition-based maintenance scheduling for a key component of a fleet of aircraft undergoing base maintenance, with a particular focus on technician resource limitations. Each aircraft has a predefined operation schedule and a limited service lifetime, by the end of which it retires and is replaced by a new aircraft of the same type. We model the problem as a discrete-time Markov Decision Process, where the objective is to minimize the long-run average cost arising from maintenance and potential failures. Due to the high-dimensional state space, we adopt the Whittle index framework for Restless Bandit problems, decomposing the fleet-level scheduling problem into a collection of single-aircraft subproblems. Each subproblem features a two-dimensional state space defined by aircraft service age and component degradation level, complicating the establishment of indexability due to the lack of monotonicity in service age. In response, we reformulate each subproblem as a finite-horizon dynamic program with a one-dimensional state. This allows us to efficiently compute Whittle indices via an existing algorithm, which is enhanced to verify indexability in the same time. The resulting index policy is shown to be optimal for problems with a fleet of two identical aircraft, and it comfortably outperforms the benchmark heuristics in all the other scenarios considered in an extensive numerical experiment.

Title: A robust conditional assessment of performance trends in education and training systems of European regions
Authors: Fernando J. Osório, Flávia Barbosa, Giovanna D’Inverno, Ana S. Camanho
Abstract: This paper proposes a robust conditional approach based on a range directional ‘Benefit-of-the-Doubt’ (BoD) model to monitor the evolution of performance from 2020 to 2023 in the education and training systems of 200 European regions, including 180 at NUTS2 level. The methodological framework first establishes an ‘ideal’ performance point, representing the most ambitious level between empirically observed best practices and aspirational benchmarks identified by experts or policymakers. It then introduces an environmentally adjusted Malmquist Productivity Index specifically adapted to a BoD framework, enabling the analysis of temporal dynamics while disentangling performance changes from contextual influences. The results indicate that overall performance in Europe is improving, largely driven by productivity gains at the frontier. However, efficiency losses remain widespread, as many regions fail to converge towards best practices observed among comparable peers, even when operating under relatively favourable conditions.

Title: Measuring firm-level and sectoral marginal abatement costs: A dual-programming by-production approach
Abstract: A novel non-parametric DEA methodology based on a by-production specification of the technology is developed for computing firm and sector-level MACs. The by-production technology independently captures features of a standard neo-classical sub-technology that produces a good output using productive inputs (including emission-causing inputs such as fossil fuels) and a sub-technology that shows the generation of bad outputs/emissions due to the use of emission-causing inputs in production. Using dual linear-programming, MAC is computed directly as the multiplier of the emission constraint of the primal-problem, where the firm or the sector maximises its objective function subject to its technological and emission constraints. This is in contrast to the conventional directional distance function (DDF)-based shadow price approach implemented under weak or related disposability assumptions, which (i) abstracts from capturing the link between emission generation and usage of emission-causing inputs, (ii) using dual linear-programming, measures MAC as ratio of two multipliers of a primal-problem linked to revenue-function duality, (iii) captures, under the non-parametric approach, the trade-off between the good and bad outputs along a constant-DDF (constant-inefficiency) surface rather than along the technological frontier. In non-parametric DEA-based approaches, we show that one can expect a convex range of firm or sector-level MACs. The sector achieves allocative efficiency when the intersection of the firm-level ranges of MACs is non-empty. Our methodology is applied to derive plant-level and sectoral MACs in the Indian coal-based thermal power sector. A Monte Carlo study is also done to compare the MAC values obtained under our and the conventional DDF-based approaches.

Title: The vehicle routing problem with zone tariffs: A matheuristic framework and insights into detour limit design
Authors: Niklas Tuma, Manuel Ostermeier, Alexander Hübner
Abstract: Companies commonly outsource transportation logistics to logistics service providers (LSPs) to reduce complexity and leverage economies of scale. The coordination between shippers and LSPs for regional distribution is typically organized through zone-based tariffs, in which shippers propose joint customer deliveries to an LSP. This approach decouples customer allocation and pricing from the delivery sequence, simplifying planning. To minimize costs, shippers must form customer clusters that meet capacity and specific distance constraints, known as detour limits. These detour limits ensure reasonable driving distances within a customer cluster. Despite their widespread application in practice, zone tariffs have received little research attention to date. Early related research either addresses dedicated case applications with a specific single detour limit or relies on exact methods suited only for small instances. In contrast, general real-world applications involve hundreds of customers and heterogeneous detour limit options. We address this gap by tailoring an Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search–based matheuristic that features problem-specific operators and two adaptive mechanisms. Combining heuristic tour generation with a set partitioning model, our approach efficiently handles multiple detour limits. Numerical studies, including a case study and benchmark instances with up to 1000 customers, demonstrate the approach's scalability and effectiveness. This study provides the first comprehensive analysis of how different detour limitations relate and affect routing efficiency as well as zone tariff design, revealing key trade-offs between cost and travel distance. We identify an efficiency threshold with moderate detour values, offering actionable guidance for the design of real-world zone-based tariffs.

Title: The location set covering disruption problem
Authors: Richard A. Sheldon, Brian J. Lunday, William N. Caballero
Abstract: This research proposes a new, relevant adversarial location problem and examines variants that relax complete and perfect game theoretic assumptions. The location set covering disruption problem (LSCDP) represents a Stackelberg game wherein the leader disrupts access to at most q out of n possible facility locations, after which the follower solves a perturbed location set covering problem (LSCP). Acknowledging the perturbed LSCP may not be feasible, the proposed LSCDP model represents a leader seeking to lexicographically maximize the value-weighted demands that cannot be covered and the follower's minimal cost of facilities required to cover remaining demands. Whereas the LSCDP adopts a complete and perfect game theoretic framework, we also develop a problem variant accounting for unawareness, a refinement of incomplete information. In the latter variant, qc≤q of the leader's disruptions are initially unknown to the follower, not just with regard to their number and locations but to even their potential existence. This research identifies suitable solution methods for both of these variants, and empirical testing evaluates the methods to derive relevant insights.

Title: A two-stage consensus reaching model with graph convolutional network based for large-scale group decision-making
Authors: Shaojian Qu, Huagui Yong, Ying Ji
Abstract: In the context of large-scale group decision-making (LSGDM) on social network, traditional clustering methods cluster experts based on opinion similarity, ignoring trust level and closeness of relationships between experts. Most feedback regulation systems fail to simultaneously consider both individuals and subgroups, thereby constraining the efficiency of reaching consensus. Furthermore, most existing consensus models do not take into account the improvement of global consensus level while controlling cost and ignoring adjustment cost uncertainty. To tackle these problems, this paper presents a two-stage consensus reaching model based on graph convolutional network (GCN). It combines opinion similarity, trust level, and relationship closeness using graph structure modeling and multi-layer convolutions, enabling effective grouping. The feedback mechanism includes different adjustment strategies: for individuals, a robust minimum cost consensus model was constructed; for subgroups, a comprehensive identification mechanism is introduced to select those subgroups with lower consensus levels, harmonious internal relationships, and a higher willingness to adjust. Subsequently, an optimization model is applied to adjust the selected subgroups, with the goal of minimizing the cost and maximizing the increase of the global consensus level. Finally, a numerical example validates the practicality and effectiveness of the proposed model, and a comparative analysis demonstrates its superiority.

Title: Analysing the interactions between demand side and supply side investment decisions in an oligopolistic electricity market using a stochastic equilibrium model
Abstract: Electricity consumers worldwide are investing in self-sufficiency technologies like solar photovoltaics and battery storage, often in markets dominated by oligopolistic generating firms that also consider generation investments. Previous models in the literature have not considered investment decisions on both the demand and the supply sides, nor the interactions between them. In this work, we study the interactions between investment decisions on both sides, and we investigate how price-making behaviour on the supply side affects these interactions. We introduce a novel stochastic equilibrium problem to model several players in an oligopolistic electricity market. On the supply side, we consider generating firms that make operational and investment decisions. On the demand side, we consider both industrial and residential consumers. This model enables us to examine how market power, feed-in premiums, and consumer prosumption influence self-sufficiency investments, consumer costs, and generation portfolios. It also allows us to explore how the interactions among these factors affect outcomes such as wholesale prices and carbon emissions. We apply the model to a case study of a stylised Irish electricity system in 2030. Our results demonstrate that price-making on the supply side increases investment in self-sufficiency on the demand side, which in turn reduces carbon emissions and lessens the increase in prices resulting from the presence of market power. We also find that both market power and self-sufficiency alter the investment decisions made by generation firms. Counter-intuitively, we also observe that the absence of a feed-in premium increases investment in solar generation on the demand side.

Title: Analyzing the greenium term structure of twin government bonds
Authors: Lorenzo Mercuri, Edit Rroji, Ilaria Stefani
Abstract: Green bonds provide financial backing for low-carbon initiatives and facilitate the transition towards a greener economy. The greenium effect refers to the potential premium that bondholders are willing to forgo when investing in green securities compared to investments with similar characteristics such as maturity, coupon rate, and issuer credit profile. Despite recent interest in the literature on this topic, the determinants and dynamics of the greenium effect remain inadequately understood, particularly regarding its term structure and geographical dependencies. In this paper, we propose a mathematical framework for the definition of the greenium term structure by employing an affine GARCH model for the interest rate. We then compute semi-analytical bond price formulas that are used for the likelihood estimation of model parameters. Empirical analyses using German and Danish twin bonds show that greenium is maturity specific. In particular, for short maturities, fluctuations in greenium dynamics align with the implementation of European directives aimed at accelerating renewable energy adoption.

Title: How to interpret near-cost-optimal energy futures economically? Linking modelling to generate alternatives and market equilibria
Authors: Jonas Finke, Christoph Weber, Valentin Bertsch
Abstract: Energy system models (ESMs) are used in many planning problems of the energy transition. On the one hand, cost-minimising, linear ESMs have a strong connection to profit-maximising agents in competitive markets. This allows for an economic interpretation of modelling results and, under certain assumptions, guarantees their economic feasibility. On the other hand, modelling to generate alternatives (MGA) generates diverse, near-optimal solutions to address structural and parametric uncertainties inherent to ESMs. However, MGA changes the mathematical model formulation and thus, at first sight, jeopardises the economic interpretation and economic feasibility of model results. This paper therefore links MGA and market equilibria to derive an economic interpretation of near-cost-optimal energy futures. First, we introduce a rigorous market-equilibrium interpretation of a linear cost-minimising ESM. Second, we prove equivalence between ESMs with MGA and cost-minimising ESMs with slightly modified cost terms. Third, we link both results to show that ESMs with MGA are equivalent to cost-minimising ESMs with additional cost or revenue terms, which in turn are equivalent to market equilibria of profit-maximising agents that face these additional costs or revenues. For investors, the MGA alternatives are optimal and exactly recover costs if the additional costs or revenues are imposed respectively provided by governments. Finally, we demonstrate and validate our theoretical findings numerically for a multi-national power system model. The novel economic interpretation improves modellers’ understanding of near-cost-optimal energy futures as well as the societal and economic feasibility of energy transition strategies.

Title: A Primal-Dual Interior-Point algorithm for nonlinear ACOPF with adaptively reformulated Volt-Var constraints
Authors: Maria Teresa Vespucci, Paolo Pisciella, Marco Rossi, Giacomo Viganò, Diana Moneta
Abstract: The increasing penetration of generation from renewable energy sources in distribution networks poses significant challenges for voltage regulation and network operation. Automatic volt-var control is widely adopted to address voltage issues; however, its integration into optimization-based distribution network management frameworks is often addressed through simplified approximations or multi-stage coordination schemes, which may compromise physical accuracy or computational efficiency. We develop an Interior-Point-based solution approach that embeds volt-var curves directly within a nonlinear AC optimal power flow (ACOPF) formulation, enabling coordinated centralized and local control in power distribution networks. The resulting formulation allows solving the problem without the use of linearizations, convex relaxations, or mixed-integer representations. An extensive computational study covering a large set of distribution network instances demonstrates the scalability, robustness, and practical applicability of the proposed approach.

Title: A branch-and-cut algorithm for job-shop scheduling under Time-of-Use pricing and a peak power limit
Authors: Marouane Felloussi, Xavier Delorme, Paolo Gianessi
Abstract: We address the job-shop scheduling problem under Time-of-Use pricing and a peak power limit, with the objective of minimizing total energy costs. To solve this problem, we propose a period-indexed mixed-integer linear programming formulation that reduces the number of variables compared to traditional time-indexed approaches, at the expense of an exponential number of constraints required to enforce the peak power limit. For this reason, we embed the formulation in a branch-and-cut scheme, where peak-power constraints are added only when violated. In addition, the formulation is strengthened with valid inequalities to improve the root relaxation and enumeration tree exploration. The proposed Branch-and-Cut incorporates clique-forbidding cuts, derived from minimal covers of the knapsack polytope associated with the peak-power constraint. We further extend this approach by deriving cuts from arbitrary valid inequalities of the peak-power polytope, and implement a problem-specific cut selection strategy inspired by established metrics in the literature to add the most effective lazy cuts. The resulting framework addresses the structural challenges of energy-aware job-shop scheduling while advancing exact methods in this domain.

Title: Dynamic pricing and learning with censored demand
Authors: Haitao Liu, Ping Cao, Jinpeng Liang, Wenyu Wang
Abstract: We study a single-product pricing problem where lost sales are unobservable, and prices are discrete. The demand is price-dependent, but the seller lacks prior knowledge of the demand-price relationship and demand distributions. The objective is to dynamically experiment with prices and learn from censored sales data to identify the optimal price that maximizes revenue. We propose two revenue distribution estimation methods: one is suitable for general and nonparametric demand, and the other is specifically designed for Gaussian demand. For nonparametric demand, we develop a machine learning model using artificially generated uncensored data to approximate revenue distributions. For Gaussian demand, we derive closed-form expressions for the mean and variance of censored revenue, allowing for the estimation of unknown parameters. Using the large deviations theory, we establish optimality conditions under infinite testing periods and develop a dynamic price-testing policy. Under mild assumptions, we show that the asymptotic allocation obtained by the proposed policy converges to the optimal allocation. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our algorithms outperform traditional methods, providing robust solutions under a variety of demand distributions, including Gaussian, Gamma, Weibull, and mixed distributions. Our findings reveal significant interactions between inventory levels and the number of learning rounds, offering valuable managerial insights for price optimization with censored demand.

Title: Platform strategies for luxury brands operating in second-hand market under digital product passport regulation
Authors: Umang Varshney, Amit Karamchandani, Tsan-Ming Choi, Tanmoy Kundu, Rohit Kapoor
Abstract: The EU's Digital Product Passport (DPP) regulation, effective from 2027, will require luxury brands to disclose key information, such as product origin, materials, and ownership history. This mandated transparency is expected to enhance consumer trust in second-hand luxury purchases. Consequently, luxury brands are strategically responding by engaging with the second-hand market while preserving brand exclusivity and consumer trust. This study employs a game-theoretic analytical modelling approach to evaluate four second-hand platform (SHP) strategies under DPP, namely no platform collaboration (e.g., Prada and Louis Vuitton), collaboration with blockchain authentication (e.g., partnering with platforms like Vestiaire Collective), proprietary multi-brand platforms (e.g., Richemont's model), and proprietary mono-brand platforms (e.g., Oscar de la Renta). Our analysis reveals that the optimal strategy depends on two key factors, i.e., the luxury experience provided during second-hand sales and consumer preference for DPP usage. For instance, brands with an inimitable luxury experience should avoid SHP collaboration to preserve exclusivity, while those with the possibility of replicable experiences could benefit from operating proprietary SHP. Additionally, when DPP usage is limited to authentication, collaboration with external SHP is recommended; however, if consumers value DPP for ownership transparency, a proprietary SHP becomes the optimal choice. Notably, brand exclusivity peaks under an optimal pricing strategy when consumers display moderate interest in DPP ownership and obtain modest utility gain from product comparisons. This study provides actionable insights for luxury brands to strategically navigate the second-hand market, leveraging the DPP regulation to enhance consumer trust while maintaining brand exclusivity.

Title: An efficient divide-and-conquer enhanced metaheuristic for operating room scheduling: A real-world case study
Authors: Marc Chouraqui, Salma Makboul, Alice Yalaoui, Farouk Yalaoui, Lionel Amodeo, Virginie Roger
Abstract: This paper proposes an efficient resolution method to solve the Operating Room (OR) allocation and scheduling problem under real-world hospital constraints using a divide-and-conquer enhanced metaheuristic approach. The objective is to assign a set of elective surgeries to appropriate ORs and intra-day time slots while satisfying practical constraints such as surgeon availability, room compatibility, setup-dependent times, and limiting surgeon idle time to a specified threshold, aiming to minimize the makespan and surgeon's overtime. The problem is modeled as an integer linear programming formulation with proven NP-hard complexity and integrated lower bound calculations. By decomposing the scheduling task into smaller, independent subproblems, the proposed divide-and-conquer strategy significantly improves the performance of the underlying Iterated Local Search metaheuristic. Extensive experiments based on real data from a partner hospital demonstrate the method's scalability and superiority over classical metaheuristics related to OR scheduling approaches in the literature, making it practical for real-world deployment.

Title: Real-time decision-support using simulation (RtS) for operational responsiveness in urgent and emergency care: Bridging the gap between conventional simulation and digital twins
Authors: Alison Harper, Navonil Mustafee, Joe Viana
Abstract: Conventional simulation models in healthcare are typically parameterised using historical data, limiting their ability to support responsive, real-time operational decision-making.
