They are therefore poorly suited to dynamic, high-pressure environments such as urgent and emergency care, where decisions must reflect the current system state. In this paper, we introduce real-time decision-support using simulation (RtS), a methodology that integrates real-time operational data into a discrete-event simulation model to enable context-aware, short-term decision-making. The model integrates partial real-time data feeds with historically derived distributions using a novel data fusion and model initialisation approach. By continuously aligning the simulation with the evolving system state, RtS enhances situation awareness and enables the evaluation of adaptive interventions whose implementation influences subsequent system behaviour. We implement the technical component of our RtS framework through a proof-of-concept model of an Urgent Care Network comprising multiple emergency and urgent care facilities. We evaluate resource-neutral operational policies designed to support short-term adaptation under conditions of rising demand. Our results demonstrate that, under the modelled high-demand conditions, normal emergency department operations can be restored within a 4-hour period through the implementation of two adaptive policies. By operationalising RtS in a service-based setting and demonstrating its effectiveness relative to conventional simulation, our findings provide healthcare stakeholders and OR practitioners with both the technical foundations and the scholarly framing needed to engage in mainstream discussions on deploying RtS as a step-change solution toward simulation enabled digital twins in complex sociotechnical systems.

Title: A generalized data-driven production planning model: algorithmic foundation and simulation-based performance assessment
Abstract: Production planning models must consider the non-linear relationship between resource workload and cycle times when timing work releases to meet demand. This is particularly crucial in semiconductor manufacturing where cycle times are of the order of ten weeks and subject to fluctuations at high utilization levels. Data-driven (DD) production planning formulations have been proposed to address this issue as an alternative to clearing function (CF)-based formulations. DD models characterize a production system through a set of discrete system states representing the multivariate relationship between work in process (WIP) and throughput of all products under steady-state conditions. The cycle times are usually not negligible in relation to the period length. The WIP-throughput relationship alone does not sufficiently capture the congestion behavior of the system under these conditions. The planning model must also correctly identify the periods in which the throughput will be realized as output. We investigate the temporal relationship of WIP and output under different cycle time regimes, and propose the concept of flow patterns that specify the expected input and output quantities over several periods based on the WIP at a specific point in time, and extend the concept of system states. To accommodate these patterns, we establish a DD planning formulation that generalizes previous DD models and outperforms other DD variants and the Allocated CF (ACF) formulation in computational experiments using a large-sized wafer fab model.

Title: Tokenizing creativity in open communities
Authors: Fernando S. Oliveira, Su Jung Jee
Abstract: Open communities, where individuals share and evaluate creative content, often face challenges in maintaining high-quality contributors over the long term. This study examines the effective governance of Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs), an emerging organizational paradigm that may address this issue. Built on blockchain technology, DAOs operate through decentralized and automated decision-making, using cryptographic tokens to reward contributors transparently. Assuming that transparent and collectively determined reward mechanisms can encourage participation, we develop an agent-based model with reinforcement learning to simulate the long-run implications of diverse DAO governance structures. Our models account for the cumulative process of reward acquisition and behavioral adaptation, shaping the evolution of such communities. We juxtapose three DAO scenarios, each characterized by its approach to distributing engagement rights that shape community evolution: Egalitarian (equitable rights distribution), Merit-based (rights based on reputation), and Property-based (rights contingent on investment). These models are compared with traditional open communities that lack reward mechanisms. Our findings underscore the potential of tokenizing creativity to sustain open communities. Notably, the Merit-based DAO exhibits high engagement rates and weak concentration of governance decisions compared to other governance structures. Meanwhile, the Property-based DAO presents a viable alternative by fostering exploratory learning and inclusive reward distribution for creators, albeit with relatively low engagement.

Title: Constrained optimal execution problem in limit order book market with stochastic market depth
Authors: Weiping Wu, Chengneng Jin, Jianjun Gao, Jiajia Yan
Abstract: This work addresses the constrained optimal execution problem in a limit order book (LOB) market with stochastic market depth. Motivated by empirical observations that LOBs often exhibit random patterns, we propose using a Markov chain to model the shape parameters of the LOB. This model encompasses several established cases, including those with block-shaped market depth and nonlinear impact functions. Additionally, recognizing that execution policies in practical applications are typically constrained around nominal policies, we introduce execution bounds into the problem formulation. For the LOB model with infinite resilience and random block-shaped market depth, we derive an explicit optimal policy by exploiting the state separation property inherent in its structure. For the LOB with finite resilience and a general shape, we present two numerical methods. The first method employs approximate dynamic programming, incorporating efficient value function approximation via the Regress-Later Least Squares Monte Carlo approach. The second method utilizes model predictive control, reformulating the problem as a nonlinear programming task. Numerical experiments demonstrate the efficiency of our methods. Furthermore, leveraging our one-sided trading policy, we extend the model to two-sided trading and demonstrate that our execution framework precludes opportunities for price manipulation.

Title: Modeling and analysis of lot streaming and lot splitting in the flexible job-shop scheduling problem
Abstract: The first aim of this paper is to provide an overview on how lot streaming and lot splitting, i.e. when jobs (or lots) are divided into sublots, can be applied to the flexible job-shop scheduling problem (FJSP). Lot streaming corresponds to the case where the sublots must be processed consecutively on the machines, whereas lot splitting allows sublots to be scheduled independently. The latter is particularly interesting in the FJSP, as sublots can be assigned to different machines. We investigate different variants of lot streaming and lot splitting, related to the consistency of the sublot sizes, of the sublot orders for lot streaming and of the sublot assignments for lot splitting. The differences between these variants are discussed and the associated mathematical models are proposed. Afterwards, we conduct extensive computational experiments on classical instances in the literature to analyze the impact of each variant and of some key parameters. For instances solved to optimality, lot streaming achieves significant improvements of over 20%, while lot splitting is able to provide additional savings of 8% on average. Recommendations are derived based on the numerical results and on practical considerations associated to the implementation of lot streaming and lot splitting. Finally, some conclusions and perspectives are provided.

Title: How much harder are indifference adjustments? An experiment on the cognitive effort in multi-criteria decisions
Authors: Wolfgang Haidinger, Florian A.D. Burnat, Juergen Branke, Walter J. Gutjahr
Abstract: This study investigates the cognitive effort required for indifference adjustments (IAs) compared to preference statements (PSs) in multi-criteria decision analysis. While IAs provide substantially more preference information than PSs do, the empirical question of whether the additional cognitive burden is justified remains underexplored. We conducted a field experiment with 83 Austrian roofing professionals who made product decisions about roofing tiles. Participants evaluated products described by 2-4 attributes using both the PS and IA methods, with response time and subjective difficulty ratings as effort measures. Surprisingly, we found that IAs required only 10%–20% more cognitive effort than PSs despite their significantly higher information yield. The effort difference increased slightly with the number of attributes, but remained modest throughout. Our findings suggest that the majority of cognitive effort in both methods stems from comprehending the alternatives rather than making an actual preference judgment or indifference adjustment. These results have important implications for multi-criteria decision support system design, suggesting that IAs offer an attractive trade-off between information gain and cognitive burden.

Title: Entry of a sustainable single-category retailer in a market with multi-category retailers
Authors: H. Sebastian Heese, Eda Kemahlıoğlu-Ziya, Olga Perdikaki
Abstract: New sustainability-marketed firms have emerged in the grocery and consumer packaged-goods categories in response to consumers’ rising preferences for sustainable products. Motivated by this trend in the retail industry, we study how the entry of a new firm that sells an assortment of sustainable consumer goods in one category affects consumers’ channel choices and the existing competing retailers’ market shares across different product categories. We analytically characterize consumers’ shopping preferences in a market with a premium-price retailer and a low-price retailer that each sell two different types of product offerings—packaged goods and fresh goods. We then consider how the entry of a sustainable-product online retailer, which operates only in the packaged-goods category and offers a limited selection, affects consumer preferences, and how the sustainable entrant should price its offering. We find that the low-price retailer becomes more vulnerable after the entry of the sustainable firm, as such entry decreases the retailer’s sales at least weakly in both product categories. In contrast, a brick-and-mortar retailer that charges premium prices and offers more sustainable fresh products can benefit in both the fresh-product and packaged-goods categories from the entry of a sustainable-product competitor. Our findings suggest that the sustainable firm can gain a larger share in highly competitive markets with low price differentials between the two existing retailers in the two product categories, and when customers are not inclined to visit multiple stores to complete their shopping. We identify two pricing strategies for the entrant. When the entrant’s product offering is highly attractive, it is optimal to charge a relatively higher price to extract profit from a larger customer base; when its offering is less attractive, a lower price is optimal to ensure market penetration. Our findings highlight the importance of cross-category interactions in retail competition and provide insights for both sustainable entrants and incumbent retailers.

Title: Selecting return insurance and online channel modes for a capital-constrained manufacturer
Authors: Kebing Chen, Qianyao Zhou, Shengbin Wang, Dong Lei
Abstract: For clothing sold online, the high return rate poses a distinct challenge compared with other product categories. A liberal return policy helps alleviate consumers’ purchase uncertainty and increase their willingness to pay, yet it also imposes a substantial financial burden on companies. To address this issue, we examine a basic supply chain system that consists of a capital-constrained manufacturer and an online platform and explore the manufacturer's online channel mode selection and return insurance strategy. First, we demonstrate that the manufacturer's financing strategy is influenced not only by the level of her initial capital but also by the return insurance cost and the sales mode. Second, we find that when the return insurance cost is sufficiently low, offering return insurance becomes viable, and doing so effectively shifts a substantial portion of the shopping cost to consumers. The choice of online channel mode then determines which party bears responsibility for providing the return insurance service. We show that when the platform's commission rate is high, the manufacturer may avoid profit loss in the agency mode, but should prioritize consumer satisfaction and effectiveness of the platform's marketing effort. Third, our analysis indicates that while the platform's marketing effort consistently increases the manufacturer's profit, it does not always benefit the platform, especially when the manufacturer has limited production capital. Finally, we examine the robustness of our results by extending the baseline model to more realistic settings and consider three key extensions: two alternative financing modes, manufacturer-bearing return costs, and marketing cost sharing.

Title: Deep reinforcement learning for order-tote-robot coordination in multi-tote storage and retrieval systems with sequential picking stations
Authors: Yuexin Kang, Jie Shao, Mingzhe Li, Peng Yang, Rui Chen
Abstract: Multi-tote storage and retrieval systems (MTS/RSs) with sequential picking stations feature a sorting conveyor that connects multiple picking stations, thereby reducing tote-handling effort and maximizing tote utilization. Given the tight coupling among orders, totes, and robots in such systems, order fulfillment can greatly benefit from the joint scheduling of these components. This study investigates the joint order-tote-robot scheduling problem in MTS/RSs with sequential picking stations. We formulate an integrated mixed-integer linear programming model to capture the unique operational characteristics. To address the complex coordination problem, we propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based scheduling framework, designed to adaptively respond to diverse search states and make high-quality sequential decisions. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our model and the superior performance of the proposed DRL-based algorithm. Compared to widely used multi-stage decision-making approaches, our method achieves up to a 71.46% reduction in makespan on large-scale instances. Our findings show that MTS/RS efficiency is more sensitive to the number of totes than to the number of orders. While increasing the number of totes significantly prolongs task completion time, variations in the number of orders have limited impact on the makespan. Additionally, increasing the number of robots initially improves performance substantially, although the marginal benefit decreases as the number grows. In contrast, varying the number of picking stations does not consistently improve performance.

Title: Non-negative autoregressive moving average models for intermittent demand: Forecast accuracy and inventory implications
Abstract: Autoregressive moving average (ARMA) models are widely used in retail demand forecasting, particularly for stationary data. However, their performance on Walmart’s demand data in the M5 competition has been low. One reason could be that ARMA models can generate negative forecasts for intermittent demand patterns, which are prevalent in the Walmart dataset used in the M5 competition. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that enables ARMA models to effectively forecast intermittent demand. Specifically, we establish conditions under which a generic ARMA model generates non-negative filters and forecasts. Additionally, we derive expressions for approximate prediction intervals, making the approach suitable for stock control applications. Through an empirical analysis of 42,686 time series from Walmart’s M5 competition data and 24,029 series from a global cosmetics retailer, we show that a simple non-negative ARMA(1,1) model significantly outperforms standard benchmarks in both point forecasts and prediction intervals. Moreover, the empirical inventory performance analysis shows that the non-negative ARMA(1,1) leads to the highest inventory efficiency as compared to all the benchmarks considered in the paper. These findings underscore the potential of ARMA models to effectively forecast intermittent demand when non-negativity is enforced.

Title: Logic-based Benders decomposition for local and short food distribution
Authors: Pierre Montalbano, Pierre Desport, Yannick Kergosien, Ameur Soukhal, Patricia Coutelle
Abstract: In Europe, short food supply chains have been recognized as a cornerstone of the transition toward a more sustainable food system. New actors emerge to facilitate the relationship between producers and institutions such as catering services. They typically operate within a restricted area, possessing detailed knowledge of producers’ inventories, delivery capacities, and the catering’ product requirements. Their role is to allocate orders to producers and manage the distribution, possibility via a hub if deemed advantageous. Making good decisions for this problem is a difficult task due to several constraints, including delivery capacities, due dates of customers, and perishability of fresh food. Developing tools to solve this problem would enable a more efficient and sustainable coordination between local producers and collective catering services. In this study, we propose a MILP model to address the problem, and develop an exact solution method based on Logic-Based Benders Decomposition. To further enhance its efficiency, we integrate various strategies aimed at accelerating the convergence of the method. Based on a real-world case study Manger Bio Centre-Val de Loire, we evaluated our approach on semi-randomly generated instances of reasonable size. The results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms the direct resolution of the MILP using CPLEX.

Title: Optimizing the two-dimensional bandwidth problem under the maximum norm using exact and heuristic approaches
Authors: Sergio Cavero, Eduardo G. Pardo, Eduardo Rodriguez-Tello, Eric Monfroy, Claudia Vasconcellos-Gaete
Abstract: This paper addresses the Two-dimensional Bandwidth Minimization Problem (2D-BMP) using the L ∞ -norm distance, focusing on embedding a guest graph into a grid-like host graph to minimize the maximum edge distance. While previous research has emphasized theoretical aspects and regular graphs, practical methods for complex graphs remain underexplored. Solving 2D-BMP is crucial for applications such as VLSI design, network simulation, and scheduling, though its NP-hard nature poses significant challenges. We propose three exact Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) models—arithmetic, finite domain, and dichotomic optimization to efficiently solve the 2D-BMP. Additionally, we introduce the Convergence-Based Multi-start Algorithm (CBMA), a heuristic combining greedy construction and local search for approximate solutions. Our CSP exact methods found optimal solutions for 70 small benchmark instances from diverse standard graph topologies, including 21 previously unknown. On the other hand, the CBMA achieved new upper bounds, requiring moderate computational times, for 113 graphs extracted from the Harwell-Boeing Sparse Matrix Collection which present larger and more complex structures.

Title: Improved approximation for min-max k-path cover with neighborhoods: Leveraging refined geometric spanning and adaptive recombination
Authors: Jun Wu, Feng Chu, Zhen Yang, Yongxi Cheng
Abstract: We study the min–max k-path cover problem with neighborhoods (min–max k-PCPN) in the Euclidean plane. Departing from classic discrete-point routing, this problem models customers as service neighborhoods (fixed-radius disks), where demand is satisfied by visiting any point within the geometric region. To address the resulting structural complexity, we propose a search-and-partition framework centered on an adaptive recombination mechanism with a refined geometric spanning strategy. Specifically, this approach hinges on (i) a tightened asymptotic bound for the generalized minimum spanning tree with neighborhoods (GMSTN), which serves as a refined geometric spanning backbone, and (ii) an adaptive recombination mechanism that dynamically partitions neighborhoods and reassembles them into cost-balanced paths based on the spanning backbone. By leveraging the synergy between these two components, our framework yields a new fixed-parameter tractable asymptotic approximation algorithm for the min–max k-PCPN. Furthermore, we generalize our methodology to several related min–max k-path and k-tree cover problems, consistently improving upon the best-known (asymptotic) approximation ratios.

Title: A best-worst method-based FlowSort approach for multi-criteria sorting problems
Authors: Xiao-Hong Pan, Shi-Fan He, Ying-Ming Wang, Jafar Rezaei
Abstract: Best-Worst Method (BWM) is a behaviorally-inspired decision-making method supporting decision-makers to evaluate and prioritize alternatives based on a set of criteria. This study introduces a novel version of BWM, incorporating concepts from the FlowSort method, which is designed to classify alternatives. Given a set of alternatives characterized with a number of criteria, first, a set of limiting profiles, as multi-criteria vectors, is defined by the decision-maker. Using these limiting profiles, pairwise comparisons are conducted between the two reference limiting profiles (best and worst), and the other limiting profiles. These pairwise comparisons form the basis to derive the priorities of the limiting profiles, which are the foundation of establishing criterion-specific value functions. Then, the criterion-wise value scores of alternatives are derived from the value functions. Subsequently, the outranking degrees between alternatives and reference limiting profiles are calculated based on a V-shape function. Following this, a min–max optimization model is established to infer classification indices. Finally, by exploring the relationships between classification indices of limiting profiles and alternatives, several assignment rules are developed to classify alternatives into different classes. The proposed method is applied to a supplier classification problem, and its performance is compared with several existing multi-criteria sorting methods. Its practical applicability is further demonstrated through a real-world case study on university assessment.

Title: Multi-objective performance optimization for picker-to-parts order picking with heterogeneous pickers, scattered storage, and order line splitting
Authors: Zhongqiang Ma, René de Koster, Debjit Roy, Guohua Wu
Abstract: Although robotic order-picking systems are increasingly applied in distribution centers, most of them are still manual. In such warehouses, it is a challenge to pick large amounts of orders efficiently, while meeting tight deadlines. We address the joint decision problem of grouping orders with due times into batches, assigning the “right” picker to pick a batch in a particular sequence, and also identifying the optimal pick location for that picker, assuming products are scattered over storage locations, where each location has a limited inventory of the product. We abbreviate the integrated problem as the JOSPLRP (the Joint Order batching, batch Sequencing, Picker selection, Location selection (with potential order line splitting), and Routing Problem) and formalize it as a mixed integer programming model to minimize total order-picking time, makespan, and tardiness simultaneously, or separately. We also introduce a metaheuristic ALNS-VNS-DP to solve large-scale and benchmark instances. Our method performs similarly or better than Gurobi, sequential optimization, and a state-of-the-art method (for a simplified version of the problem) in solution quality and computation time. Experiments with real-world e-commerce orders show that integrated optimization substantially improves efficiency (in the unit-demand case, the four objectives improve between 1.05% and 20.4% over the sequential approach). Using storage scattering, optimal picker assignment and location selection can substantially improve objectives. Order batching is beneficial even under tight deadlines, though optimal batch sizes depend on the order profile.

Title: Data-driven arrival time suggestion for drivers in trucking platform of export containers
Authors: Zhen Tan, Ziyi Zhong, Zhehua Liu, Hao Luo, Jie Yu, Huan Jin
Abstract: Trucking platforms have emerged in recent years for improving export freight logistics. As bilateral platforms, they need to balance the satisfaction of exporters and truck drivers. A typical scenario is that given the required start loading time of the container at the exporter's warehouse, the platform can make an arrival time suggestion to the assigned driver for reducing the expected time cost for both the exporter and the driver. This decision problem is nontrivial due to uncertainties in drivers’ punctuality and stay times at the warehouses as well as partial schedule and truck information possessed by the platform. Thus, we propose an arrival time suggestion model (ATSM) which computes the suggested arrival time in real-time by solving a stochastic program based on contextual information once a new pick-up task is assigned. Both feature matching and residual-based strategies are proposed for constructing the predictive probability distributions. We prove properties of the single- and bi-objective formulations and design efficient algorithms for common families of punctuality distributions illustrated by numerical examples. Experiments on a real dataset show that the proposed ATSM can potentially reduce the average total time cost by 2.95∼7.58% against historical decisions over various parameter settings. Optimal decision patterns are affected by different task-, driver- and warehouse-specific features. The impacts of key algorithm and model parameters are also discussed, leading to various managerial insights. Our single-objective stochastic program is a novel variant of the newsvendor problem whose theoretical properties and new implications for data-driven decision strategies are discussed, which may be of separate interest.

Title: Competing under antitrust regulations: Can non-discriminatory operations be an alternative for on-demand ride service firms?
Abstract: There are a growing number of antitrust proceedings against major on-demand ride service providers alleging unfair business practices. Ride-hailing platforms that operate with two types of capacities have been at the receiving end of some of these litigations. When platforms prioritise their “leased” drivers over “independent” drivers, it can have serious repercussions. Such prioritisation, while potentially more profitable, raises ethical concerns and legal issues due to its discriminatory nature. In light of these issues, we examine the implications of platforms switching over to non-discriminatory operating policies (NDOPs). Specifically, we explore the consequences of competing with NDOPs on platforms’ performance. Using a two-stage game, we analyse the effect of competition and NDOPs in a duopolistic setting. Contrary to conventional wisdom, our analysis shows that dual-capacity platforms (DPs) can sustain optimal profits under certain conditions. Adopting NDOPs, however, shrinks the operational flexibility of DPs. Our analysis further shows that the shrinkage is lowest when the competition is intense. We also provide an estimate to the managers on the shrinkage DPs can experience with NDOPs. We believe these results can motivate platforms to transition to NDOPs.

Title: Rules for consistent aggregation: With application to cost efficiency decompositions
Authors: Bert M. Balk, José L. Zofío
Abstract: This study offers a complete discussion of existing and novel rules for consistent aggregation, here interpreted as rules ensuring that measurement scores for units can somehow be added or averaged so that their sum or mean has the same structure and interpretation as the unit-level scores. Examples are the denominator rule and the numerator rule, but there are many more, dependent on the choice of aggregation function, either the arithmetic, harmonic or geometric mean, and associated weights, either symmetric or asymmetric. Additionally, when the aggregates are decomposed, this can be done based on equal or unequal weights for the different components. Several of these general rules have appeared dispersedly in the literature to evaluate applied research in fields such as index numbers, efficiency measures, productivity analysis, cross-efficiency measures, and composite indicators. To address this fragmentation, we present a unified framework for assessing and comparing these rules, highlighting their individual characteristics. In addition, we conduct an empirical application that brings all the decompositions together and compares them using a common dataset of financial institutions. From a methodological standpoint, the overall conclusion is that for consistent decomposition a geometric mean, based on symmetric weights — so that there is no need to distinguish between denominator and numerator rules — is advisable. Consistent factorial decompositions appear then also straightforward.

Title: A matheuristic augmented ɛ-constraint framework for a bi-objective Multi-Depot Cumulative Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem
Authors: Eduardo Segredo, Samuel Nucamendi-Guillén, Gara Miranda, Eduardo Lalla-Ruiz
Abstract: In this work, we extend the Multi-Depot Cumulative Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (MDCCVRP) to consider two objectives. Besides its cumulative aspect, i.e., minimizing the sum of customers’ waiting time, we also consider the travel cost minimization. To tackle this problem, we propose a novel matheuristic framework, called Math-AUGMECON-II, consisting of two stages. In the first stage, a multiobjective memetic algorithm based on the well-known Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) is used to obtain an approximation to the Pareto front. This approximation of the Pareto front is then optimized in a second stage using the Augmented ɛ ɛ -Constraint II (AUGMECON-II) approach. The performance of NSGA-II, AUGMECON-II, and Math-AUGMECON-II is evaluated by their application to a set of well-known instances of the MDCCVRP with different sizes. The analyses based on different metrics, such as the number of solutions, hypervolume, and set coverage, reveal that AUGMECON-II is a suitable choice for small instances, while Math-AUGMECON-II is more appropriate to deal with medium and large instances, including instances with a reduced fleet size. Finally, a trade-off evaluation was carried out to examine the extent to which enhancing one objective impacts the other. It revealed that improving latency leads to an increase in travel cost, while improving travel cost results in a deterioration of latency. This highlights the asymmetric compromise between both objectives.

Title: An Explore-Then-Commit strategy for revenue management via sequential estimation
Authors: Jeunghyun Kim, Chihoon Lee, Dongyuan Zhan
Abstract: We introduce and analyze a sequential Explore-Then-Commit (ETC) strategy for revenue management that balances the trade-off between learning about demand and maximizing revenue. Assuming the demand function belongs to a parametric family with unknown parameters, we derive a closed-form stopping rule based on observed Fisher information that allows the decision maker to adaptively determine when to stop price experimentation and commit to a price, eliminating the need to specify a fixed sample size in advance. We show that the proposed algorithm outperforms any fixed sample size ETC procedure in terms of regret and achieves asymptotically optimal min–max regret, a robustness guarantee that no predetermined sample size procedure can attain. We extend the algorithm to a parametric choice model with multiple products and to a network revenue management setting with nonparametric demand and finite resource capacities. Numerical experiments confirm the practical benefits of our approach across all settings.

Title: Pitfalls in radial efficiency decomposition for parallel production systems
Abstract: The data envelopment analysis (DEA) radial model is able to measure the system and division efficiencies of the parallel production system composed of several divisions at the same time. Moreover, the system efficiency can be decomposed into a weighted average of the division efficiencies. However, there is a pitfall in determining the target point for calculating radial division efficiencies, which may obtain negative values under variable returns to scale as discussed in the literature. This paper analyzes the reason that causes the decomposition to fail and develops a model to calculate the correct radial division efficiencies. It is proven that the possibly erroneous radial division efficiency decomposed from the radial system efficiency is less than or equal to the correct radial division efficiency under both constant returns to scale and variable returns to scale. Furthermore, the correct radial division efficiency is less than or equal to the division-specific radial efficiency under constant returns to scale and is equal to the division-specific radial efficiency under variable returns to scale.

Title: Deadlock-free integrated flexible job shop and multiple robots scheduling problems
Authors: Yonghuan He, Hoi-Lam Ma, Sai-Ho Chung
Abstract: In smart manufacturing environments, recognizing the interdependency between machine production and robot routing is crucial for avoiding inefficiencies and deadlocks, especially in no-buffer systems. Deadlocks arise from circular waiting conditions, where each process in a loop waits for a resource held by the next. In this paper, we address the flexible job shop scheduling problem, incorporating multi-robot coordination and deadlock-avoidance considerations, with the objective of minimizing the exit time, that is, the total duration required to complete all jobs and return them to the load/unload area. We propose a branch-and-check heuristic to solve the problem. In this approach, we decompose the problem into a master problem, which determines machine assignment and operation sequencing, and a mixed-integer subproblem, which addresses robot routing. To enhance the algorithm's performance, we introduce valid inequalities, a matheuristic for warm-starting, and several heuristic strategies to accelerate convergence, including heuristic-induced inequalities and fixed-assignment constraints added in later iterations. Computational results demonstrate that our algorithm achieves optimality gaps within 0.8% while reducing computation time by up to 95.7% compared to warm-started CPLEX. Furthermore, we compare our algorithm to an alternative method with fewer variables in the master problem. Our findings also indicate that properly improved robot and machine flexibility can further enhance system performance.

Title: Optimizing parallel machine location and scheduling with sequence-dependent setup times via logic-based benders decomposition
Authors: Yun Wang, Peng Wu, Zhe Yuan, Yeming Gong, Ajay Kumar
Abstract: This study introduces a novel problem in parallel machine location and scheduling that considers one key practical factor: sequence-dependent setup times. Its objective is to minimize the makespan by optimally selecting machine locations, assigning jobs to these machines, and determining the operation sequences, while accounting for the challenging sequence-dependent setup time constraints. We first construct a new compact mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model with a stronger linear relaxation lower bound, which is then strengthened with a set of valid inequalities derived from its structural properties. To solve practical-sized instances more efficiently, we propose an exact, customized full-feature logic-based Benders decomposition algorithm (FLBBD). The FLBBD incorporates three advanced features: (i) we propose new valid lower and upper bounds to further shrink the search space of the FLBBD; (ii) we propose a tailored constraint programming approach to efficiently solve NP-hard subproblems; (iii) we propose specialized combinatorial and analytical cuts to further accelerate the solution process. Detailed experimental results show that (i) The proposed FLBBD algorithm can solve a significantly greater number of instances to optimality compared with the off-the-shelf MILP solver CPLEX and BD incorporated within CPLEX; (ii) The FLBBD algorithm finds feasible solutions for 100% instances whereas CPLEX and BD solve only 81.17% and 57.65% instances; (iii) The FLBBD algorithm attains a smaller average optimality gap of 4.89%, in contrast to the 59.10% and 26.09% average optimality gap observed for CPLEX and BD; and (iv) The derived valid inequalities reduces 6.67% computational time and 62.37% optimality gap compared with CPLEX.

Title: Fair and effective dynamic allocation under stochastic supply and demand
Abstract: Motivated by humanitarian operations such as food and vaccine distribution, we introduce the fair and effective dynamic allocation under stochastic supply and demand (FEDA-SSD) problem, where real-time resource allocation decisions need to be made under uncertainty. We model the problem as a finite-horizon Markov decision process, in which decisions must be made at pickup and demand points, with supply and demand realizations revealed only upon arrival at each node. With limited vehicle capacity and insufficient total supply, the challenge is to allocate the collected items effectively and equitably. We propose the radial basis function with value function approximation (RBF-VFA) solution framework, employing stage-specific radial basis function interpolants within a backward recursive dynamic programming approach. By training separate models for each decision point and propagating approximations backward, our method enables efficient, near-optimal decision-making. Numerical experiments on empirical and randomly generated instances demonstrate that our RBF-VFA outperforms the best known benchmark for this problem. Our findings provide several managerial insights: we show how conservative early rationing triggers capacity-induced downstream waste, we demonstrate how optimal policies adapt to realized system-wide supply-to-demand ratios, and that the spatial positioning of downstream high-variance demand points alters optimal early allocations.

Title: Branch-price-and-cut for the vehicle routing problem with simultaneous delivery and pickup, time windows, and load-dependent cost
Abstract: The vehicle routing problem with load-dependent cost is an extension of the classical capacitated vehicle routing problem in which the cost of traveling along an arc is dependent on the load carried by the vehicle. For the benefit of generalization, this work considers the vehicle routing problem with simultaneous delivery and pickup, time windows, and load-dependent cost (VRPSDPTW-LDC). We utilize both continuous and discontinuous monotonically non-decreasing load-dependent cost functions. These cost structures are justified by real-life applications: First and foremost, transportation cost rises in load due to increasing fuel cost. In addition, cost functions may also show discontinuities due to toll-by-weight schemes, weight restricted passage, and lift axles that may be raised when the vehicle is empty or lightly loaded, therefore decreasing tire wear. We employ a fully equipped branch-price-and-cut algorithm to solve the VRPSDPTW-LDC. A major complication in its development is the consistent handling of the load-dependent cost in the column-generation subproblem when solved by bidirectional labeling algorithms. Indeed, in the VRPSDPTW-LDC, the precise load on board is not known when a partial path is constructed. We provide a unifying description of the associated resource extension function for forward and backward labeling. In several computational experiments, we analyze algorithmic components of the branch-price-and-cut algorithm, and give managerial insights on the impact of the cost structure on key metrics such as total cost, the number of routes, and the average load carried in an optimal solution.

Title: Analyzing the potentials of car-free zones in Munich
Authors: Vladimir Stadnichuk, Maximilian Schiffer, Grit Walther
Abstract: Car-free zones (CFZs) are designed to reduce urban air pollution by restricting vehicle access and promoting sustainable transportation. City authorities implement CFZs to support pedestrians, cyclists, and public transport, aiming to achieve sustainability goals in transportation. However, the introduction of CFZs requires strategic planning to balance the benefits against potential negative impacts on businesses and private vehicle users. Our research addresses this challenge by focusing on the interrelation between city authorities establishing CFZs and network users adjusting their travel behaviors in response. We employ a bilevel optimization model, with the first level representing city authorities’ decisions on CFZ locations and the second level reflecting network users’ adaptations. To make this bilevel model computationally tractable, we develop novel acceleration techniques based on smart path enumeration. We validate the proposed model and derive managerial insights from a case study in Munich, Germany. We study the impact that CFZs of varying sizes have on external cost savings and user mode choice. Furthermore, we investigate how restricting displaced car traffic from CFZs influences our results.

Title: Pareto fronts for privacy-utility trade-offs in multi-query systems
Authors: Yi Yin, Guangquan Zhang, Hua Zuo, Jie Lu
Abstract: Multi-query systems have become a common paradigm for enabling flexible access to sensitive data. However, their openness introduces privacy risks, most especially from attribute inference attacks (AIAs), where adversaries infer sensitive attributes by analyzing strategically crafted queries. While defenses such as differential privacy (DP) and query limit help mitigate these risks, determining appropriate privacy parameters, particularly the privacy budget ϵ and the maximum query limit N , to protect privacy while maintaining data utility remains a significant challenge. To address this trade-off, we first introduce a bilevel optimization framework for multi-query systems. We construct a realistic interaction model involving a query-based system (QBS) server, users, and a QueryCheetah-based attacker to capture real-world multi-party dynamics under advanced threat scenarios. Within this framework, the upper level is formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem that seeks to defend against the attacker while satisfying utility requirements by selecting appropriate privacy configurations. The lower level simulates an attacker that optimizes its attribute inference strategy under these configurations. To solve the upper-level optimization problem, we design a task-aware adaptive Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) to search for Pareto-optimal configurations. The algorithm leverages the monotonicity of privacy and utility metrics, and incorporates dynamic search space pruning and direction-guided mutation to enhance search efficiency and improve solution quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework can significantly enhance search efficiency and optimization precision given advanced AIA threats.

Title: An exact algorithm for public transport line planning considering passenger and operational costs and lost demand
Authors: Siv Marie Cartland Hansen, Rowan Hoogervorst, Otto Anker Nielsen, Richard Martin Lusby, Evelien van der Hurk
Abstract: Line planning in public transport is the strategic problem of selecting lines and their operating frequencies. This problem is important as it defines the passenger service, based on available connections and expected travel times, and drives operational cost in terms of the number of vehicles required. This paper presents a line planning model that minimizes the weighted sum of passenger travel time, including in-vehicle time and frequency-dependent waiting and transfer times, and operating costs for the public transport agency. Unlike traditional approaches that assume demand to be fixed, our approach requires a minimum service level for demand to be captured, ensuring that services are provided only when they are attractive to users and cost-efficient to operate. The introduced capacity constraints ensure sufficient capacity on the lines and help guide the trade-off between expected demand on selected lines and their frequencies. The resulting mixed-integer program presents a challenging combinatorial problem as the number of passenger paths grows rapidly in relation to the number of lines and frequencies considered. To address this, we propose an iterative exact algorithm that utilizes a reduced problem representation and dynamically expands it with additional frequencies and paths. Evaluated on four networks with varying complexity and cost trade-offs, our method achieves significant speed-ups and tighter bounds compared to solving the complete model directly by CPLEX, particularly when operator and passenger costs are more evenly balanced in the objective. Furthermore, we demonstrate how accounting for lost demand leads to more efficient resource use from an overall perspective.

Title: Accelerated Benders Decomposition for the Two-Level Generalized Median Tour Problem
Authors: Nickolas Gueller, Bruno Fanzeres, Rafael Martinelli
Abstract: This work addresses the Two-Level Generalized Median Tour Problem (TLGMTP), a recently introduced extension of the Generalized Median Tour Problem (GMTP) motivated by complex logistics challenges such as multi-level health care systems. The TLGMTP poses significant computational challenges due to its hierarchical structure and the presence of fixed-charge decisions, which increase the complexity of exact solution methods. We propose a Benders Decomposition (BD) framework enhanced with a suite of acceleration techniques, including a Branch-and-Benders-Cut scheme for efficient tree exploration, subproblem normalization for stronger feasibility cuts, an adaptive in-out stabilization procedure, a set of valid inequalities to tighten the formulation, and a novel cut filtering mechanism to manage the model size. Computational experiments on 41 GTSP-Lib instances demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed approach. Our framework not only outperforms the existing Branch-and-Cut algorithm but also solves significantly larger instances previously unsolved. In particular, across all instances optimally solved by both methods, the BD approach achieved solutions 1.7 times faster. Compared to the automatic Benders implementation available in CPLEX, our method was more than 3.4 times faster. To further extend the study, we introduce new asymmetric and large-scale symmetric instances, solving a particularly challenging case with 575 nodes and 115 clusters, the largest to date. Furthermore, by adapting the input data, the same framework is applied to GMTP, achieving new optimal solutions for large instances. This study highlights the potential of BD to tackle hierarchical network design problems, offering a scalable and effective alternative to classical exact methods.

Title: Delivery-time benchmark design in food delivery platforms
Abstract: Online food-delivery platforms rely on delivery-time benchmarks to manage service quality and customer expectations. This paper studies how the design of these benchmarks affects operational decisions when delivery outcomes are uncertain and lateness is penalized more heavily than early delivery is rewarded. We model a platform that chooses dispatch intensity over time while performance is evaluated against a benchmark that may either remain fixed or updated based on recent deliveries. The analysis shows that benchmarks which adapt to recent performance can reduce dispatch effort: when a series of fast deliveries causes future service standards to become more demanding, a forward-looking food-delivery platform may restrain current dispatch intensity, such as courier prioritization or surge deployment, to limit exposure to higher penalties from subsequent late orders. In volatile environments where delivery times are heavily influenced by traffic, restaurant delays, or weather, fixed externally anchored benchmarks perform better by insulating service standards from noise. In more stable settings where performance is predictable and improvements persist, internally adaptive benchmarks perform better by allowing standards to reflect underlying capability. We provide sufficient conditions for preference of each regime and develop an asymptotic characterization showing why optimal benchmark design tends to select externally anchored or internally adaptive regimes, rather than intermediate hybrids, as the state space grows. We illustrate the theory using two stylized delivery environments that represent distinct operational regimes commonly faced by food-delivery platforms.

Title: A unifying approach to shift design and rotating workforce scheduling
Abstract: In many organizations, human resources are a primary cost driver. Therefore, careful scheduling of this resource is paramount. The shift design and scheduling process involves several steps from the recognition of staffing requirements to the deployment of an operational schedule. Based on the staffing requirements and shift design constraints, a set of workable shifts is devised. The shift scheduling process then determines the number of employees and assembles these shifts into a shift schedule, consisting of work shift and rest sequences. Due to their complexity, shift design and shift scheduling problems are often decomposed. This study investigates an integration of shift design and scheduling, focusing specifically on the rotating workforce scheduling problem. In addition to the shift design objective, we model an ergonomics objective for the quality of the schedule. We propose a compact network flow formulation and graph representation that ensures feasible shift designs by modeling the schedule as an Eulerian cycle of work and rest sequences. Experiments indicate that our approach is able to quickly solve problem instances based on benchmark sets for the shift design and rotating workforce scheduling problem. Furthermore, our results indicate that integrated planning improves ergonomics compared to a sequential approach.

Title: A matheuristic for integrated scheduling of manufacturing assembly, product transport, and material supply
Authors: Bilgenur Erdogan, Quang-Vinh Dang, Mehrdad Mohammadi, Ivo Adan
Abstract: With Industry 4.0 advancements, production environments are becoming increasingly automated. However, integrating smart robots introduces new scheduling challenges for efficiently coordinating tasks such as manufacturing assembly, product transport, and material supply. Unlike previous studies that address these tasks separately or in pairs, we address their simultaneous scheduling in a pull-based production line, where assembly tasks depend on product delivery by automated guided vehicles (AGVs) and material supply by autonomous mobile robots (AMRs). The problem is to assign product transport tasks to AGVs and material supply tasks to AMRs, sequence these tasks on each robot, and schedule assembly tasks at workstations, with the objective of minimizing the makespan. We formulate a mixed-integer linear programming model, and develop a matheuristic based on iterated local search and linear programming to tackle computational complexity of larger instances. Using a real battery manufacturing case study, we evaluate the efficacy of our methods in varying fleet sizes, the number of jobs, and the number of assembly lines. Our computational results reveal that the proposed matheuristic significantly outperforms current practice, with makespan reductions of 22% on average.

Title: Large neighborhood search for the two-dimensional irregular bin packing problem
Authors: Jianming Wang, Kuan Xu, Zhouwang Yang
Abstract: This paper investigates the two-dimensional irregular bin packing problem with limited rotations, focusing on efficiently packing irregular, potentially non-convex polygons into the fewest number of fixed-dimension bins. The problem is decomposed into two subproblems: polygon assignment and single-bin packing. To solve the assignment problem, we propose a large neighborhood search (LNS) approach featuring large-perturbation operators that explore a far broader neighborhood than existing methods. To initialize the LNS, we design a two-stage construction procedure that combines the best-fit rule with a round-robin scheme, providing a high-quality starting solution. We also introduce an adaptive strategy that fixes the LNS parameters automatically from the characteristics of the initial solution, improving balanced performance and reducing the need for manually selecting operator frequencies across diverse instances. For the single-bin packing problem, we apply an overlap-minimization technique each time assignment feasibility is evaluated. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that, under the closest comparable time budget, the proposed approach achieves better average results than previous methods for every bin size. Moreover, the extended-run results demonstrate the strong improvement potential of the proposed method: it obtains the best-known results in 56 out of 66 instances and improves the objective value by an average of 2.9% over the previous state of the art. Extensive experiments further validate the contribution of each module and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method for the two-dimensional irregular bin packing problem.

Title: Dynamic task allocation of heterogeneous aircraft for wildfire suppression via deep reinforcement learning
Authors: Jia Yuan, Quan Shao, Jianhong Sun, Vedpal Arya
Abstract: Heterogeneous aircraft, including drones, helicopters, and fixed-wing planes, are playing an increasingly important role in wildfire suppression operations. However, efficient resource allocation remains challenging due to dynamic fire propagation, diverse operational capabilities, and competing objectives. This paper develops a task allocation model that integrates aircraft performance attributes with the evolving characteristics of fire spread and introduces a deep reinforcement learning framework based on Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). The framework enables adaptive policy learning in high-dimensional and uncertain environments. Simulation experiments, calibrated with real geographical and meteorological data, show that the PPO-based algorithm converges up to 40% faster, reduces task completion time by more than 10%, and increases overall task benefits by approximately 22% compared with classical optimization and evolutionary approaches. These findings provide actionable decision support for emergency command departments, enabling rapid and scientifically-grounded deployment of aerial firefighting resources in complex and uncertain wildfire scenarios.

Title: Environmental efficiency under materials balance: A minimum-distance directional slack approach
Authors: Hirofumi Fukuyama, Stavros Kourtzidis, Roman Matousek, Nickolaos G. Tzeremes
Abstract: This study develops a two-stage environmental–economic framework for U.S. states over 1998–2017 within a materials-balance setting. In the first stage, we construct a convexified materials-balance technology in which undesirable outputs are directly linked to an emission-generating input through materials-balance conditions, and we derive an environment-oriented sub-vector efficiency measure in the spirit of Hampf and Rødseth (HR). The resulting radial environmental efficiency scores are then used to transform the pollution-related variables and define a second benchmark technology from which we obtain a materials-balance-based minimum-distance directional slack inefficiency (minDistDSI) measure. This dual structure permits a comparison between a conventional frontier perspective and a minimum-distance perspective, thereby distinguishing deeper structural inefficiency from proximity to feasible improvement targets. In the second stage, we embed both indices in a Bayesian difference-in-differences design with staggered policy adoption and event-study diagnostics to assess the causal effects of state environmental interventions. The results indicate meaningful reductions in major air pollutants, whereas average policy effects on the efficiency indices are modest and imprecisely estimated. Overall, the evidence supports a tiered policy approach in which minimum-distance benchmarks guide attainable short-run improvements, while the HR-based measure identifies longer-run environmental performance gains requiring broader structural adjustment.

Title: Improving manufacturer energy efficiency: The effects of bank downside risk management and government incentives
Authors: Wei Jin, Chengfu Wang, Qinhong Zhang, Wenli Wang
Abstract: Energy efficiency (EE) improvement in energy-intensive manufacturing industries delivers substantial economic and environmental benefits. However, credit constraints arising from banks’ downside risk management may impede manufacturers’ EE investment. Using a two-period decision framework, we investigate whether and how government incentives can alleviate such underinvestment. We show that investment-based and savings-based incentives targeting the manufacturer are equally effective in promoting EE investment, but they exacerbate the savings intensity gap induced by the bank's downside risk management. To correct this distortion, we introduce a guarantee-based incentive aimed at the bank and demonstrate that it effectively narrows the savings-intensity gap while generating synergistic value when combined with either of the manufacturer-targeted incentives. Further comparative analysis reveals that, to achieve a given savings target, the savings-based incentive yields higher manufacturer profitability but exposes the bank to greater downside risk. Moreover, the investment-based incentive exhibits higher cost efficiency than the savings-based incentive when the target is mildly modest. Under credit constraints, supplementing either manufacturer-targeted incentive with the guarantee-based instrument improves cost efficiency and renders the comparative outcomes similar to those observed in the credit-unconstrained scenario. These findings remain robust when extending the model to settings with ex-ante production decisions, tax-deduction incentives, and volatile energy prices. Overall, these insights offer valuable guidance for policymakers designing effective incentives to enhance EE and support decarbonization in energy-intensive industries.

Title: Stable formulations for the Capacitated Facility Location Problem with Customer Preferences
Authors: Concepción Domínguez, Juan de Dios Jaime-Alcántara
Abstract: In the Simple Plant Location Problem with Order (SPLPO), the aim is to open a subset of plants to assign every customer taking into account their preferences. Customers rank the plants in strict order and are assigned to their favorite open plant, and the objective is to minimize the location plus allocation costs. Here, we study a generalization of SPLPO named the Capacitated Facility Location Problem with Customer Preferences (CFLCP) where a limited number of customers can be allocated to each facility. We consider the global preference maximization setting, where the customers preferences are globally maximized. We define three new types of stable allocations, namely customer stable, pairwise stable and cyclic-coalition stable allocations, and we provide two mixed-integer linear formulations for each setting. In particular, our cyclic-coalition stable formulations are Pareto optimal in a global-preference maximization setting, in the sense that no customer can improve their allocation without making another one worse off. We assess the performance of the proposed formulations and the quality of the resulting stable allocations through extensive computational experiments. As an additional contribution, we present a novel formulation that provides maximum-cardinality Pareto-optimal matchings for the Capacitated House Allocation problem.

Title: The value of platform-based digital certification in the value-added tax system
Authors: Yaobin Wu, Chenyu Wang, Xiangfeng Chen
Abstract: Traditional value-added tax (VAT) systems often suffer from inefficiencies in input tax deduction due to unverifiable costs stemming from informal upstreams, thereby reducing fiscal transparency and distorting the tax liability. We investigate how platform-based digital certification can mitigate such tax frictions and create value for the supply chain. A game-theoretical model is developed involving a manufacturer, a platform, and the government to analyze the strategic interactions among production decision, certification pricing, and tax collection. The results show that incomplete input VAT causes losses for both the manufacturer and the platform while also reducing government tax revenue in high-cost industries. The adoption of platform certification expands the manufacturer's feasible cost range, establishes optimal pricing strategies for the platform, and creates conditions under which both firms and the government can achieve Pareto-improvement outcomes. Further extensions, considering differentiated VAT policy, platform certification cost, and firm competition, confirm the robust value of platform certification and demonstrate their impacts on the Pareto-improvement regions for both firms and all three parties. The findings indicate that platform certification serves as an effective tool for enhancing VAT traceability, increasing corporate profits, and boosting government tax revenue.

Title: An explainable dynamic programming framework for interpreting optimal condition-based maintenance policies
Abstract: This study investigates the optimization of condition-based maintenance (CBM) for k-out-of-N systems operating under stochastic degradation and monitored through periodic inspections. The system model accounts for economic dependencies among components within the k-out-of-N system structure, emphasizing group maintenance policies that balance cost efficiency and reliability. To enhance interpretability, we propose an Explainable Dynamic Programming (XDP) framework that decomposes the optimal average cost and associated bias functions into interpretable cost channels: preventive maintenance, corrective maintenance, setup, and system failure costs. The proposed Decomposed Relative Value Evaluation algorithm operationalizes this approach, ensuring that each channel's contribution is computed in a DP-consistent and additive manner. Beyond standard operations-research post-optimality tools, we benchmark XDP against traditional cost breakdowns and sensitivity analysis. While these conventional approaches provide parameter-level shares and response-to-perturbation insights, XDP yields an exact decomposition of the baseline optimal long-run cost into channel-wise contributions and explains state-dependent action choices through cost-channel drivers. The XDP framework enables rigorous comparison between the optimal CBM policy and a widely used heuristic policy, revealing how and why heuristic rules deviate from optimality. Numerical experiments on an aircraft engine system show that the optimal policy achieves a lower total average cost and a more balanced cost distribution across maintenance channels, and that XDP highlights the dominant cost drivers and their trade-offs. Overall, the proposed XDP methodology bridges the gap between dynamic programming–based CBM optimization and practical interpretability, offering a transparent and analytically grounded approach for decision-making in complex reliability systems.

Title: Supply chain dynamics under the proportional order-up-to replenishment policy: The role of the lead time
Authors: Geng Cui, Stephen M. Disney, Naoto Imura, Katsuhiro Nishinari
Abstract: We investigate how lead time affects supply chain dynamics under the proportional order-up-to (POUT) policy, a linear extension of the celebrated order-up-to (OUT) policy. We reveal how auto-correlated demand processes — commonly observed in practice and widely studied in the literature — influence the effect lead time has on a supply chain's dynamics and economic performance. Our key findings challenge the conventional understanding of lead time. We show that reducing lead time does not always decrease order and net stock variances; instead, the impact of lead time reduction depends on the interaction between demand correlation and the POUT policy's proportional controller. Moreover, we identify an even–odd lead time effect, whereby the parity of lead time influences the impact of lead time reduction, as well as the choice of the optimal proportional controller for maximising economic performance. These results contrast with the perception that lead time reduction always improves supply chain performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate that modifying the POUT policy by replacing the lead-time-ahead demand forecast with the mean demand eliminates the even–odd lead time effect. This modification also enhances economic performance in certain scenarios.

Title: A column generation-based heuristic algorithm for home healthcare scheduling and routing with synchronization and workload balance
Authors: Marzieh Amini Rarani, Ehsan Nikbakhsh, Mehdi Mahnam, Seyed Hessameddin Zegordi
Abstract: Home healthcare includes medical and support services provided in the homes of patients and people in need to help them manage their conditions, maintain comfort, and reduce the need for in-person visits to medical centers. Based on field observations of home healthcare centers and a review of existing literature, this study develops a mathematical model for scheduling and routing caregivers within a daily planning horizon. The proposed model optimizes scheduling and coordination for patients requiring two caregivers, minimizing the time difference between their arrivals. It also considers high-priority patient visits, workload balance among caregivers, reduced working time, and patient satisfaction factors such as preferred time windows, gender preferences, and caregiver–patient loyalty. In addition, we incorporate caregiver fatigue and time-dependent travel time to develop a more realistic model. To efficiently tackle the proposed problem, we design a heuristic approach based on column generation that employs a customized labeling algorithm to solve the caregiver's routing sub-problem. To ensure solution integrity and feasibility, the algorithm incorporates several novel features. Testing on generated instances demonstrates significant reductions in computational time (up to 99%) and near-optimal solution gaps (0.53% for small instances and -2% for large ones). Finally, a case study confirms the model's effectiveness, showing a 22.9% improvement over the current plan and highlighting its potential for real-world applications and its ability to enhance similar systems.

Title: Evaluating disruption risks at the chokepoints of the maritime transport network to support re-routing decision-making
Authors: Tao Wen, Yu-wang Chen, Jingchuan Ma, Tahir Abbas Syed, Arijit De
Abstract: Maritime transport is crucial to global trade and economic stability, yet natural hazards and human-induced disruptions at key chokepoints pose significant risks to the reliability of the global maritime network. To address this challenge, we develop an agent-based model to examine how chokepoint disruptions affect vessel-level operations and re-routing decision-making and how these micro-level responses affect system-wide transport performance and trade flows. The model incorporates heterogeneous vessel characteristics, including estimation deviation and sensitivity to disruption, to represent adaptive routing under uncertainty. We evaluate the effects of disruption duration, estimation deviation, and vessel sensitivity on system performance, measured by recovery time, additional sailing distance, and delayed freight weight. Results show that even short-term disruptions can induce detours amounting to millions of additional kilometers, increasing operational costs and fuel consumption, and that the system may require one to two months to return to normal operations. We further analyze joint disruptions of the Suez and Panama Canals under various scenarios to demonstrate that disruption timing significantly affects recovery and disruption severity. These findings offer actionable guidance for vessel operators and logistics firms on when proactive re-routing is beneficial, and they inform port authorities and supply-chain stakeholders in designing contingency plans and improving risk management.

Title: Measuring environmental efficiency using refined semi-disposability and inefficiency assumptions of undesirable outputs
Authors: Junfei Chu, Yanhua Dong, Shaonan Wu, Weijiao Wang
Abstract: Assessing environmental efficiency is crucial for identifying emission reduction potential and establishing benchmark targets, providing organizations with clear pathways to meet their emission reduction goals. This paper introduces a new approach for assessing environmental efficiency of decision-making units (DMUs) by rigorously examining every production axiom for undesirable outputs. We begin by identifying certain limitations in the existing formulation of the semi-disposability assumption. In its current form, the assumption appears to lack full mathematical rigor and may not adequately capture the freely disposable portion of undesirable outputs, making it resemble more an inefficiency assumption rather than a semi-disposability assumption. To address this problem, we redefine the semi-disposability axiom using a formulation that more accurately reflects its physical meaning and distinguishes it from the existing formulation. Additionally, we clarify the distinctions between strong disposability and inefficiency axioms for undesirable outputs and propose a practical inefficiency axiom with a compliance bound. Using these refined production axioms and some conventional ones, we construct a new production possibility set (PPS) as well as models for environmental efficiency evaluation under both constant returns to scale (CRS) and variable returns to scale (VRS) scenarios. We also demonstrate the efficiency monotonicity property of the models and show how the environmental efficiency of each DMU is decomposed into environmental managerial efficiency and environmental technical efficiency. Finally, the proposed approach is then validated and compared with existing models through a numerical example and a case study of China's Thermal Power Industry.

Title: Robust valuation and optimal harvesting of forestry resources in the presence of catastrophe risk and parameter uncertainty
Authors: Ankush Agarwal, Christian Oliver Ewald, Yihan Zou
Abstract: We determine forest lease value and optimal harvesting strategies under model parameter uncertainty within stochastic bio-economic models that account for catastrophe risk. Catastrophic events are modeled as a Poisson point process, with a two-factor stochastic convenience yield model capturing the lumber spot price dynamics. Using lumber futures and US wildfire data, we estimate model parameters through Kalman filtering and maximum likelihood estimation and specify the model parameter uncertainty set as the 95% confidence region. We numerically determine the forest lease value under catastrophe risk and parameter uncertainty using reflected backward stochastic differential equations (RBSDEs) and establish conservative and optimistic bounds for lease values and optimal stopping boundaries for harvesting. Numerical experiments further explore how parameter uncertainty, catastrophe intensity, and carbon sequestration impact the lease valuation and harvesting decision. In particular, we explore the costs arising from this form of uncertainty in the form of a reduction of the lease value. These are implicit costs which can be attributed to climate risk, and are likely to become more significant as forestry resources play a larger role in the energy transition. We conclude that in the presence of parameter uncertainty, it is better to lean toward a conservative strategy reflecting, to some extent, the worst case than being overly optimistic. Moreover, our results suggest that convenience yield plays a substantial role in determining optimal harvesting strategies within the two-factor model adopted in this study.

Title: Integrating real options analysis with ε-constraint optimization for multi-objective decision-support: A case study on investment in offshore electrification
Authors: Olga Noshchenko, Verena Hagspiel, Maria Lavrutich
Abstract: This paper introduces a novel multi-objective real options approach for optimal investment planning, focusing on economic and environmental aspects of polluting projects’ decarbonization under market uncertainty. The approach integrates real options analysis with the multi-objective optimization method, where emissions are treated as an ε-constraint, a predefined upper limit representing an emission limit set by the company. By using such an integrated approach, the research addresses the dilemma between a project's profitability and environmental performance. The proposed methodology is applied to a case study of offshore platform electrification on the Norwegian Continental Shelf, where offshore wind power electrification is considered a key strategy to meet emissions reduction targets. The model aims to identify optimal investment decisions allowing to balance emissions constraints and project profitability while considering fluctuating commodity and CO 2 allowance prices. The results highlight the potential for decarbonization and the effectiveness of setting and committing to environmental targets at the firm level. Meanwhile, the sensitivity analysis of different renewable energy technology scenarios underscores the critical role of technological development in driving further decarbonization.

Title: The impact of ancillary services in green hydrogen investment valuation
Authors: Lars Erik Lunde Halbrendt, Maria Lavrutich, Inger Kristine Melhus, Ståle Størdal
Abstract: As the share of intermittent renewable energy sources increases, there is a growing need for flexible resources to maintain grid stability. Green hydrogen, produced by electrolysis, is recognized as a key flexible resource because of its easily adjustable production process. However, previous studies often deem investments in green hydrogen production unprofitable, largely because they tend to overlook the potential revenue from ancillary services. This paper addresses this gap by examining the impact of integrating ancillary services into the investment strategy for a green hydrogen production plant. We link a stochastic price model with an hourly resolution optimization and a real options valuation to quantify the benefits of co-optimizing hydrogen production and ancillary service participation for hydrogen plants in Norway and Germany. Our results show that optimizing the electrolyzer's daily production to include participation in ancillary services markets substantially raises the project's NPV and eliminates the value of delaying investment. In contrast, without ancillary services, spot-price volatility creates an incentive to delay investment. This effect is stronger in Germany than in Norway due to more volatile spot prices. This highlights the complementary role of real-options valuation and participation in the ancillary services markets, where ancillary service revenues act as an operational hedge, smoothing cash flows and reducing price volatility, thereby reducing the incentive to postpone investment.

Title: Optimal investment in an energy storage system
Authors: Marta Castellini, Chiara D’Alpaos, Fulvio Fontini, Michele Moretto
Abstract: Renewable energy production plays a crucial role in the energy transition. However, many renewable energy sources are intermittent, and there is often a mismatch between energy production and consumption, which can be partially solved by storage. In this paper we investigate the investment decision in a photovoltaic (PV) power plant coupled with a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), namely an Energy Storage System (ESS). We aim to investigate the relationship between the net present value (NPV) of the investment and the technical implications related to the maximum amount of energy to be stored while also accounting for the impact of energy prices. In our setting an ESS is connected to the national power grid. Energy can be produced, purchased from the grid, stored, self-consumed, and fed into the grid. PV production and energy consumption loads evolve stochastically over time. In addition, as BESSs are costly, the energy stored has an opportunity cost, which depends on the prices of energy purchased from the grid and energy fed in and sold to the grid, respectively. However, BESS can significantly contribute to increasing ESSs’ managerial flexibility and ESSs’ value. We investigate the optimal size of a BESS that minimizes ESSs’ net operating costs. We also provide insights into the optimal operating strategy of an ESS. Our results show that the net operating costs of an ESS are relatively small. They decrease for increasing selling prices of energy, whereas they increase with increasing volatility of the stock of energy stored in the battery.

Title: Locational marginal value of battery network
Authors: Xinjiang Chen, Puxiang Tan, Yu Yang, Guannan He
Abstract: The battery network, including stationary energy storage (SES) and mobile energy storage (MES), is gaining attention for the role in improving power system flexibility and resilience. However, most studies focus on SES or fail to evaluate the economic contributions of MES to node operations. Additionally, the impact of battery degradation caused by frequent charging and swapping on the value of MES is often overlooked. To address these gaps, we propose a framework to evaluate the locational marginal value (LMV) of a battery network, defined as the cost reduction achieved by adding one unit of battery capacity with a specific state of health (SOH) to MES at a given node.
