We define functions for battery energy efficiency and capacity based on SOH and develop a model to optimize battery network and power system dispatch, considering battery charging and swapping coordination. Analytical expressions for LMV are derived, capturing their dependence on system operating states and conditions. The LMV is decomposed into three components: the energy storage component, the energy transportation component, and the locational marginal price component. Using data from China's power systems, we validate the LMV theory through numerical experiments, revealing that using batteries with different SOH results in a 20 % difference in the LMV of the battery network, demonstrating its accuracy and value in guiding MES deployment.

Title: Out of the black into the green? Modeling the pathways for regional coal transitions
Authors: Dieter Grass, Michael Kuhn, Omkar Patange, Alexia Prskawetz, Stefan Wrzaczek
Abstract: Coal is a major contributor to anthropogenic carbon emissions and climate change. Coal mining and combustion are also leading causes of premature mortality due to local air pollution. Conversely, coal is central to many regional economies that rely on its mining, power generation, industrial use and exports. With accelerating climate change and continuously high air pollution within many coal-centered economies, the urgency for coal phase-out has become more prominent in recent years. This has put pressure on coal-dependent regional economies to implement energy transitions in a time bound manner. This paper studies optimal pathways for a coal phase-out within a small, open, regional economy consisting of a coal extraction sector, an energy sector composed of both coal-based and renewable power generation, and a final goods sector that relies on coal and electricity. Taking the perspective of a social planner who maximizes regional welfare and employing optimal control theory, we study the conditions under which coal extraction and fossil power generation are phased out, depending on preferences, cost and price structures. We also provide a systematic analysis of the dynamic processes associated with the transition out of coal of (formerly) coal-based regional economies, including the scope for multiple equilibria that may reflect stalling transitions. Our results will be relevant for regional governments in undertaking a transition away from coal in a way that safeguards regional welfare and at the same time contributes to global climate goals.

Title: Rank-1 transition uncertainties in constrained Markov decision processes
Authors: V Varagapriya, Vikas Vikram Singh, Abdel Lisser
Abstract: We consider an infinite-horizon discounted constrained Markov decision process (CMDP) with uncertain transition probabilities. We assume that the uncertainty in transition probabilities has a rank-1 matrix structure and the underlying uncertain parameters belong to a polytope. We formulate the uncertain CMDP problem using a robust optimization framework. To derive reformulation of the robust CMDP problem, we restrict to the class of stationary policies and show that it is equivalent to a bilinear programming problem. We provide a simple example where a Markov policy performs better than the optimal policy in the class of stationary policies, implying that, unlike in classical CMDP problem, an optimal policy of the robust CMDP problem need not be present in the class of stationary policies. For the case of a single uncertain parameter, we propose sufficient conditions under which an optimal policy of the restricted robust CMDP problem is unaffected by uncertainty. The numerical experiments are performed on randomly generated instances of a machine replacement problem and a well-known class of problems called Garnets.

Title: A data-driven distributionally robust optimization approach for the core acquisition problem
Authors: Cheng-Hu Yang, Xiao-Li Su, Xin Ma, Srinivas Talluri
Abstract: Reusing electric vehicles (EV) batteries that reach the end of their useful first life is an environmental and cost-competitive option; however, the process of recycling EV batteries is not yet mature. Due to complex electrochemical reactions and physical conditions, the quality of used EV batteries (cores) is highly uncertain. The remanufacturer needs to make the acquisition decision under quality distributional ambiguity. Perfect quality distribution of cores cannot be known to the remanufacturer in practice. We develop distributionally robust optimization models based on phi-divergence measures and the imprecise Dirichlet model (DRO-IDM) to derive robust decisions. First, we find that the bounds of quality probability intervals are identified solely based on the collected data by introducing the imprecise Dirichlet model. The derived finite-sample boundary can reduce the scope of the uncertainty set and avoid the no-direction search issue. Second, our models can hedge against distributional uncertainty, reduce the probability of a robust solution that deviates from the optimal solution, and correct bias in decision making. Third, we extend the DRO-IDM to develop data-driven models, that can reassess the value of multisource quality information to improve the estimation accuracy of core quality and maximize the remanufacturer's profit. Our study provides new insights for remanufacturers: the new remanufacturing process proposed in our work can assist remanufacturers in utilizing the values of cores without disassembly; the information-aware algorithm can offer the remanufacturing sector a valuable tool for efficiently filtering out invalid information in optimizing acquisition decisions; this capability empowers decision-makers to leverage multiple sources of information and expedite the process of digital transformation in remanufacturing; our approach can also provide a manner of integrating information fusion and distribution learning into remanufacturing.

Title: Problem of locating and allocating charging equipment for battery electric buses under stochastic charging demand
Authors: Sadjad Bazarnovi, Taner Cokyasar, Omer Verbas, Abolfazl (Kouros) Mohammadian
Abstract: Bus electrification plays a crucial role in advancing urban transportation sustainability. Battery Electric Buses (BEBs), however, often need recharging, making the Problem of Locating and Allocating Charging Equipment for BEBs (PLACE-BEB) essential for efficient operations. This study proposes an optimization framework to solve the PLACE-BEB by determining the optimal placement of charger types at potential locations under the stochastic charging demand. Leveraging the existing stochastic location literature, we develop a Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Program (MINLP) to model the problem. To solve this problem, we develop an exact solution method that minimizes the costs related to building charging stations, charger allocation, travel to stations, and average queueing and charging times. Queueing dynamics are modeled using an M/M/s queue, with the number of servers at each location treated as a decision variable. To improve scalability, we implement a Simulated Annealing (SA) and a Genetic Algorithm (GA) allowing for efficient solutions to large-scale problems. The computational performance of the methods was thoroughly evaluated, revealing that SA was effective for small-scale problems, while GA outperformed others for large-scale instances. A case study comparing garage-only, other-only, and mixed scenarios, along with joint deployment, highlighted the cost benefits of a collaborative and a comprehensive approach. Sensitivity analyses showed that the waiting time is a key factor to consider in the decision-making.

Title: A prudent framework for understanding risk-awareness in demand response
Abstract: We show that risk-aware behaviors in demand response originate from superquadratic state-dependent cost functions and price uncertainty with skewed distributions. We obtain such results through developing a novel theoretical demand response framework that combines non-anticipatory multi-stage decision-making with superquadratic cost functions. We introduce the concept of prudent demand, defined by a positive third-order derivative of the cost function, which is the first principle for risk-averse behavior despite a risk-neutral objective. Our analysis establishes that future price uncertainty affects immediate consumption decisions, and the extent of this response scales proportionally with the skewness of the price distribution. We visualize our theoretical findings through numerical simulations and illustrate their practical implications using a real-world case study.

Title: Strategic investment in electricity markets: Robust optimization versus stochastic programming
Authors: Álvaro García-Cerezo, Afzal S. Siddiqui, Trine K. Boomsma, Raquel García-Bertrand, Luis Baringo
Abstract: Decarbonization policies have spurred the adoption of variable renewable energy (VRE) technologies such as wind and solar power. To enable flexible resources and accommodate VRE’s intermittency, electricity markets are shifting toward renewable-aware dispatch based on stochastic optimization. However, strategic firms may exploit such market structures to manipulate prices to their advantage. To complement the extant literature, we compare investment decisions as well as worst-case profits and losses in the context of generation expansion by a strategic firm that uses either risk-averse stochastic programming or robust optimization. The former is a bi-level optimization problem, whereas the latter is a tri-level problem. Our contributions are threefold in addressing policy and methodological challenges. First, we demonstrate that using robust optimization instead of stochastic programming generally leads to investment plans with a higher share of VRE because it serves as a hedge during undesirable realizations with low consumer willingness to pay and high marginal costs for conventional generation. Second, a regret analysis shows that the worst-case profit is significantly reduced if an investor uses expansion decisions from stochastic programming, highlighting the importance of selecting a methodology aligned with the main objective of the investor. The effect is especially pronounced if decisions stem from a social planner, thereby indicating how a conventional, centralized perspective may fail to reflect private incentives for generation expansion in evolving electricity markets. Third, the analysis of strategic behavior necessitates state-of-the-art decomposition techniques such as the constraint generation-based algorithm and the column-and-constraint generation algorithm for the bi- and tri-level problems, respectively.

Title: Power-gas infrastructure planning under weather-induced supply and demand uncertainties
Authors: Rahman Khorramfar, Dharik Mallapragada, Saurabh Amin
Abstract: Implementing economy-wide decarbonization strategies based on decarbonizing the power grid via variable renewable energy (VRE) expansion and electrification of end-uses requires new approaches for energy infrastructure planning that consider, among other factors, weather-induced uncertainty in demand and VRE supply. An energy planning model that fails to account for these uncertainties can hinder the intended transition efforts to a low-carbon grid and increase the risk of supply shortage especially during extreme weather conditions. Here, we consider the generation and transmission expansion problem of joint power-gas infrastructure and operations planning under the uncertainty of both demand and renewable supply. We propose two distributionally robust optimization approaches based on moment (MDRO) and Wasserstein distance (WDRO) ambiguity sets to endogenize these uncertainties and account for the change in the underlying distribution of these parameters that is caused by the climate change, among other factors. Furthermore, our model considers the risk-aversion of the energy planners in the modeling framework via the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) metric. An equivalent mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) reformulation of both modeling frameworks is presented, and a computationally efficient approximation scheme to obtain near-optimal solutions is proposed. We demonstrate the resulting DRO planning models and solution strategy via a New England case study under different levels of end-use electrification and decarbonization targets. Our experiments systematically explore different modeling aspects and compare the DRO models with stochastic programming (SP) results.

Title: Robust collaborative routing problem with time-dependent travel times and uncertain service durations for home services
Authors: Li Jiang, Xiaoning Zang, Changyong Liang, Xiang Fang
Abstract: Balancing cost efficiency with high service quality has become a challenge for service providers in the rapidly growing home service sector, where tasks are time-sensitive and affected by traffic conditions and uncertain service durations. To address this, we propose a robust collaborative routing model that integrates time-dependent travel times and uncertain service durations, enabling multiple providers to optimize routes jointly, reduce costs, and improve service reliability. The proposed model captures two major sources of uncertainty: (i) time-dependent travel times arising from urban traffic congestion and (ii) stochastic service durations due to personalized task requirements. To handle these complexities, we propose a route-based robust optimization framework with a master problem and multiple pricing problems and incorporate individual rationality constraints to ensure sustainable long-term collaboration. A robust branch-price-and-cut algorithm is developed to solve the model, integrating column generation for the master problem with a tailored robust labeling algorithm for the pricing problems. Computational experiments on benchmark and real-world instances validate the efficiency and effectiveness of our method in handling uncertainty. Results also reveal a key trade-off: while collaboration considerably reduces total cost and fleet size, it may increase the risk of service delays. Our approach addresses this by incorporating tunable robustness parameters, which offer decision-makers a practical means to balance cost efficiency with service reliability.

Title: Geometric optimization of wildlife corridors on grid-based landscapes using integer programming
Authors: Chao Wang, Jorge A. Sefair, Robert J. Fletcher
Abstract: Conservation corridors play a critical role in mitigating biodiversity loss by linking fragmented habitats. A central challenge in designing these corridors lies in satisfying ecological requirements through geometric constraints such as connectivity, redundancy, width, and size. In this study, we propose a mixed-integer programming model that integrates these geometric features into the corridor design process, with the objective of maximizing corridor utility over a grid-based landscape. To enhance computational performance, we develop a Branch-and-Cut algorithm supported by a bound-improving heuristic, valid inequalities, and a variable reduction preprocessing routine. We evaluate our approach on a real-world landscape aimed at protecting the Florida panther, as well as on a suite of computer-generated landscapes. Results show that the algorithm can efficiently produce near-optimal solutions for instances with up to 3000 patches within a two-hour time limit.

Title: Taxing emissions and de-risking investments in renewables: Insights from electricity markets
Abstract: We investigate the optimal design of CO 2 taxation policies along with renewable energy de-risking instruments in the context of decarbonizing power sectors that are subject to investment risk. We develop a two-stage multi-period stochastic equilibrium model that captures endogenous investment decisions regarding production and storage assets. Some market fundamentals, such as demand, prices, and production profiles, are risky. Furthermore, investors are risk-averse and the financial market is incomplete inasmuch as it lacks sufficient risk-sharing instruments. The model integrates economic and environmental incentives through a multi-objective framework based on social welfare and emissions, allowing for the characterization of the Pareto-optimal frontier for de-risking/emissions-taxation policies. As a proof of concept, we apply the model to a stylized representation of the French power system, considering a diverse mix of generation and storage technologies. Our results show that de-risking instruments and CO 2 taxes are imperfect substitutes and must be optimized jointly to avoid suboptimal outcomes—such as over-investment in renewable production, market distortions induced by excessive de-risking, or insufficient emissions reductions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that commonly used de-risking instruments in Europe may lead to spot-market inefficiencies and welfare losses. Our findings provide actionable policy guidance by identifying optimal de-risking/emissions-taxation combinations and quantifying the performance gap in current European policies relative to the Pareto frontier.

Title: From the ivory tower to the field: The impact of humanitarian operations research on humanitarian practice
Abstract: Since the first publications on humanitarian operations, researchers have been concerned about the impact of our research on humanitarian practice. This paper seeks to better understand the gap between research and practice and, thus, how to narrow it. We incorporate not only the research perspective, through a review of 640 abstracts in humanitarian operations and a survey of the author community, but also the practitioner perspective, through 18 interviews with experienced humanitarian practitioners and a review of 131 practitioner conference proceedings. We assess the extent of practice impact, and find limited but important instances. We identify new barriers to achieving practice impact from the practitioner perspective. Finally, we develop a framework for describing the depth and reach of practice impact achieved by a research project, with a description of many ways in which such impact may be (and has been) achieved. We hope these efforts enable greater researcher accountability to practitioners and clearer paths to practice impact for the field.

Title: Dynamic incentive mechanisms on renewable power consumption with generators’ competition
Authors: Shuqin Xu, Qi Xu, Devika Kannan, Kannan Govindan
Abstract: The growing penetration of renewable energy into the power grid has heightened competition between renewable and conventional generators. To facilitate renewable power consumption and carbon emissions reduction, and to ensure a higher quality of power supply, this paper considers that the energy trading platform incentivizes competitive power generators to improve electricity supply quality by offering dynamic incentive contracts. This study examines how to formulate dynamic incentive contracts with considering competition between power generators over electricity supply quality. It compares dynamic contracts with and without competition, as well as static contracts under competition. Additionally, case studies from China and Australia's power sectors are analysed. The results demonstrate that dynamic contracts enhance renewable energy consumption as competition intensity increases. Compared to the non-competitive scenario, dynamic contracts incorporating competition incentivize power generators to deliver higher electricity supply quality. When the potential share of green electricity demand exceeds a certain threshold, Australia achieves higher renewable electricity trading volumes and consumption levels than China. As competition intensifies, China must more promptly take measures to meet the required share of green electricity demand to achieve its 2030 renewable energy targets. Furthermore, the study contributes to the revenue management field and finds that dynamic contracts outperform static contracts, supporting the United Nations 2030 Sustainable Development Goals. Renewable energy consumption performs significantly better under dynamic contracts.

Title: Multicomponent biogas membrane separation by superstructure optimization
Authors: Bernardetta Addis, Veronica Piccialli, Christophe Castel
Abstract: This study addresses the challenge of membrane separation for biogas upgrading in a multicomponent system containing a small fraction of N 2 . The final product of the process is biomethane, which is the biogas after separation and purification, where all species in addition to methane have been removed. The minimal purity of CH 4 that allows transport and use is generally 98%. We aim to design a system that meets this purity requirement while maximizing biomethane recovery from the feed gas. To achieve this, we employ a superstructure optimization approach that balances performance with industrial feasibility and robustness. The problem is formulated as a Mixed Integer Non-Linear Programming (MINLP) model, incorporating cubic equality constraints derived from discretized differential equations governing membrane physics. Furthermore, the model allows to enforce industrial operability requirements (no small flows, reduced number of splits). Due to the difficulty of general solvers to tackle the resulting MINLP, we propose an ad-hoc solution procedure. After enumerating all viable industrial configurations, a global optimization algorithm determines the optimal design parameters and operating conditions to maximize recovery without compromising the purity threshold of 98% CH 4 . The advanced MEMSIC module is used for numerical simulation to evaluate the practical feasibility of optimized solutions. The numerical results highlight the increased complexity of the three-gas system compared to simpler two-gas scenarios, underscoring the need for sophisticated modeling and optimization techniques.

Title: Optimization-augmented machine learning for vehicle operations in emergency medical services
Abstract: Minimizing response times to meet legal requirements and serve patients in a timely manner is crucial for Emergency Medical Service (EMS) systems. Achieving this goal necessitates optimizing operational decision-making to efficiently manage ambulances. Against this background, we study a centrally controlled EMS system for which we learn an online ambulance dispatching and redeployment policy that aims at minimizing the mean response time of ambulances within the system by dispatching an ambulance upon receiving an emergency call and redeploying it to a waiting location upon the completion of its service. We propose a novel combinatorial optimization-augmented machine learning pipeline that allows to learn efficient policies for ambulance dispatching and redeployment. In this context, we further show how to solve the underlying full-information problem to generate training data and propose an augmentation scheme that improves our pipeline's generalization performance by mitigating a possible distribution mismatch with respect to the considered state space. Compared to existing methods that rely on augmentation during training, our approach offers substantial runtime savings of up to 87.9% while yielding competitive performance. To evaluate the performance of our pipeline against current industry practices, we conduct a numerical case study on the example of San Francisco's 911 call data. Results show that the learned policies outperform the online benchmarks across various resource and demand scenarios, yielding a reduction in mean response time of up to 28%.

Title: Pure Nash equilibrium market recommendations
Abstract: New business models help sellers make better decisions by communicating information about market prices. However, sellers’ inability to coordinate greatly reduces the efficacy of this information and can lead to market failures. We study the feasibility and benefits of providing equilibria as recommendations in economies where sellers face price uncertainty, information scarcity, and an inability to coordinate. We describe a general model in which sellers wish to sell some quantity of a good at one of several markets with elastic prices, and show that while a pure Nash equilibrium may not necessarily exist, an approximate equilibrium always exists under mild assumptions on the market concentration. We describe an algorithm that a market planner can use to recommend approximate equilibria to sellers, and compare the recommended (approximate) equilibria to selling strategies identified from a survey of onion and potato farmers in India. Using real data on India's agricultural markets, we show that the recommended strategy outperforms the other strategies in terms of seller welfare, geographic price dispersion, market volume concentration, and several metrics of individual farmer welfare improvements. We use parameterized data to show that the framework is robust to imperfect market penetration, is fair to smaller farmers, and captures nearly all of the welfare from a welfare-maximizing allocation.

Title: Simple games with one minimal winning vector
Abstract: Every simple game is a monotonic Boolean function. For the other direction, we just have to exclude the two constant functions. The enumeration of monotone Boolean functions with distinguishable variables is also known as Dedekind's problem. The corresponding number for nine variables was determined by two disjoint research groups in the recent literature. Considering permutations of the variables as symmetries, we can also speak about non-equivalent (or non-isomorphic) monotone Boolean functions (or simple games). Additionally, the recent determination of the number of non-equivalent monotone Boolean functions with nine variables and a summary of the previous history on the problem are also discussed in the recent literature. Here, we consider simple games with a unique minimal winning vector. A closed formula for the number of such games is found as well as its dimension in terms of the number of players and equivalence classes of players.

Title: Do social relationships lead to bias in group decision-making? A simulation analysis based on screening-selection model
Authors: Xue Feng, Shifeng Liu, Yuan Xu, Xiaopu Shang
Abstract: In the group decision-making (GDM) process, social networks play a crucial role in facilitating communication and information exchange among decision-makers (DMs). However, most existing GDM models primarily focus on interactions among DMs, while neglecting the social relationships between DMs and the alternatives being evaluated (named “reviewees”). As decision-making environments grow more complex and involve numerous alternatives, traditional single-stage GDM models often struggle to balance efficiency and accuracy. To address the above limitations, we propose a screening-selection GDM (SS-GDM) model, which integrates both the social trust network among DMs and the social relationships between DMs and reviewees, thereby capturing how social factors influence opinion dynamics and consensus formation across two distinct yet interconnected stages: the screening stage and the selection stage. A numerical case and comparative analyses demonstrate the practical application and advantages of the proposed SS-GDM method. Simulation experiments further indicate that social trust and opinion similarity are the key drivers in shaping group opinions and promoting consensus. However, the social relationships between DMs and reviewees can lead to bias during the screening stage. In contrast, the selection stage characterized by open communication can weaken such bias. Additionally, when reviewees exhibit high capability, such bias tends to diminish. Overall, this model enhances our understanding of how social networks influence GDM processes and provides actionable strategies to improve fairness and reduce bias in real-world GDM scenarios, such as excluding DMs with close social ties to reviewees, anonymizing reviewee information during the screening stage, and encouraging open communication during the selection stage.

Title: Substitute recommendations and in-transit order cancellations
Abstract: Online retail platforms are implementing in-transit order cancellations (ITOC) through digital logistics such as delivery interception. Although originally designed to reduce return losses for sellers and enhance consumer experience, platforms have repurposed ITOC into a marketing tool that creates additional revenue by using substitute recommendations to induce consumers to cancel initial orders and purchase substitutes. This study analytically examines how the interplay of substitute recommendations and ITOC affects the profits of downstream platform and upstream seller in an agency-based supply chain. Our findings show that platforms benefit from ITOC even when recommending inferior substitutes, while sellers benefit under conditions of high value losses from returns and low consumer return hassle costs. Furthermore, when premium substitutes are recommended, ITOC may create a conflict of interest between platforms and sellers, whereas recommending inferior substitutes better aligns their interests. Our study highlights that substitute recommendations and ITOC can be complementary, enabling platforms to balance seller interests and their profits.

Title: An active three-way concept-cognitive computing system for dynamic financial fraud detection
Authors: Yun-Long Mi, Yi Qu, Huan Zhu, Zongrun Wang, Gang Kou, Yong Shi
Abstract: Fraud detection is a popular topic in financial services, and has been extensively studied in different areas such as accounting and finance, information systems, business intelligence, and data mining. However, most machine learning methods rely on supervised learning and assume a balanced class distribution within the data. This ignores the problems of evolving data over time, between-class imbalance, and label scarcity in the fraud detection process. Crucially, these methods cannot obtain outstanding detection prediction performance due to their failure to address the dynamic data with limited labels and class imbalance. Therefore, we propose a novel dynamic fraud detection method: active three-way concept-cognitive computing system (atC3S). It comprises constructing an initial learning model, making fraud predictions, active three-way concept learning, and updating the learning model. The atC3S leverages an active three-way concept learning method, concept-center neighborhood, and concept-dynamic optimization strategies to improve the effectiveness of dynamic fraud detection. Experimental results on several real-world financial fraud datasets show that atC3S can demonstrate excellent performance on discriminating between fraudulent and nonfraudulent detections under label scarcity and class imbalance scenarios. Finally, excessive requests for label information from experts are not the most cost-effective strategy considering the label acquisition cost.

Title: The impact of technology spillover and diffusion on competing manufacturers’ market expansion strategies
Authors: Hui Huang, Bin Liu, Naimeng Liu
Abstract: In technology-asymmetric markets, technology upgrading may help weak manufacturers expand, but it can also intensify rivalry with powerful incumbents. Weak manufacturers may rely on passive technology spillover, whereas powerful manufacturers may respond through deliberate technology diffusion under profit sharing. This paper develops a two-stage Stackelberg game to examine how these two upgrading paths jointly shape market encroachment and firms’ strategic incentives. A distinctive feature of our framework is that competition intensity is endogenous to the technology gap, so technology upgrading affects not only perceived product quality but also the intensity of rivalry. We show that technology spillover does not uniformly improve the weak manufacturer's market expansion outcome. Although spillover improves product appeal, it can also intensify competition enough to reduce the profitability of substantial encroachment. However, we also find that technology spillover may broaden the boundary of substantial encroachment when the spillover level remains relatively low. Technology diffusion is sustained under a narrower set of conditions. It becomes attractive when the weak manufacturer's cost disadvantage is limited, and the technology gap is sufficiently small, and it may arise either as a jointly preferred arrangement or as a defensive response to unmanaged spillover. We further characterize the implementable range of profit-sharing terms and show that technology diffusion may be strategically desirable yet contractually infeasible when technological or cost asymmetry is too large. These findings clarify how alternative upgrading paths reshape market encroachment and when rival upgrading can be sustained through contract-based governance.

Title: Chance-constrained battery management for electric bus scheduling
Authors: Léa Ricard, Guy Desaulniers, Andrea Lodi, Louis-Martin Rousseau
Abstract: The adoption of electric buses introduces challenges related to limited driving range, extended charging times, and strict battery management requirements. These requirements — often set by battery leasing companies or warranty providers — typically include recommended ranges for the battery's state-of-charge (SoC). This study addresses these challenges by proposing a novel chance-constrained model for the electric vehicle scheduling problem that accounts for stochastic energy consumption and battery management guidelines. The model ensures compliance with recommended SoC ranges while optimizing operational costs. A tailored branch-and-price heuristic with stochastic pricing problems is developed. Computational experiments on realistic instances show that the stochastic approach offers good trade-offs between operational costs and compliance with battery management guidelines, reducing costs by up to 10% compared to a deterministic worst-case benchmark. In contrast, we show that relying on expected energy consumption yields solutions with a near-certain probability of violating SoC guidelines, rendering such an approach unsuitable for practical use.

Title: Two approaches for real-time robust rolling stock rescheduling given disruption duration uncertainty
Authors: Joris Wagenaar, Evelien van der Hurk, Richard Lusby, Marie Schmidt
Abstract: In railway planning, effective disruption management tools can limit the impact of a disruption. A key challenge is that disruption durations are typically uncertain, leading to inefficiencies such as unnecessary shunting, seat-shortages, end-of-day inventory mismatches, and trip cancellations. To address this challenge, we propose two different approaches for incorporating robustness in real-time rolling stock rescheduling under uncertain disruption duration, an aspect that is typically assumed to be known in existing rescheduling models. The first approach, Light trip robustness (LTR) requires that a pre-specified percentage of critical trips are robust with respect to their incoming composition across different disruption durations. The second approach, Strict composition robustness (STR), ensures feasibility across all possible disruption durations without further changes to compositions or shunting operations. Both methods extend a well-known rolling stock rescheduling model by explicitly accounting for multiple possible disruption durations. We develop an online evaluation framework and conduct a computational study using real-world data from the Dutch railway network. Our results demonstrate that explicitly accounting for disruption duration uncertainty can significantly reduce rescheduling costs when disruptions last longer than initially expected. For instance, the STR model achieves up to 21% lower total costs compared to models that do not consider robustness, while the LTR model offers flexibility and performs well under moderate uncertainty. However, these benefits can come at a cost when the initially expected disruption duration is accurate. Overall, our results show that robust rolling stock rescheduling can significantly improve operational resilience and reduces the need for reactive updates. The appropriate level of robustness should be chosen based on the likelihood of disruption duration extensions.

Title: The collect-and-process vehicle routing problem with completion time minimization: An application in home healthcare
Abstract: Home healthcare (or simply homecare) refers to providing medical services to individuals in their homes rather than in a hospital or in outpatient clinics. This system is convenient for the public authorities, which reduces the operational costs of medical facilities, is beneficial for the environment because it prevents patients from going to a hospital, and is comfortable for patients who can receive medical assistance without leaving their houses. In this work, we deal with clinical exams such as blood sampling, which requires collecting a sample from the patient and delivering it to a laboratory where it must be processed and analyzed. Currently, healthcare professionals collect all the samples and then deliver them to the labs at the end of the day. This results in an inefficiency in the processing system, in which labs are overloaded in the late afternoon and are not working during the first part of the day. To better balance lab workload and provide timely results to the patients, we introduce the Collect-and-Process Vehicle Routing Problem with Completion Time minimization, in which each lab has a maximum processing capacity for each time slot, and samples exceeding this capacity are postponed to the next slot. The goal is to provide a routing and scheduling plan that minimizes a sample’s average completion time. We provide a formulation of the problem and a fast procedure to compute tight lower bounds. To efficiently and effectively handle large-sized instances, we develop a multi-neighborhood local search matheuristic. Results show the high-quality performance of the proposed method. Insights indicate that it is more convenient to visit labs at the end of the time slot than to visit them at the beginning and exploit the residual time to collect further samples. Another insight is that solutions containing well-balanced routes in terms of route duration are preferable with respect to unbalanced ones.

Title: Exact methods and a scalable heuristic for a hierarchical bi-objective two-agent scheduling problem
Authors: Shijin Wang, Ruihe Liu, Yihong Hu, Feng Chu
Abstract: This paper studies a hierarchical bi-objective two-agent scheduling problem motivated by a practical Print-on-Demand (POD) production setting. The primary objective is to minimize the total number of tardy jobs, and the secondary objective is to minimize the absolute difference in average weighted tardiness between the two agents, thereby capturing an efficiency–fairness trade-off. We formulate two mixed integer programming (MIP) models using position-based and time-indexed decision variables, and strengthen them with five valid inequalities (VIs). To solve medium-scale instances to optimality, we develop a tailored decomposition-based cutting-plane (CP) method enhanced with three infeasibility cuts and one no-good cut. For larger instances, we design a two-stage heuristic combining tardy-pattern search and sequence refinement. Computational experiments evaluate the valid inequalities, the efficiency–fairness trade-off, the limits of the exact methods, the dispatching-rule baselines, and the heuristic scalability. The results show that the position-based MIP formulation enhanced with all VIs reduces average solution times for small instances by about 97%. They further reveal that allowing only one or two additional tardy jobs can reduce the fairness imbalance. The exact CP method solves most instances with up to 50 jobs within one hour and can prove optimality for many tested instances with 80 and 100 jobs, although with more variable runtimes. The heuristic outperforms baseline dispatching rules andobtains high-quality solutions for instances with up to 1000 jobs within seconds. These results provide a scalable solution framework for fairness-aware real-world POD scheduling.

Title: Scheduling in distributed two-machine permutation flow shops for maximizing the total early work subject to arbitrary due dates
Authors: Xin Chen, Yongkang Zhao, Xinbo Liu, Bertrand M.T. Lin, Jacek Blazewicz
Abstract: This study addresses the problem of maximizing total early work in distributed flow shops that are composed of multiple identical distributed two-stage flow shops. The total early work criterion quantifies the cumulative benefit of scheduling jobs relative to their arbitrary due dates. To tackle this challenge, we first present a mixed integer linear programming (MILP) model to formalize the problem. We establish that the general problem is computationally intractable and prove that even a simplified scenario involving a single flow shop remains strongly NP-hard. However, for the special case where the number of due dates is constant, we introduce a pseudo-polynomial time dynamic programming algorithm, demonstrating that the problem is then weakly NP-hard. Furthermore, we design two meta-heuristic approaches, a genetic algorithm and an ejection chain algorithm, to generate high-quality scheduling solutions. Computational experiments reveal that the genetic algorithm outperforms the ejection chain algorithm in terms of scheduling quality, though it requires a longer running time.

Title: Minimizing maximum regret in two-stage facility location with site preparation costs
Abstract: This paper introduces the two-stage capacitated facility location problem under demand and facility construction cost uncertainty with site preparation costs. In the first stage, the decision maker decides whether to pay site preparation costs to obtain an option for potential future utilization of a facility at each candidate site. In the second stage, after demand and facility construction costs are known, the decision maker decides whether to execute each option and construct a facility at each prepared site, and simultaneously allocates demands across the utilized facilities. We use a robust optimization framework with budgeted uncertainty sets to formulate a mixed-integer linear program and develop a column-and-constraint generation algorithm, incorporating a Benders decomposition approach, to solve the resulting minimax regret problem. We conduct numerical tests to identify the relationship between problem conditions and the optimal solution’s properties. We further examine the performance of the minimax regret solution evaluated against the minimax cost objective (and vice versa), and find that minimax cost solutions exhibit higher worst-case regret for instances with a large percentage of fixed cost associated with the first-stage decision and one of the following conditions: (a) small transportation cost, (b) large total facility cost, or (c) a large number of potential facilities. The minimax regret model appears to hedge against the potential regret of overinvestment in the first stage by preparing fewer facilities and increasing capacity utilization, at the expense of larger travel distances.

Title: Robust extensible bin packing and a convex knapsack problem
Authors: Noam Goldberg, Michael Poss, Yariv N. Marmor
Abstract: We study a robust extensible bin packing problem, under a budget uncertainty model where item sizes lie in the intersection of a box with a one-norm ball. We design an algorithm based on the column-and-constraint generation framework, which alternates between solving a master robust bin-packing problem with a finite uncertainty set and solving a separation problem. We show that the separation is strongly NP-hard given solutions to the continuous relaxation of the master problem. Then, focusing on the separation problem for the integer master problem, we show that this problem becomes a special case of the continuous convex knapsack problem, which is known to be weakly NP-hard. Next, we prove that our special case remains NP-hard. We develop a pseudo-polynomial dynamic program (DP) and a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for our special case whose running times match those of the binary knapsack problem. Finally, our computational study shows that the DP can be significantly more efficient in practice compared with solving the problem with specially ordered set (SOS) constraints using advanced mixed-integer programming (MIP) solvers. Our experiments also demonstrate the application of our separation problem method to solving the robust extensible bin packing problem, including separating based on approximate master solutions in intermediate iterations. We further enhance the algorithm by proposing custom symmetry breaking inequalities, valid when bins have identical costs per unit of excess capacity. Finally, a case-study, based on real elective surgery data, demonstrates the potential advantage of our model compared with the actual schedule and optimal nominal schedules.

Title: Multi-objective online convex optimization via joint gradient descent
Authors: Jieyuan Guo, Lizhen Shao, Fangyuan Zhao
Abstract: In this paper, we study multi-objective online convex optimization, where a learner repeatedly makes decisions in the presence of multiple conflicting objectives. We introduce a novel multi-objective regret based on ɛ-nondominance, which measures the uniform translation of the cumulative vector loss required to reach the offline weakly nondominated set in hindsight. We further show that, by applying convex duality, this regret admits an equivalent minimax representation, which reveals an underlying saddle-point structure and provides a tractable basis for regret analysis and algorithm design. Based on this equivalent formulation, we develop an Online Joint Gradient Descent (OJGD) algorithm that performs descent-ascent updates to handle multiple conflicting objectives online. Under standard convexity assumptions, OJGD is shown to achieve sublinear regret. Experimental results on convex learning problems, non-convex multi-task benchmarks, and real-world online streaming data from recommender systems demonstrate favorable performance compared with existing approaches.

Title: An alternating direction method of multipliers for utility-based shortfall risk portfolio optimization
Authors: Rufeng Xiao, Zhiping Li, Rujun Jiang
Abstract: Utility-based shortfall risk (UBSR), a convex risk measure sensitive to tail losses, has gained popularity in recent years. However, research on computational methods for UBSR optimization remains relatively scarce. In this paper, we propose a fast and scalable algorithm for the UBSR-based portfolio optimization problem. Leveraging the Sample Average Approximation (SAA) framework, we reformulate the problem as a block-separable convex program and solve it efficiently via the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). In the high-dimensional setting, a key challenge arises in one of the subproblems -- a projection onto a nonlinear feasibility set defined by the shortfall-risk constraint. We propose two semismooth Newton algorithms to solve this projection subproblem. The first algorithm directly applies a semismooth Newton iteration to the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) system of the projection problem. The second algorithm employs an implicit function transformation of semismooth functions to reduce the problem to a univariate equation involving the Lagrange multiplier and achieves global superlinear convergence with enhanced numerical stability under mild regularity conditions. Theoretical convergence guarantees of the proposed algorithms are established, and numerical experiments demonstrate a substantial speedup over state-of-the-art solvers, particularly in high-dimensional regimes.

Title: Transportation-energy integration: Strategic, tactical and operational decision optimization
Authors: Xuan Yang, Xiang T.R. Kong, George Q. Huang, Lóri Tavasszy
Abstract: Transportation-Energy Integration (TEI) has become increasingly important as low-carbon mobility relies on the joint operation of transportation systems and electricity/hydrogen/multi-energy infrastructures. This paper provides a comprehensive review of peer-reviewed journal research on TEI published between 2010 and 2026. The review is organized into four parts: strategic-level planning, tactical-level coordination, operational-level execution, and cross-level integration. For each part, we synthesize representative decision problems, coupling mechanisms, modeling choices, and solution approaches, and we identify level-specific research gaps. Building on these gaps, we propose a structured research agenda in the form of research perspectives for each part, covering adoption-endogenous planning and physics-aware strategic models, scalable centralized optimization for tactical coordination with decentralized mechanism design, feasibility-first optimization-learning control for operations, and full-stack integration of cross-level decisions.

Title: Editorial Board
Portfolio optimization with decreasing absolute risk aversion stochastic dominance constraints
Authors: Miloš Kopa, Thierry Post, Jana Junová
Abstract: An optimization method is developed for constructing investment portfolios which stochastically dominate a given benchmark for all decreasing absolute risk-averse investors, using Quadratic Programming. The method is applied to a standard data set of historical returns of equity industry portfolios. The proposed optimization method improves upon the performance of mean-variance optimization by tens to hundreds of basis points per annum out of sample, depending on whether short sales are allowed. The improvements critically depend on imposing the complex condition of Decreasing Absolute Risk Aversion in addition to the simpler conditions of global risk aversion and decreasing risk aversion.

Title: Optimizing online grocery service: From customer understanding to multichannel profitability
Authors: Daniela Fernandes, Fábio Neves-Moreira, Pedro Amorim, Jan C. Fransoo
Abstract: We study the optimal online service for grocery retailers operating both physical and online stores. The challenge lies in optimizing the size of the online assortment and the delivery fees to maximize profitability across channels, while considering customer, operational, and market dynamics. Using transaction data from a major grocery retailer, we employ an alternative-specific conditional logit model to investigate how delivery fees, assortment size, network characteristics, and customer needs influence store choice and spending across physical and online channels. We develop a profitability model that incorporates online service variables, customer behavior, and operational costs, enabling us to explore optimal strategies under various conditions. By identifying favorable conditions for the online store and analyzing optimal service variables, we provide actionable insights for retailers. Our findings challenge common practices in omnichannel retail. We show that delivery fees should not merely cover costs but can be strategically set higher, particularly for retailers with strong offline presence. Additionally, while reducing fulfillment costs improves profitability, its impact is smaller than expected. Multichannel retailers can offset these costs by passing them on to customers, with minimal overall demand loss, as some customers opt to shop in physical stores rather than abandoning the retailer entirely. Lastly, maximizing the online assortment may not always be optimal, particularly if the operational inefficiencies and costs outweigh the value customers place on variety. Our methodological framework provides retailers the opportunity to align their online services with customer preferences and operational constraints and to leverage customer data in shaping their omnichannel strategies.

Title: Feature selection in linear support vector machines via a hard cardinality constraint: A scalable conic decomposition approach
Authors: Immanuel Bomze, Federico D’Onofrio, Laura Palagi, Bo Peng
Abstract: In this paper, we study the embedded feature selection problem in linear Support Vector Machines (SVMs), in which a cardinality constraint is employed, leading to an interpretable classification model. The problem is NP-hard due to the presence of the cardinality constraint, even though the original linear SVM amounts to a problem solvable in polynomial time. To handle the hard problem, we first introduce two mixed-integer formulations for which novel semidefinite relaxations are proposed. Exploiting the sparsity pattern of the relaxations, we decompose the problems and obtain equivalent relaxations in a much smaller cone, making the conic approaches scalable. To make the best usage of the decomposed relaxations, we propose heuristics using the information of its optimal solution. Moreover, an exact procedure is proposed by solving a sequence of mixed-integer decomposed semidefinite optimization problems. Numerical results on classical benchmarking datasets are reported, showing the efficiency and effectiveness of our approach.

Title: Rethinking green technology interventions: Strategic motivations under uncertain regulations
Authors: Chong Huang, Shaofu Du, Wenzhi Tang
Abstract: Governments increasingly rely on industry capability to assess the feasibility of implementing stricter environmental regulations. Rather than passively awaiting their imposition, this trend incentivizes firms to shape future regulations through green activities. To investigate how firms with different cost structures and market power strategically adopt and invest in green technology under uncertain regulations, this paper proposes a three-period game model. The equilibrium outcomes reveal the strategic motivations behind green technology adoption. Specifically, when unit green cost is high, technology-leading firms voluntarily adopt green technology to lobby for stricter regulations, thereby raising rivals’ costs and strengthening their competitive advantage. Conversely, when unit green cost is low, these firms adopt green technology to preempt potential threats from technology-following firms, who could dominate the green market through early adoption. Interestingly, our findings show that green technologies most likely to face industry resistance are not the most expensive, but those with moderate production costs. In such cases, regulatory uncertainty fosters tacit collusion, where competing firms collectively resist green technology adoption to reduce regulation probability and improve profits, even though adoption is economically feasible. To counter this strategic resistance, this paper identifies the most effective intervention mechanisms, such as subsidies or penalties. The results suggest that the optimal intervention strategy differs from the traditional approach of subsidizing high-cost green technologies and penalizing low-cost ones. Instead, it should focus on leveraging firms’ strategic motivations for voluntary green adoption. These insights are vital for governments to design more effective and feasible environmental regulations.

Title: A rollout strategy for electric vehicle charging stations in urban European environments: Ensuring long-term sustainability
Authors: Bryan Coulier, Hatice Çalık, Thijs Becker, Greet Vanden Berghe
Abstract: The electrification of the transportation sector is a key component of the global transition to green energy. As European countries increasingly adopt Electric Vehicles (EVs), they are in the process of rapidly deploying EV Charging Stations (CSs) to meet ever-increasing demand. However, the current approach to CS deployment is highly reactive and typically requires a manual case-by-case response from city planners. This reactive strategy stems from a lack of tools to provide a full understanding of the situation and the consequences of different rollout strategies. There are two key questions concerning the long-term sustainability of the current approach: (i) how certain can we be that decisions currently being made regarding CS placement will not eventually lead to detrimental strain on the electricity grid and (ii) what financial savings are possible by adopting an integrated approach to CS deployment which simultaneously considers both the demand for CSs as well as their impact on the grid. In this paper we investigate how to deploy CSs while mitigating electricity grid congestion and maximizing the utilization of valuable resources. We introduce a decision support algorithm for optimal CS placement within European low-voltage networks. The computational results for large-scale urban instances demonstrate that an integrated rollout strategy results in significant cost savings and reduces grid congestion. By comparing our integrated approach against the current strategy adopted by city planners, we provide valuable insights concerning how to avoid foreseeable problems and achieve cost-effective, future-proof CS infrastructure deployment.

Title: Energy transitions under anti-environmentalism via Markov chain modeling
Authors: Simone Marsiglio, Tatyana Perevalova, Marco Tolotti
Abstract: We analyze the effects of anti-environmentalism on the likelihood of success of the energy transition required to achieve sustainable development. We study the adoption process related to a green technology in a population formed by two sub-groups, environmentalists and anti-environmentalists, who are and are not concerned with environmental outcomes, respectively. The individual adoption decision is determined by environmental attitudes and social factors such that there exist important feedback effects within and between groups. The complexity of social dynamics and the underlying uncertainty may lead the presence of even a small group of anti-environmentalists to preclude the achievement of a green transition, especially when such agents strongly oppose the new technology or when the noise in the stochastic dynamics is sufficiently large. From a policy perspective, this implies that fighting the spread of anti-environmentalism, despite its marginal role in our society, is essential to promote a greener future.

Title: The value of nuclear power plants’ flexibility: A multistage stochastic dynamic programming approach
Abstract: In future power systems dominated by intermittent renewable generation, nuclear power plants will increasingly need to follow uncertain loads. However, regulatory and technical constraints limit the frequency of load-following operations, making their efficient allocation crucial. This paper explores the economic value of nuclear flexibility by modeling it as a stock constraint within a stochastic dynamic programming framework. We show how non-convex constraints at the reactor-scale translate to the fleet level through a linearized approximation, allowing for the analysis of multiple reactors operating under flexibility constraints. Applying this model to the French electricity system in 2035 using the Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming (SDDP) algorithm, we estimate a marginal value of EUR 100/MW for the current flexibility level of the French nuclear fleet. Our results show that increased nuclear flexibility enhances system-wide cost efficiency and improves the integration of renewables, with solar generation seeing the largest benefits. However, our findings suggest a potential misalignment with the profit-maximizing goals of individual nuclear operators, which may deter them from increasing flexibility despite its necessity for the system.

Title: Endogenous directed technical change for energy transition
Authors: Younes Ben Zaied, Wided Mattoussi, Alessandro Marra
Abstract: The finite nature of certain fossil fuels, which are essential inputs in production, imposes a substantial constraint on the economy's long-term growth potential. This paper develops an endogenous directed technical change model under uncertainty regarding the timing of a potential backstop technology discovery. The model directs R&D towards increasing the probability of a technological breakthrough, triggering thereby a transition from a fossil fuel-dependent economy to one powered by cleaner, renewable energy sources. We derive analytical solutions using a general optimal control framework allowing to establish the Pontryagin (maximum principle) first-order optimality conditions, complemented with an adequate numerical assessment to a model of the optimal allocation of national economic resources between consumption, investment, and R&D. We identify the optimal time paths for consumption in both the pre- and post-backstop adoption economies, the depletion rate of fossil fuels, investment in R&D, and the utilization rate of the substitute, under two scenarios: when energy input and physical capital are substitutes in production, and when they are complements.

Title: Measuring carbon emission performance in China's energy market: Evidence from improved non-radial directional distance function data envelopment analysis
Authors: Yinghao Pan, Jie Wu, Chao-Chao Zhang, Muhammad Ali Nasir
Abstract: The most complex challenge facing the energy market is identifying effective solutions to reduce CO 2 emissions (CEs) and enhance environmental performance (EP). Coal production within the power sector is the primary source of these emissions. In this study, we developed a novel linear programming model that accounts for undesirable outputs to assess the EP of 15 power enterprises in eastern China from 2016 to 2020. In addition, we employed a global non-radial Malmquist-Luenberger productivity index (GNML) to analyse the mechanisms influencing changes in efficiency among these enterprises. Our findings indicate that, while the EP of the power industry in eastern China improved, it remains at a relatively low level and exhibits instability. Moreover, technological efficiency (TE) and scale efficiency (SE) play a significant role in determining production efficiency within the sector. Therefore, it is essential for industry managers to implement standardized production management regulations, enhance technological development and scale investments, and strengthen control over unintended emissions that could facilitate energy transition.

Title: Efficiency-inducing lump sum taxation in non-renewable resource industries
Authors: Hassan Benchekroun, Luca Colombo, Paola Labrecciosa
Abstract: This paper studies the design of efficiency-inducing lump-sum taxes in common-pool non-renewable resource industries. Although fixed payments such as royalties, rents, and lease fees play a central role in real-world resource taxation, their theoretical properties remain largely unexplored. We develop a dynamic Cournot model in which firms exploit a shared exhaustible stock and pay a lump-sum tax that depends solely on the current resource level. We characterize the tax that decentralizes the social planner's extraction path under both open-loop and closed-loop information structures. When marginal extraction costs are independent of the resource stock, the optimal tax under open-loop strategies is positive and exceeds the corresponding tax under closed-loop strategies. In contrast, when extraction costs decline with the stock, the optimal tax in both information structures may be positive or negative, with its sign determined by a threshold of industry concentration, which varies across the two settings. Closed-form solutions for linear and iso-elastic demands reveal that the optimal tax can be strictly negative (resp. positive) even in the interval of resource stocks where the laissez-faire equilibrium output is higher (resp. lower) than the social planner's solution.

Title: A pairwise-frontier-based classification framework for two-group classification
Authors: Qianying Jin, Kristiaan Kerstens, Ignace Van de Woestyne, Zhongbao Zhou
Abstract: Mathematical programming-based methods are widely used to generate separating boundaries in two-group classification problems. While nonlinear boundaries may often yield better performance, they typically require pre-specifying a nonlinear functional form. This contribution proposes a novel pairwise-frontier-based classification (PFC) framework that approximates nonlinear separating boundaries without the need for such a specification. The proposed PFC framework clarifies the role of axioms in classification, providing a clear basis for axiom selection based on problem characteristics. Building on this, PFC methods with nonconvex (NC) frontiers are developed, ensuring that the overlap is not artificially enlarged. To further minimize overlap, certain training observations are deliberately controlled to misclassify, provided that the total misclassification cost does not increase. This enables the extension from hard frontiers to more stable soft frontiers. The applicability of the proposed PFC methods is validated through simulation studies and real-life datasets. The results show that the proposed PFC methods are competitive with some well-established classifiers. Specifically, the PFC-NCSoft method demonstrates superior average performance and greater stability, making it particularly suitable for imbalanced classification tasks.

Title: A Bayesian approach to probability default model calibration: Theoretical and empirical insights on the Jeffreys test
Abstract: The calibration of Probability of Default (PD) models is a cornerstone of model risk management, ensuring alignment between predicted and observed default rates, as required by credit risk regulation and supervisory practices. This paper examines the Jeffreys test as a Bayesian alternative to traditional frequentist methods for the assessment of PD model calibration. Unlike classical binomial tests, which often rely on normal approximations and exhibit poor coverage in low-default or small-sample portfolios, the Jeffreys test constructs credible intervals using a non-informative prior, improving robustness and interpretability. We provide a systematic and regulator-aligned assessment of the Jeffreys test in internal validation settings, with particular emphasis on low- and zero-default segments, small-sample grades, and environments with drifting default risk. Through Monte Carlo simulations, we compare its performance with standard approaches such as the Clopper–Pearson interval and normal approximations, highlighting its superior coverage properties in sparse-data regimes. We further illustrate the approach through two complementary empirical applications: a Low-Default Portfolio constructed from publicly available Standard & Poor's corporate rating histories, and a U.S. mortgage credit portfolio based on the Freddie Mac Single-Family Loan-Level dataset. These applications show how Jeffreys credible intervals and the Jeffreys p-value provide transparent diagnostics of calibration and conservatism at the grade or pool level.

Title: The Truck–Drone Hurdle Relay Problem in a Euclidean space
Authors: Alf Kimms, Christin Münch, Fabian Wilschewski
Abstract: In this work, we study the Truck–Drone Hurdle Relay Problem in a Euclidean space (TDHRP), which is particularly relevant in the context of disaster relief. In this problem, a drone is tasked with the delivery of relief supplies in a disaster-stricken area, while being supported by trucks along its way with transportation and battery exchanges. Trucks and drone need to work together, as the partially damaged road network prevents the trucks from reaching the destination, and as the distance from the depot to the destination is far too great for the drone to cover in one flight. We develop a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) for the TDHRP, where we apply a geometric approach that includes trajectory planning for the drone, as opposed to the common assumption in truck–drone delivery that the vehicles operate on a graph. The geometric approach allows the drone to be launched and recovered on any position along the roads, to model the drone velocities as continuous variables, and to ensure collision avoidance. To reduce computation times, we develop an exact row-generation solution method with six different strategies on adding rows. In an extensive computational study with instances with up to ten trucks and 300 obstacles or no-fly zones, two strategies are shown to yield faster median computation times then the complete MILP.

Title: Further improvements of MorK algorithms for identifying the Kemeny median rankings
Authors: Ivano Azzini, Nicola Morandi, Giuseppe Munda
Abstract: This article presents new theoretical and computational developments of the MorK algorithms developed by Azzini and Munda (2020) for finding Kemeny median rankings. Our enhanced Mork-Exact algorithm identifies all Kemeny median rankings for instances with up to 45 alternatives within a reasonable amount of searching time, improving upon the previous tractability threshold of 14. Our MorK-Heuristic algorithm consistently shows a better approximation performance, which we have exhaustively analyzed through a wide range of position-based measures of error. To the best of our knowledge, no such measures of error have been considered before in the related literature. Notwithstanding the NP-hardness of the relevant problem, our results greatly extend the use of the MorK algorithms for practical applications.

Title: Joint improvement of rationality and representativeness in Group Decision Making with the Analytic Hierarchy Process
Authors: Juan Aguarón, María Teresa Escobar, José María Moreno-Jiménez
Abstract: Two of the most relevant issues in multifactor decision-making are rationality and representativeness. Rationality refers to the consistency of individuals when incorporating their preferences into the formal model (individual coherence) whilst representativeness refers to the compatibility or the individuals’ acceptance of the collective position (group coherence). This paper presents for the first time in the literature a unified (methodologically) and closed (mathematically) framework for the joint improvement of rationality and representativeness in a local AHP-Group Decision Making context in which the collective position is given by a group pairwise comparison matrix. Based on maximising efficiency, the proposal works with slight modifications in relative terms, uncommon in this field, of the judgements of the collective matrix without modifying the initial individual positions. Optimisation results for the judgement that most rapidly increases the efficiency and the value that achieve the maximum improvement are provided. Significant improvements are attained and valuable information for learning and negotiation is gathered. The flexibility of this unified and closed framework allows its adaptation to different interests and situations. Simulation studies and illustrative examples demonstrate the robustness, effectiveness and potential of the framework.

Title: Computational adversarial risk analysis for general security games
Authors: J.M. Camacho, R. Naveiro, D. Rios Insua
Abstract: This paper provides an efficient computational scheme to handle general security games from an adversarial risk analysis perspective. Two cases in relation to single-stage and multi-stage simultaneous defend-attack games motivate our approach to general setups which uses bi-agent influence diagrams as underlying problem structure and augmented probability simulation as core computational methodology. Theoretical convergence and numerical, modeling, and implementation issues are thoroughly discussed. A disinformation war case study illustrates the relevance of the proposed approach.

Title: Automated preference determination in graph model for conflict resolution based on text extraction
Authors: Shawei He, Huan Song, Binran Ji
Abstract: The determination of preferences is a critical step of modelling strategic conflicts within the framework of Graph Model for Conflict Resolution (GMCR) and can significantly affect the results of equilibrium. In the existing GMCR methodologies, preferences are determined based on human judgement, affecting the credibility of equilibrium for guiding decision makers (DMs) to handle conflicts. In this paper, a novel approach is developed based on Natural Language Processing (NLP) to extract text from websites for automatically determining preferences. Algorithms are designed for the first time to convert online text into the preference statements in the option prioritization structure within the paradigm of GMCR. Three types of preference statements are constructed. This novel methodology is applied to air carbon negotiation, suggesting guidance of actions for DMs regarding how to be involved into the international carbon mitigation in aviation industry. Comparing with the existing preference modelling approaches within GMCR, our methodology can be utilized for determining preferences with more efficiency and credibility.

Title: Managing perishable production systems with extended shelf life: The role of sustainability
Abstract: A common way to reduce the waste from expired raw materials in perishable supply chains is to transform perishable raw materials into relatively non-perishable end products with extended shelf life. We consider how to coordinate production and ordering for a periodic-review serial inventory/production system in which the perishable raw material is transformed into a non-perishable end product over a finite planning horizon. When the lifetime of the raw material has a fixed lifetime, we first derive a condition that ensures the optimality of the first-in first-out policy. More interestingly, we find that if the unit expiration cost exceeds a threshold in a period, a raw material no-disposal policy is optimal and the value function in each subsequent period is decomposable under a state transformation. As a result, in each of these periods, the optimal production policy is an age-differentiated base-stock policy and the optimal ordering policy is a base-stock policy. Thus, a high unit expiration cost not only makes the supply chain more sustainable but also can simplify the operational strategy significantly. Our results provide operational guidelines and insights on managing this type of perishable production systems and improving sustainability.

Title: Optimizing multimodal deliveries with synergistic drone network design
Abstract: Drone-based deliveries offer significant potential to improve delivery times due to rapid deployment and independence from road conditions. However, pure drone-based cargo deliveries are expensive and restricted by drone’s limited cruising range. On the other hand, pure truck freight services are efficient in well-developed road networks. To address the issue of inefficient delivery times in remote areas, we study a synergistic truck-drone network design problem that improves service performance at minimal cost. We propose an optimization model that minimizes drone investment cost while meeting delivery-time targets for the longest routes. Our model uses an M/G/ k queueing system to account for the waiting time during drone transportation, with the general service time distribution stemming from the heterogeneous travel time between the drone station and the discharging locations. To handle the nonlinearity of waiting time, we apply discretization and power-function approximations. The resulting nonlinear model remains tractable for solvers such as Gurobi. Through a case study conducted with order information data from a major e-commerce platform in Shaanxi, China, we find that our drone network design has the potential to improve the delivery time performance by 17.17% at an economical price. Furthermore, extending the cruising range from 80 km to 120 km improves delivery time by 36.33%. We also discuss managerial insights on infrastructure design, truck-drone synergy, drone technology, and how prioritizing different portions of the longest deliveries alters the resulting design.

Title: Long-distance electric freight truck path planning with uncertain charging station waiting times
Abstract: This paper addresses a shortest-path problem for long-haul electric freight trucks traveling through charging stations with uncertain waiting times. We propose a Dynamic Programming-based ’Proactive’ policy that builds upon a threshold-based online recourse mechanism to mitigate long waits. This policy finds a dynamic set of paths exploiting the probabilistic nature of the problem, minimizing total trip cost (waiting, travel, and charging). Our findings indicate that the proposed policy reduces waiting times by 24% while improving system performance by 27%, with further gains achievable through communication infrastructure.

Title: The value of information in stochastic-dynamic RoRo ship cargo handling
Authors: Arne Heinold, Teresa Marquardt, Catherine Cleophas, Frank Meisel
Abstract: This paper addresses the planning of loading and unloading processes, also termed stevedoring, for Roll-on/Roll-off (RoRo) ships. We consider a setting where we sequence operations, assign tugs to handle trailers, and determine the cargo positions on the ship and in the yard. In real-world settings, the outcomes of these decisions are strongly affected by stochastic uncertainty, such as considering the type of cargo to unload or traffic congestion on the ship. To account for this, we formulate the problem as a sequential decision process and describe two feature-based policy function approximations for the decision-making. We propose an effective heuristic for designing policies in an offline learning process. We evaluate this approach in a case study at the Port of Kiel, Germany, simulating the service operations of a three-deck RoRo ship. Compared to industry benchmark policies, the proposed policies reduce the ship’s turnaround time by up to 26 min (8.8%). Additionally, we apply our methodology to illustrate the value of various levels of information availability. The results show that information on process completion times, especially for vehicle entry and exit at both the ship and the yard, has the potential to shave off turnaround time by an additional 8%. Yet, the availability of information on the incoming ship’s stowage plan is an important precondition for tailored policies capable of achieving such reductions, especially when there is a surplus of tug-handled cargo.

Title: Discount replenishment opportunities with limited capacity: Optimal policy and pricing dynamics
Authors: Bram J. De Moor, Robert N. Boute, Stefan Creemers, Joren Gijsbrechts
Abstract: We study an inventory model with occasional discounts on the fixed order cost, where a random capacity constraint limits the quantity ordered at the discount. We prove that the optimal policy resembles a can-order policy, characterized by a unique reorder, can-order, and order-up-to level. However, the random capacity constraints on the discount offers add complexity: the optimal policy features additional thresholds for inventory levels between the reorder and can-order point that determine when to use the discount.
